$b=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "In part 1, we found that $p(15)=225a+15b.$ So, we need to solve the equation $225a+15b=4\,050$ for the parameter $b.$

We need to isolate the variable $b.$ To do this, we treat $a$ as though it were a constant and apply the addition and multiplication principles as usual.

First, we subtract $225a$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}225a+15b & =4\,050 \\ 225a+15b-225a & =4\,050-225a \\ 15b & =4\,050-225a\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide both sides of the equation by $15:$

$$
\begin{aligned}15b & =4\,050-225a \\ \frac{15b}{15} & =\frac{4\,050-225a}{15} \\ \frac{\cancel{15}b}{\cancel{15}} & =\frac{4\,050}{15}-\frac{225a}{15} \\ b & =270-15a\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $b=270-15a.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-187ca06a-34b2-52f2-bb4c-69c7613a1bfe"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-187ca06a-34b2-52f2-bb4c-69c7613a1bfe" :answer-field/id #uuid "187ca06a-34b2-52f2-bb4c-69c7613a1bfe" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-d436335e-8de5-5c08-ac68-22272df80bd8" :answer-field/choices ["answer-d436335e-8de5-5c08-ac68-22272df80bd8"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d436335e-8de5-5c08-ac68-22272df80bd8" :answer/id #uuid "d436335e-8de5-5c08-ac68-22272df80bd8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "270-15a" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186073752 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-b42bde79-43e7-5e0d-aa7f-ed2b4b36837d"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-b42bde79-43e7-5e0d-aa7f-ed2b4b36837d" :question/id #uuid "b42bde79-43e7-5e0d-aa7f-ed2b4b36837d" :question/math-academy-id "q-167218" :question/problem "The coefficients $a$ and $b$ also satisfy the equation $100a+15b=4\,800.$ Find the values of $a$ and $b.$

{{field-1}}

$b\,=$
{{field-2}}" :question/worked-solution "We have the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}b=270-15a \\ 100a+15b=4\,800\end{aligned}
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. 

Notice that the first equation is already solved for $b:$

$$
b=270-15a
$$

So, we replace $b$ in the second equation and solve for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}100a+15b & =4\,800 \\ 100a+15(270-15a) & =4\,800 \\ 100a+4\,050-225a & =4\,800 \\ -125a+4\,050 & =4\,800 \\ -125a & =750 \\ a & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $a=-6$ into $b=270-15a,$ we can then find the value of $b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}b & =270-15(-6) \\ b & =360\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $a=-6,\,b=360.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-152e2f23-0e18-55aa-a6f1-c39bead952a2" "answer-field-ee0751b7-37b1-5581-b463-69aae210a148"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-152e2f23-0e18-55aa-a6f1-c39bead952a2" :answer-field/id #uuid "152e2f23-0e18-55aa-a6f1-c39bead952a2" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-283112f9-9ffe-5a11-bbfc-a5ba098b6d08" :answer-field/choices ["answer-283112f9-9ffe-5a11-bbfc-a5ba098b6d08"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-283112f9-9ffe-5a11-bbfc-a5ba098b6d08" :answer/id #uuid "283112f9-9ffe-5a11-bbfc-a5ba098b6d08" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-ee0751b7-37b1-5581-b463-69aae210a148" :answer-field/id #uuid "ee0751b7-37b1-5581-b463-69aae210a148" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-967fdc49-d3aa-54f3-af09-6a561f202139" :answer-field/choices ["answer-967fdc49-d3aa-54f3-af09-6a561f202139"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-967fdc49-d3aa-54f3-af09-6a561f202139" :answer/id #uuid "967fdc49-d3aa-54f3-af09-6a561f202139" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "360" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068701 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-527dba5f-2797-5f00-97de-509f725bd58d"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-527dba5f-2797-5f00-97de-509f725bd58d" :question/id #uuid "527dba5f-2797-5f00-97de-509f725bd58d" :question/math-academy-id "q-167219" :question/problem "Determine the weekly profit if the company produces $24$ wooden tables in a week.

Therefore, the company will earn $$5\,184.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-3bf53a58-c815-5351-a1ce-001a880e2d2f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-3bf53a58-c815-5351-a1ce-001a880e2d2f" :answer-field/id #uuid "3bf53a58-c815-5351-a1ce-001a880e2d2f" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-8bd929a1-7008-59ac-9b18-94c80aab8fb4" :answer-field/choices ["answer-8bd929a1-7008-59ac-9b18-94c80aab8fb4"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8bd929a1-7008-59ac-9b18-94c80aab8fb4" :answer/id #uuid "8bd929a1-7008-59ac-9b18-94c80aab8fb4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5184" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064323 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-497dcd2a-064b-5508-ade6-dffd4f30752c"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-497dcd2a-064b-5508-ade6-dffd4f30752c" :question/id #uuid "497dcd2a-064b-5508-ade6-dffd4f30752c" :question/math-academy-id "q-167220" :question/problem "The manager wants to determine the number of wooden tables the company should produce per week to make a weekly profit of $\$4\,800.$ The required number of wooden tables $x$ is the solution to the equation

$$
6{x}^{2}-360x+4\,800=0.
$$

This equation can be factored as $\,$$6\cdot ($
{{field-1}} $)=0.$" :question/worked-solution "We factor $6{x}^{2}-360x+4\,800$ using the greatest common factor (GCF).

Computing the GCF, we get

$$
\text{GCF}(6{x}^{2},360x,4\,800)=6
$$

Then, we rewrite each term in the original expression as a product with the $\text{GCF}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}6{x}^{2}-360x+4\,800 & = \\ 6\cdot ({x}^{2})+6\cdot (-60x)+6\cdot (800)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the $\text{GCF}$ outside the parentheses and keep the remaining terms inside:

$$
\begin{aligned}6\cdot ({x}^{2})+6\cdot (-60x)+6\cdot (800) & = \\ 6({x}^{2}-60x+800)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing expression is ${x}^{2}-60x+800.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-56c69cd5-07d2-598b-b43c-0e186d6e3185"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-56c69cd5-07d2-598b-b43c-0e186d6e3185" :answer-field/id #uuid "56c69cd5-07d2-598b-b43c-0e186d6e3185" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-820e6076-fcaa-5c6f-b5f8-e29610fe3682" :answer-field/choices ["answer-820e6076-fcaa-5c6f-b5f8-e29610fe3682"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-820e6076-fcaa-5c6f-b5f8-e29610fe3682" :answer/id #uuid "820e6076-fcaa-5c6f-b5f8-e29610fe3682" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(x-20)(x-40)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054658 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-f01f8f3f-d44f-517a-a672-79bef06856d4"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-f01f8f3f-d44f-517a-a672-79bef06856d4" :question/id #uuid "f01f8f3f-d44f-517a-a672-79bef06856d4" :question/math-academy-id "q-167221" :question/problem "Find the minimum number of wooden tables the company needs to produce per week to make a weekly profit of $\$4\,800.$

{{field-1}}$\,$ wooden tables per week." :question/worked-solution "From part 5, the required number of wooden tables $x$ is the solution to the equation

$$
6\cdot ({x}^{2}-60x+800)=0.
$$

Dividing this equation by $6,$ we have

$$
{x}^{2}-60x+800=0.
$$

To solve this equation, we want to find a factor pair of the constant term $(800)$ that also adds up to the coefficient of the linear term $(-60).$ The required factors are $(-20)$ and $(-40).$

Using this factor pair, we write the linear term as $-60x=-20x-40x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-60x+800 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-20x-40x+800 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately and then factor the expression completely:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-20x-40x+800 & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}-20x)+(-40x+800) & =0 \\ x(x-20)-40(x-20) & =0 \\ (x-20)(x-40)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the solutions are $x=20$ or $x=40.$ Since we require the minimum solution, we conclude that the company needs to produce $20$ wooden tables per week to make a profit of $$4\,800.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-69bddd2d-4ab6-5d13-b5cd-247cb058b864"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-69bddd2d-4ab6-5d13-b5cd-247cb058b864" :answer-field/id #uuid "69bddd2d-4ab6-5d13-b5cd-247cb058b864" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-81d6fadc-c6fc-54df-85f4-906ea6060968" :answer-field/choices ["answer-81d6fadc-c6fc-54df-85f4-906ea6060968"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-81d6fadc-c6fc-54df-85f4-906ea6060968" :answer/id #uuid "81d6fadc-c6fc-54df-85f4-906ea6060968" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "20" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133748 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-f85c7e50-3cac-5133-ab86-e4e54ecc65fa"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-f85c7e50-3cac-5133-ab86-e4e54ecc65fa" :question/id #uuid "f85c7e50-3cac-5133-ab86-e4e54ecc65fa" :question/math-academy-id "q-167222" :question/problem "The company wants to increase its output by implementing a new production model. The number of wooden tables ${a}_{n}$ produced in the $n$th week since the implementation of the new model is given by the arithmetic sequence

$$
{a}_{n+1}={a}_{n}+4,\,{a}_{1}=12,\,n\ge 1
$$

What is the explicit formula for the $n$th term of this arithmetic sequence?

${a}_{n}=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The explicit formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}+(n-1)d,\,n\ge 1,
$$

so we need to determine the first term ${a}_{1}$ and the common difference $d.$

We are given that the first term is ${a}_{1}=12,$ and we can use the recursive rule to compute the second term as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & ={a}_{1}+4 \\  & =12+4 \\  & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Using the first and second terms, we can compute the common difference:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={a}_{2}-{a}_{1} \\  & =16-12 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now we substitute ${a}_{1}=12$ and $d=4$ into the formula for the $n$th term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =12+(n-1)(4) \\  & =12+4n-4 \\  & =4n+8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is

$$
{a}_{n}=4n+8,\,n\ge 1.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c3549239-369c-5dc5-b97f-5b91a23e416d"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-c3549239-369c-5dc5-b97f-5b91a23e416d" :answer-field/id #uuid "c3549239-369c-5dc5-b97f-5b91a23e416d" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-d7608f3d-23f5-549b-a860-02910a5e6580" :answer-field/choices ["answer-d7608f3d-23f5-549b-a860-02910a5e6580"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d7608f3d-23f5-549b-a860-02910a5e6580" :answer/id #uuid "d7608f3d-23f5-549b-a860-02910a5e6580" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4n+8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "multistep-bb1bcb11-dd3e-5ef2-acf5-2bd2feb4ce5d" :multistep/id #uuid "bb1bcb11-dd3e-5ef2-acf5-2bd2feb4ce5d" :multistep/context "The sales manager of a company that produces wooden furniture analyses the weekly profit made by creating $x$ wooden tables per week. $$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(\frac{7}{x}+\frac{4}{{x}^{3}})}{(3+\frac{12}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & \to \frac{0+0}{3+0} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0.05a-0.2b=0.04 & |\times 100 \\ 0.12a-1.2b=0.24 & |\times 100\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}5a-20b=4 \\ 12a-120b=24\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that if we multiply the first equation by $-2$ and divide the second equation by $3,$ we will get a $40b$ term in the first equation that can cancel with the $-40b$ term in the second equation:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}5a-20b=4 & |\,\times (-2) \\ 12a-120b=24 & |\,÷3\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}-10a+40b=-8 \\ 4a-40b=8\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $b$-variable and allows us to solve for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-10a+\cancel{40b} & =-8 \\ 4a-\cancel{40b} & =8 \\ (-10a+4a) & =(-8+8) \\ -6a & =0 \\ a & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $a=0$ into the equation $5a-20b=4$ to solve for $b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5a-20b & =4 \\ 5(0)-20b & =4 \\ -20b & =4 \\ b & =-\frac{4}{20} \\ b & =-0.2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $a=0,\,b=-0.2.$ So,

$$
a+b=0+(-0.2)=-0.2.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a297791d-ebee-5b0c-89e6-af072a20920b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

$$
\frac{-19}{5-3p}=-2.

$$

$$

$$

$$

- The third component can be found using a special limit:

$$

"Find ${lim}_{t\to \infty }[g(t)+2f(t)]$ given that $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are defined as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =\frac{{t}^{2}}{1-{t}^{2}}\,i+(1+\frac{1}{t})\,j+{t}^{-2}\,k \\ g(t) & =2\,i+{e}^{-t}\,j+{(1+\frac{1}{t})}^{t}\,k\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \infty }f(t) & =({lim}_{t\to \infty }\frac{{t}^{2}}{1-{t}^{2}})\,i+({lim}_{t\to \infty }(1+\frac{1}{t}))\,j-({lim}_{t\to \infty }{t}^{-2})\,k, \\ {lim}_{t\to \infty }g(t) & =({lim}_{t\to \infty }2)\,i-({lim}_{t\to \infty }{e}^{-t})\,j+({lim}_{t\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{t})}^{t})\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's find the limits one-by-one.

$$
\begin{aligned} & {lim}_{t\to \infty }\frac{{t}^{2}}{1-{t}^{2}}={lim}_{t\to \infty }\frac{1}{\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}-1}=-1 \\  & {lim}_{t\to \infty }(1+\frac{1}{t})=1+{lim}_{t\to \infty }\frac{1}{t}=1 \\  & {lim}_{t\to \infty }{t}^{-2}={lim}_{t\to \infty }\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}=0 \\  & {lim}_{t\to \infty }2=2 \\  & {lim}_{t\to \infty }{e}^{-t}=0 \\  & {lim}_{t\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{t})}^{t}=e\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \infty }f(t) & =-1\,i+1\,j+0\,k \\  & =-i+j, \\ {lim}_{t\to \infty }g(t) & =2\,i+0\,j+e\,k \\  & =2\,i+e\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the limit of each function:

$$

\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 2}[f(t)\times g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to 2}f(t)\times {lim}_{t\to 2}g(t) \\  & =⟨-2,-2,2⟩\times ⟨5,2,4⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -2 & -2 & 2 \\ 5 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 5 & 4\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}|k \\  & =((-2)\cdot 4-2\cdot 2)\,i-((-2)\cdot 4-5\cdot 2)\,j+((-2)\cdot 2-5\cdot (-2))\,k \\  & =-12\,i+18\,j+6\,k \\  & =⟨-12,18,6⟩\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4a9c7ac2-4c78-5bd6-ac32-375910d4abbb"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-4a9c7ac2-4c78-5bd6-ac32-375910d4abbb" :answer-field/id #uuid "4a9c7ac2-4c78-5bd6-ac32-375910d4abbb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-7eacfd82-115e-5369-9ea0-e0661e38dc5a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-7eacfd82-115e-5369-9ea0-e0661e38dc5a" "answer-37a1710a-45e4-557c-9442-1e74ba9112ce" "answer-e9e869f0-043f-53a7-9d36-e47ddd23102f" "answer-3f8fd679-95eb-5199-ba6a-a1cfb67ca9ca" "answer-bbc42210-6e93-5e95-b495-30f65a2b1ba3"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7eacfd82-115e-5369-9ea0-e0661e38dc5a" :answer/id #uuid "7eacfd82-115e-5369-9ea0-e0661e38dc5a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "⟨-12,18,6⟩" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-37a1710a-45e4-557c-9442-1e74ba9112ce" :answer/id #uuid "37a1710a-45e4-557c-9442-1e74ba9112ce" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "⟨-18,12,6⟩" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e9e869f0-043f-53a7-9d36-e47ddd23102f" :answer/id #uuid "e9e869f0-043f-53a7-9d36-e47ddd23102f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "⟨-2,8,6⟩" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3f8fd679-95eb-5199-ba6a-a1cfb67ca9ca" :answer/id #uuid "3f8fd679-95eb-5199-ba6a-a1cfb67ca9ca" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "⟨12,8,9⟩" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bbc42210-6e93-5e95-b495-30f65a2b1ba3" :answer/id #uuid "bbc42210-6e93-5e95-b495-30f65a2b1ba3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "⟨5,2,4⟩" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-33768c70-a4a8-56c5-b929-58df88c6ba1b" :question/id #uuid "33768c70-a4a8-56c5-b929-58df88c6ba1b" :question/math-academy-id "q-78268" :question/problem "Find the limit ${lim}_{t\to 1}[f(t)\cdot g(t)]$ given that $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are defined as:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{t-1} \\ \frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t}{t} \\ \frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t}{t}\end{aligned}],\,g(t)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{t}^{2}-2t+1}{t+1} \\ \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t}{t+1} \\ \frac{{e}^{t+1}}{t+1}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}\,(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{t-1}) \\ {lim}_{t\to 1}\,(\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t}{t}) \\ {lim}_{t\to 1}\,(\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t}{t})\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}\,(\frac{(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)^{′}}{(t-1)^{′}}) \\ {lim}_{t\to 1}\,(\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t}{t}) \\ {lim}_{t\to 1}\,(\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t}{t})\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}\,(\frac{1}{t}) \\ \frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi }{1} \\ \frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi }{1}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Note that for the first component of ${lim}_{t\to 1}f(t)$ we used L'Hopital's Rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}g(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}\,\frac{{t}^{2}-2t+1}{t+1} \\ {lim}_{t\to 1}\,\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t}{t+1} \\ {lim}_{t\to 1}\,\frac{{e}^{t+1}}{t+1}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{1}^{2}-2\cdot 1+1}{1+1} \\ \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡1+1}{1+1} \\ \frac{{e}^{1+1}}{1+1}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{{e}^{2}}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}[f(t)\cdot g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to 1}f(t)\cdot {lim}_{t\to 1}g(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{{e}^{2}}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =1\cdot 0+(-2)\cdot \frac{1}{2}+0\cdot \frac{{e}^{2}}{2} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b24006f7-dcb6-5a3e-962f-d3babb6d995e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b24006f7-dcb6-5a3e-962f-d3babb6d995e" :answer-field/id #uuid "b24006f7-dcb6-5a3e-962f-d3babb6d995e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-873d5f29-f5c3-5d96-8997-2e96d20efdab" :answer-field/choices ["answer-873d5f29-f5c3-5d96-8997-2e96d20efdab" "answer-8ccbdb14-9c0c-5f46-a3d4-ae2fd1da959c" "answer-920aaecc-64b5-5927-be63-43fbf263f51a" "answer-5f6847e3-eb2c-5cc6-9cd0-83733cfef02d" "answer-4e7082bf-94bc-5f95-a646-926615cd1b1a"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-873d5f29-f5c3-5d96-8997-2e96d20efdab" :answer/id #uuid "873d5f29-f5c3-5d96-8997-2e96d20efdab" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8ccbdb14-9c0c-5f46-a3d4-ae2fd1da959c" :answer/id #uuid "8ccbdb14-9c0c-5f46-a3d4-ae2fd1da959c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-{e}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-920aaecc-64b5-5927-be63-43fbf263f51a" :answer/id #uuid "920aaecc-64b5-5927-be63-43fbf263f51a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5f6847e3-eb2c-5cc6-9cd0-83733cfef02d" :answer/id #uuid "5f6847e3-eb2c-5cc6-9cd0-83733cfef02d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1-\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4e7082bf-94bc-5f95-a646-926615cd1b1a" :answer/id #uuid "4e7082bf-94bc-5f95-a646-926615cd1b1a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1-{e}^{2}}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-0e9c7e83-813e-5902-881b-22d16eab32e5" :question/id #uuid "0e9c7e83-813e-5902-881b-22d16eab32e5" :question/math-academy-id "q-78269" :question/problem "Find the limit ${lim}_{t\to 0}[f(t)\cdot g(t)]$ given that $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are defined as:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =⟨\frac{{t}^{2}-2t+2}{t+1},\,\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{t},\,t\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ g(t) & =⟨\frac{{e}^{2t}-1}{t},\,1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t+1⟩\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}f(t) & =⟨{lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{{t}^{2}-2t+2}{t+1},\,{lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{t},\,{lim}_{t\to 0}t\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =⟨{lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{{t}^{2}-2t+2}{t+1},\,2{lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{(2t)},\,{lim}_{t\to 0}t\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{0}^{2}-2\cdot 0+2}{0+1},\,2\cdot 1,\,0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡0⟩ \\  & =⟨2,2,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Note that for the second component of ${lim}_{t\to 0}f(t)$ we used a special limit ${lim}_{u\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡u}{u}=1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}g(t) & =⟨{lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{{e}^{2t}-1}{t},\,{lim}_{t\to 0}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,{lim}_{t\to 0}(t+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨{lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{({e}^{2t}-1)^{′}}{(t)^{′}},\,{lim}_{t\to 0}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,{lim}_{t\to 0}(t+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨{lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{2{e}^{2t}}{1},\,{lim}_{t\to 0}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,{lim}_{t\to 0}(t+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{e}^{0},\,1-\operatorname{cos}⁡0,\,0+1⟩ \\  & =⟨2,0,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Note that for the first component of ${lim}_{t\to 0}g(t)$ we used L'Hopital's Rule.

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}[f(t)\cdot g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to 0}f(t)\cdot {lim}_{t\to 0}g(t) \\  & =⟨2,\,2,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨2,0,1⟩ \\  & =2\cdot 2+2\cdot 0+0\cdot 1 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-fa331f7b-2a1a-5cc2-9b0b-49206016e7e3"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-fa331f7b-2a1a-5cc2-9b0b-49206016e7e3" :answer-field/id #uuid "fa331f7b-2a1a-5cc2-9b0b-49206016e7e3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-dfc4555a-8d25-52bb-84f7-9a18b8237849" :answer-field/choices ["answer-0e7b3ee8-302c-5bb1-a016-50116576c2f2" "answer-7f679746-4683-54bf-906e-e3418d6fd20d" "answer-dfc4555a-8d25-52bb-84f7-9a18b8237849" "answer-a18cb561-1016-5b60-a141-a208ee290e53" "answer-9a621fae-e013-5531-ad51-a186fffabdb1"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0e7b3ee8-302c-5bb1-a016-50116576c2f2" :answer/id #uuid "0e7b3ee8-302c-5bb1-a016-50116576c2f2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7f679746-4683-54bf-906e-e3418d6fd20d" :answer/id #uuid "7f679746-4683-54bf-906e-e3418d6fd20d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-dfc4555a-8d25-52bb-84f7-9a18b8237849" :answer/id #uuid "dfc4555a-8d25-52bb-84f7-9a18b8237849" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a18cb561-1016-5b60-a141-a208ee290e53" :answer/id #uuid "a18cb561-1016-5b60-a141-a208ee290e53" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9a621fae-e013-5531-ad51-a186fffabdb1" :answer/id #uuid "9a621fae-e013-5531-ad51-a186fffabdb1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-e00ec48a-b851-58e1-a999-f80b28436a4f" :question/id #uuid "e00ec48a-b851-58e1-a999-f80b28436a4f" :question/math-academy-id "q-130317" :question/problem "Find the limit ${lim}_{t\to 0}[f(t)\cdot g(t)]$ given that $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)=[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{t} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{{t}^{2}+9}{t+3}\end{aligned}],\,g(t)=[\begin{aligned}t-2 \\ \frac{3t-2}{{t}^{2}-1} \\ {2}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}3{e}^{t} \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{{t}^{2}+9}{t+3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{0} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡0 \\ \frac{{0}^{2}+9}{0+3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}g(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}\,(t-2) \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{3t-2}{{t}^{2}-1} \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}{2}^{t}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0-2 \\ \frac{3(0)-2}{{0}^{2}-1} \\ {2}^{0}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}[f(t)\cdot g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to 0}f(t)\cdot {lim}_{t\to 0}g(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =3(-2)+0(2)+3(1) \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-df762a5a-9fee-5f06-a818-ced60d8cdc38"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-df762a5a-9fee-5f06-a818-ced60d8cdc38" :answer-field/id #uuid "df762a5a-9fee-5f06-a818-ced60d8cdc38" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-67f4a994-694a-52fa-9687-ee0e3b608236" :answer-field/choices ["answer-67f4a994-694a-52fa-9687-ee0e3b608236" "answer-76d89423-c5cf-587f-afc3-f3c4191d18a9" "answer-7247832d-b063-5bbc-a125-48edef9b555a" "answer-374e28b1-9d60-5567-9006-2366cebd20ac" "answer-bc1fe512-d096-5581-975f-b0f625e130b3"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-67f4a994-694a-52fa-9687-ee0e3b608236" :answer/id #uuid "67f4a994-694a-52fa-9687-ee0e3b608236" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-76d89423-c5cf-587f-afc3-f3c4191d18a9" :answer/id #uuid "76d89423-c5cf-587f-afc3-f3c4191d18a9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7247832d-b063-5bbc-a125-48edef9b555a" :answer/id #uuid "7247832d-b063-5bbc-a125-48edef9b555a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{3}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-374e28b1-9d60-5567-9006-2366cebd20ac" :answer/id #uuid "374e28b1-9d60-5567-9006-2366cebd20ac" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bc1fe512-d096-5581-975f-b0f625e130b3" :answer/id #uuid "bc1fe512-d096-5581-975f-b0f625e130b3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115759 :question/problem "Find the limit ${lim}_{t\to \pi }[f(t)\cdot g(t)]$ given that $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are defined as:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 1+\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \frac{4t}{\pi }\end{aligned}],\,g(t)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 2+\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \pi }f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \pi }\,(\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\ {lim}_{t\to \pi }\,(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\ {lim}_{t\to \pi }\,(\frac{4t}{\pi })\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi  \\ 1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\ \frac{4\pi }{\pi }\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ {lim}_{t\to \pi }g(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \pi }\,(\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\ {lim}_{t\to \pi }\,(2+\operatorname{tan}⁡t) \\ {lim}_{t\to \pi }\,(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\ (2+\operatorname{tan}⁡\pi ) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \pi }[f(t)\cdot g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to \pi }f(t)\cdot {lim}_{t\to \pi }g(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =0\cdot (-1)+0\cdot 2+4\cdot (-1) \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186113520 :answer-field/correct 17592186113523 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186116437 :tutorial/content "To find the limit of a vector function, we compute the limit of each component individually. So, if $\mathbf f (t) = x(t) \ \mathbf {i} + y(t) \ \mathbf {j} +z(t) \ \mathbf {k}$ is our vector function, then the limit is computed as follows:

$$
\displaystyle \lim_{t\to a} \mathbf f (t) = \bigg[ \lim_{t \to a} x(t) \bigg] \mathbf {i} + \bigg[ \lim_{t \to a}y(t) \bigg] \mathbf {j} +\bigg[ \lim_{t \to a}z(t) \bigg] \mathbf {k}
$$

The limit on the left exists *if and only if* all the limits on the right exist too.

For example, suppose we are given the vector function

$$
\mathbf f (t) = \left( 5+t \right) \ \mathbf {i} +  (t^{2}-1) \ \mathbf {j} + \sin{t} \ \mathbf {k},
$$

and we want to compute the limit $\lim\limits_{t \to 0} \mathbf f (t).$ To do this, we find the limit of each component function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}f(t) & =[\,{{{lim}_{t\to 0}(5+t)}_{⏟}}_{=\,5}\,]i+[\,{{{lim}_{t\to 0}({t}^{2}-1)\,}_{⏟}}_{=\,-1}]j+[\,{{{lim}_{t\to 0}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,}_{⏟}}_{=\,0}]k \\  & =5\text{ }i+(-1)\text{ }j+0\text{ }k \\  & =⟨5,\,-1,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186116438 :tutorial/content "Many properties of limits of scalar functions extend naturally to limits of vector functions. For instance, if $\mathbf f(t)$ and $\mathbf g(t)$ are vector functions and $p,q$ are constants, then

$$
\lim_{t \to a}\left[p \ \mathbf f(t) + q \ \mathbf g(t)\right] =  p \ \lim_{t \to a}\mathbf f(t) + q \ \lim_{t \to a}\mathbf g(t).
$$

We also have the following property for the magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to a}‖f(t)‖ & =‖{lim}_{t\to a}f(t)‖,\end{aligned}
$$

where $\left\| \mathbf f(t) \right\|$ denotes the magnitude of the vector $\mathbf f(t)$." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186116439 :tutorial/content "For two vector functions, the limit of a product is equal to the product of the limits:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to a}[f(t)\cdot g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to a}f(t)\cdot {lim}_{t\to a}g(t) \\ {lim}_{t\to a}[f(t)\times g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to a}f(t)\times {lim}_{t\to a}g(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Here, $\mathbf f(t)\cdot \mathbf g(t)$ and $\mathbf f(t) \times \mathbf g(t)$ are the dot product and the cross product of $\mathbf f(t)$ and $\mathbf g(t),$ respectively." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115485 :activity/expected-seconds 840.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124437 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-4e141666-84d5-5edd-9a4e-a7cb3e788f33"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-4e141666-84d5-5edd-9a4e-a7cb3e788f33" :question/id #uuid "4e141666-84d5-5edd-9a4e-a7cb3e788f33" :question/math-academy-id "q-132581" :question/problem "A surface $S$ is defined by $z=f(x,y).$ The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $x=2.$ Given that the point $P$ with $y$-coordinate $\frac{\pi }{4}$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy-\frac{\pi }{3})$, find the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$" :question/worked-solution "The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point where $y=\frac{\pi }{4}$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(2,\frac{\pi }{4}).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(2,\frac{\pi }{4}):$ 

$$

with the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,\frac{\pi }{2})}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(1,\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,\frac{\pi }{2})} & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(1\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})-1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =2\cdot 1-1\cdot 0 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,\frac{\pi }{2})} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,\frac{\pi }{2})}(x-1) \\ z-0 & =2(x-1) \\ z & =2x-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=\frac{\pi }{2} \\ z=2x-2\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d2ed29c1-ef21-57a0-9839-78668465edfc"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "19ce6755-ce5c-5344-86b9-dca6271615dd" :question/math-academy-id "q-132608" :question/problem "The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=0.$ Given that the point $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=(y+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$" :question/worked-solution "The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=0.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(\frac{1}{2},0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(\frac{1}{2},0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(\frac{1}{2},0) & =(0+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2})+2(\frac{1}{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(\frac{1}{2},0) & ={f}_{x}(\frac{1}{2},0)(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =1(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =x-\frac{1}{2} \\ z & =x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=0 \\ z=x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=x+\frac{1}{2}$ (or $x-z+\frac{1}{2}=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $-i-k$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-(-i-k)=i+k$ is also parallel to it." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields :question/worked-solution "We can solve this equation by isolating the $(x+4)^{3}$ term and then taking the $3$rd root of each side.

First, let's isolate the $(x+4)^{3}$ term on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2(x+4)^{3} & =686 \\ (x+4)^{3} & =343\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we take the $3$rd root of each side and solve for $x.$ Since $n=3$ is odd, there is only one real solution to this equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+4)^{3} & =343 \\ \sqrt[3]{(x+4)^{3}} & =\sqrt[3]{343} \\ x+4 & =\sqrt[3]{{7}^{3}} \\ x+4 & =7 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=3.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179320 :answer-field/correct 17592186179321 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179681 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-ee997e26-088f-52b1-8913-d296b8992e92"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-ee997e26-088f-52b1-8913-d296b8992e92" :question/id #uuid "ee997e26-088f-52b1-8913-d296b8992e92" :question/math-academy-id "q-91348" :question/problem "Find the real solution to the equation ${x}^{7}=-\frac{1}{128}.$" :question/worked-solution "We can solve this equation by taking the $7$th root of each side and solving for $x.$ Since $n=7$ is odd, there is only one real solution to this equation:

"a95ee677-1642-5975-8b50-8432d56de160" :question/math-academy-id "q-97770" :question/problem "$\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-4x}}\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}-4x & =-({x}^{2}+4x) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}) \\  & =-((x+2)^{2}-4) \\  & =4-(x+2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-4x}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{4-(x+2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{2(x+2)\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x+2}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x+2}{2})\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x+2}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\frac{x+2}{2}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}-6x & =-({x}^{2}+6x) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}) \\  & =-((x+3)^{2}-9) \\  & =9-(x+3)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{(x+3)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-6x}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{3}{(x+3)\sqrt{9-{(x+3)}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x+3}{3})\sqrt{9-9{(\frac{x+3}{3})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x+3}{3})\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x+3}{3})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\frac{x+3}{3}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{(x+3)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-6x}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x+3}{3})\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x+3}{3})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot 3\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡(\frac{x+3}{3})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}

"$\int \frac{\sqrt{2}}{|x-5|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-10x+27}}\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-10x+27 & ={x}^{2}-2\cdot 5x+{5}^{2}-{5}^{2}+27 \\  & =(x-5)^{2}+2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\sqrt{2}}{|x-5|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-10x+27}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{\sqrt{2}}{|x-5|\sqrt{2+(x-5)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{2}}|\sqrt{2+2{(\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{2}}|\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{2}}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{2}}|\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{2}})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0b36eef3-f0c2-5b45-97f7-a2607c73a159"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+4x+5 & ={x}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}+5 \\  & =(x+2)^{2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int -\frac{15}{|5x-10|\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4x+5}}\,\text{d}x=-\int \frac{15}{5|x+2|\sqrt{1+(x+2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x=-3\int \frac{1}{|x+2|\sqrt{1+(x+2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x+2.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}-3\int \frac{1}{|x+2|\sqrt{1+(x+2)^{2}}}\text{d}x & =-3\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =3\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(x+2)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-96a55f92-f39f-5881-94c0-2f84b4c3471a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id \frac{1}{16-(3x+2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that

$$
\int \frac{1}{16-(3x+2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{16-16(\frac{1}{16}(3x+2)^{2})}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{16}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{4}(3x+2))}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{4}(3x+2).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3}{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{4}{3}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{16}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{4}(3x+2))}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{16}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\cdot \frac{4}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{3x+2}{4})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

"$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-2x(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].$*" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8ea9a430-3071-50b8-b617-7ec74f7a4ddc"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "701145a1-1f00-509b-9c1b-60626233c2a4" :question/math-academy-id "q-335434" :question/problem "$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=4y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-4x(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(1) \\ y(1)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}].$*

<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" height="30px" rowspan="2">$[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=\,\,$</td>
<td align="center" height="40px" width="5px"></td>

</tr>
<tr>

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-1)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-1)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-1)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-1))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-1))\, \\ \,3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-1))\,\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0f7c85fb-7d21-5d48-8f24-4c37d6bc47ea" "answer-field-9ff392b1-754b-5f5c-ad8a-af1f4c91dfa9"] :db/ensure - For $x>1,$ the function is positive and grows very slowly as we increase $x.$ We say that $y\rightarrow \infty$ (slowly) as $x\rightarrow \infty.$

- The function has the vertical asymptote $x=0.$

- The function is an increasing function.

III. $y\rightarrow\infty$ as $x\rightarrow -\infty$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's plot the graph of $y=\ln (x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)=0\,✓\end{aligned}

- Statement III is false. The function is not defined for $x<0,$ so the function is not defined as $x \to -\infty.$

I. The function passes through the point $(1,0)$

II. Its horizontal asymptote is $y=0.$

III. It passes through the point $(10,100).$" :question/worked-solution "Let's plot the graph of $y=\operatorname{log}⁡x.$

![](images/17/177d2949118515d96b6a1c49d0222a2417ab6236e8641f8d89c0cd8f6b30a592.png)

Let's go through each statement.

- Statement I is true.

- Statement II is false. The function $y=\operatorname{log}⁡x$ has no horizontal asymptote. However, it does have the vertical asymptote $x=0.$

- Statement III is false. Substituting $x=10$ into the equation of the curve gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\operatorname{log}⁡(10) \\  & =\operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{1}) \\  & =1\ne 100\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, only statement I is true." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186109039 :answer-field/correct 17592186109041 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186233519 :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true regarding the function $y={log}_{6}⁡x?$ 

I. It has no zeros

II. $y\to 6$ as $x\to \infty $

III. It has a vertical asymptote at $x=0$" :question/worked-solution "Let's plot the graph of $y={log}_{6}⁡x.$

![](images/d8/d8d3f9dc995d8801d451b15129860362efa772178cdc3ef07be5adb6a1da5c45.png)

Let's go through each statement.

- Statement I is false. The function has a zero at $x=1.$

- Statement II is false. As $x$ increases, $y$ increases without bound. Therefore, $y\to \infty $ as $x\to \infty $

- Statement III is true.

In conclusion, only statement III is true." :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b179eeb3-b9e7-569b-a20d-09ef65081dfe"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b179eeb3-b9e7-569b-a20d-09ef65081dfe" :answer-field/id #uuid "b179eeb3-b9e7-569b-a20d-09ef65081dfe" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-2d1effa9-7e1a-55a3-81d4-aac75787131d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-d9334f19-c8ae-5204-a395-20c07315d341" "answer-dd5aa106-d5f2-58b4-962e-4d9b7feff98e" "answer-5963bb65-6486-5a51-a43b-a6e3dcb86561" "answer-0b0f5b8f-e5e0-519d-aa21-ccb7de143a67" "answer-2d1effa9-7e1a-55a3-81d4-aac75787131d"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d9334f19-c8ae-5204-a395-20c07315d341" :answer/id #uuid "d9334f19-c8ae-5204-a395-20c07315d341" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-dd5aa106-d5f2-58b4-962e-4d9b7feff98e" :answer/id #uuid "dd5aa106-d5f2-58b4-962e-4d9b7feff98e" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5963bb65-6486-5a51-a43b-a6e3dcb86561" :answer/id #uuid "5963bb65-6486-5a51-a43b-a6e3dcb86561" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0b0f5b8f-e5e0-519d-aa21-ccb7de143a67" :answer/id #uuid "0b0f5b8f-e5e0-519d-aa21-ccb7de143a67" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2d1effa9-7e1a-55a3-81d4-aac75787131d" :answer/id #uuid "2d1effa9-7e1a-55a3-81d4-aac75787131d" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-96d6c320-22a1-578b-bc1b-575bf1a1c004" :question/id #uuid "96d6c320-22a1-578b-bc1b-575bf1a1c004" :question/math-academy-id "q-156742" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true regarding the function $y={log}_{8}⁡x?$

I. The domain is $x\ge 0$

II. It has no horizontal asymptotes

III. It passes through the point $(64,2)$" :question/worked-solution "Let's plot the graph of $y={log}_{8}⁡x.$

![](images/68/6811e57f1259b97448811ac9abe8d6fc7f76a52b62e685f2fa0ec36e290381b4.png)

Let's go through each statement.

- Statement I is false. From the graph, we see that the domain is $x>0.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the function $y={log}_{8}⁡x$ has no horizontal asymptote. However, it does have the vertical asymptote $x=0.$

- Statement III is true. Substituting $x=64$ into the equation of the curve gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={log}_{8}⁡(64) \\  & ={log}_{8}⁡({8}^{2}) \\  & =2{log}_{8}⁡(8) \\  & =2\,\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can just plot the exponential function and reflect it over the line $y=x.$

For example, suppose that we wish to plot the graph of 

$$
y=\log_2 x.
$$

The corresponding inverse function is $y=2^x,$ and since $y=2^x$ is a one-to-one function defined for all real $x,$ we can obtain the graph of $y=\log_2{x}$ by reflecting $y=2^x$ over the line $y=x.$ The result is shown below:

![](images/0c/0c614201798324262429f080d8e8a31bfefe58c4008bfe82e6da1b91dc158b7a.png)

Here are some key points to note about $y=\log_2(x)\mathbin{:}$

- The domain is $x>0$, and the range is $-\infty <   y <   \infty.$

- The graph has the vertical asymptote $x=0.$

- The function is an increasing function.

- The graph passes through the point $(1,0).$

- For $x>1$, the graph is positive and grows very slowly as we increase $x.$ We say that $y\rightarrow \infty$ (slowly) as $x\rightarrow \infty.$

In general, for any base $n>1,$ the graph of $y=\log_n{x}$ always has the same shape, and all of the above points are valid. We can verify that this is true by inspecting some possible graphs shown below:

![](images/91/91567f282acbc3b8390da1e4147b445018ae649d913205e59867d58ea980ff7b.png)

**Note:** The important points covered above also apply to two familiar logarithms.

- $y = \ln x = \log_e x$ is the natural logarithm. Since the base is $n=e>1,$ all of the important points covered above apply.

- $y = \log x = \log_{10} x$ is the logarithm with base $10.$ Since the base is $n=10>1,$ all the important points covered above apply." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110877 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054604 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d591e3b7-0993-5fb9-b7f0-ff97c33bf559" "question-2b9acb7e-8235-5df0-907d-863119079541"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-d591e3b7-0993-5fb9-b7f0-ff97c33bf559" :question/id #uuid "d591e3b7-0993-5fb9-b7f0-ff97c33bf559" :question/math-academy-id "q-100250" :question/problem "Find ${lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{3x}{\sqrt[3]{2{x}^{4}-5}}.$" :question/worked-solution "Applying the quotient rule, we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{3x}{\sqrt[3]{2{x}^{4}-5}}=\frac{{lim}_{x\to 2}3x}{{lim}_{x\to 2}\sqrt[3]{2{x}^{4}-5}}
$$

We calculate the limits of the numerator and denominator, separately.

For the numerator, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}3x & =3{lim}_{x\to 2}x \\  & =3\cdot 2 \\  & =6\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the root rule in the denominator, we have
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\sqrt[3]{2{x}^{4}-5} & =\sqrt[3]{{lim}_{x\to 2}(2{x}^{4}-5)} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{2(2)^{4}-5)} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{27} \\  & =3\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{3x}{\sqrt[3]{2{x}^{4}-5}} & =\frac{6}{3}=2\,.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ddff0f96-aeb7-5490-8d56-4c8b9d0de231"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "From the graph, we get that ${lim}_{x\to \,2}f(x)=3.$

From the product rule, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,2}(x-1)^{2}\,(f(x)-2)^{3}={lim}_{x\to \,2}(x-1)^{2}\cdot {lim}_{x\to \,2}(f(x)-2)^{3}.
$$

We calculate the limits of each factor, separately.

Applying the power rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,2}(x-1)^{2} & ={({lim}_{x\to \,2}(x-1))}^{2} \\  & =(2-1)^{2} \\  & ={1}^{2} \\  & =1\,,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,2}(f(x)-2)^{3} & ={({lim}_{x\to \,2}(f(x)-2))}^{3} \\  & =(3-2)^{3} \\  & ={1}^{3} \\  & =1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,2}(x-1)^{2}\,(f(x)-2)^{3} & =(1)\cdot (1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-817fc64f-fe17-5ab1-8ab5-8f8ebfd722a2"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-817fc64f-fe17-5ab1-8ab5-8f8ebfd722a2" :answer-field/id #uuid "817fc64f-fe17-5ab1-8ab5-8f8ebfd722a2" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-066cb984-e17a-5fea-af4c-48188475d862" :answer-field/choices ["answer-066cb984-e17a-5fea-af4c-48188475d862"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-066cb984-e17a-5fea-af4c-48188475d862" :answer/id #uuid "066cb984-e17a-5fea-af4c-48188475d862" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-2b9acb7e-8235-5df0-907d-863119079541" :question/id #uuid "2b9acb7e-8235-5df0-907d-863119079541" :question/math-academy-id "q-338390" :question/problem "Find the **exact** value of the limit.

Find the cosine of $∠Y.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall the definition of cosine: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡Y=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{XY}{YZ}=\frac{XY}{5}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $XY.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}XY & =\sqrt{Y{Z}^{2}-X{Z}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}-(\sqrt{7})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25-7} \\  & =\sqrt{18} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡Y & =\frac{XY}{5}=\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186075298 :answer-field/correct 17592186075301 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-b2b55850-322e-5b17-9a94-b2696bd083f6" :question/id #uuid "b2b55850-322e-5b17-9a94-b2696bd083f6" :question/math-academy-id "q-122050" :question/problem "In the right triangle $△JKL,$ $∠J$ is a right angle, $JL=8$ and $KL=12.$ Find $\operatorname{tan}⁡K.$" :question/worked-solution "The following triangle illustrates the information given.

![](images/cc/cc33327cc6d071cb6ec9ac0c10d58e57bc35f8d81b326731120cf04c18f58ec1.png)

Recall the definition of tangent: 

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡K=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}=\frac{JL}{JK}=\frac{8}{JK}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $JK.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}JK & =\sqrt{K{L}^{2}-J{L}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{12}^{2}-{8}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{144-64} \\  & =\sqrt{80} \\  & =4\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡K & =\frac{8}{4\sqrt{5}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f15bdbe8-d486-594d-b02d-d29460c4afc4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Find the tangent of $∠P.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall the definition of tangent: 

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡P=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}=\frac{QR}{PQ}=\frac{QR}{3.5}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing length $QR.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}QR & =\sqrt{P{R}^{2}-P{Q}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{12.5}^{2}-{3.5}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{156.25-12.25} \\  & =\sqrt{144} \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡P & =\frac{QR}{3.5} \\  & =\frac{12}{3.5} \\  & =\frac{120}{35} \\  & =\frac{24}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-518b1e5c-6389-594b-b333-90ba109eabdc"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-48e5a226-dec1-538c-a739-b2da6b892931" :question/id #uuid "48e5a226-dec1-538c-a739-b2da6b892931" :question/math-academy-id "q-127807" :question/problem "Which of the following vector-valued functions are continuous on $[-1,1]?$

  

$$
\begin{aligned}p(s) & =|{s}^{2}-1|\,i+\frac{s+1}{s}\,j+2{s}^{2}\,k \\ q(s) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(s-1)\,i+({s}^{2}+1)\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡s\,k \\ r(s) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡s\,i-2\operatorname{tan}⁡s\,j+\operatorname{csc}⁡s\,k\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "A vector-valued function is continuous on an interval if and only if each of its components is continuous on that interval.  

Let's consider the functions one by one. 

- The function $p(s)$ is **not** continuous on $[-1,1]$ because 
its second component, $\frac{s+1}{s},$ is undefined at $s=0$ and hence discontinuous on $[-1,1].$

- The function $q(s)$ is **not** continuous on $[-1,1]$ because 
its first component, $\operatorname{ln}⁡(s-1)$, is undefined at $s=1$ and hence discontinuous on $[-1,1].$

- The function $r(s)$ is **not** continuous on $[-1,1]$ because 
its third component, $\operatorname{csc}⁡s$, is undefined at $s=0$ and hence discontinuous on $[-1,1].$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the functions are continuous on $[-1,1].$"" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e733f8a2-e030-5a6d-ae1a-9d5ff92e104f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-e733f8a2-e030-5a6d-ae1a-9d5ff92e104f" :answer-field/id #uuid "e733f8a2-e030-5a6d-ae1a-9d5ff92e104f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-897e666e-5017-5c68-b94e-f2a61cddac86" :answer-field/choices ["answer-98a35e8c-50cb-52af-93af-e4c92463935b" "answer-8d44025a-769b-53ed-8380-a28de619549a" "answer-5f216b60-e388-51f5-ba21-e8378f9d2558" "answer-ea628c3b-5f80-5519-9722-358822a7671c" "answer-897e666e-5017-5c68-b94e-f2a61cddac86"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-98a35e8c-50cb-52af-93af-e4c92463935b" :answer/id #uuid "98a35e8c-50cb-52af-93af-e4c92463935b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "r(s)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8d44025a-769b-53ed-8380-a28de619549a" :answer/id #uuid "8d44025a-769b-53ed-8380-a28de619549a" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$p(s)$  and $q(s)$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5f216b60-e388-51f5-ba21-e8378f9d2558" :answer/id #uuid "5f216b60-e388-51f5-ba21-e8378f9d2558" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$p(s)$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ea628c3b-5f80-5519-9722-358822a7671c" :answer/id #uuid "ea628c3b-5f80-5519-9722-358822a7671c" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$q(s)$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-897e666e-5017-5c68-b94e-f2a61cddac86" :answer/id #uuid "897e666e-5017-5c68-b94e-f2a61cddac86" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "None of the functions are continuous on $[-1,1]$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115761 :question/problem "Which of the following vector-valued functions are continuous at $t=0?$

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "A vector-valued function is continuous at a point if and only if each of its components is continuous at that point.

Let's now consider the functions one-by-one.

$$

 
Hence, ${lim}_{t\to 0}\operatorname{cot}⁡t$ doesn’t exist.

- Function $g(t)$ is **not** continuous at $t=0$ since its first component $\frac{2}{t}$ is not continuous at $t=0.$

- Function $h(t)$ is continuous at $t=0$ because each of its components $2t$, $\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and ${t}^{4}$ are continuous at $t=0.$

Therefore, the answer is:

$\,$ $h(t)$ only." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186113532 :answer-field/correct 17592186113536 :answer-field/choices ["answer-c98a9e61-787a-5809-8c15-d98c6271b0d3"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c98a9e61-787a-5809-8c15-d98c6271b0d3" :answer/id #uuid "c98a9e61-787a-5809-8c15-d98c6271b0d3" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "All the functions are continuous at $t=0$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-dd43e1d4-a6c0-5d8f-9dc6-6b6b8e30eb50" :question/id #uuid "dd43e1d4-a6c0-5d8f-9dc6-6b6b8e30eb50" :question/math-academy-id "q-127809" :question/problem "Determine the interval on which the function $f(t)=⟨t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,2{e}^{t-1},\,\sqrt{5-t}⟩$ is continuous." :question/worked-solution "A vector-valued function is continuous on an interval if and only if each of its components is continuous on that interval.

interval $[0,4)\cup (4,\infty ).$ Let's study the differentiability of its components on this interval one-by-one.

- The derivative of  $\sqrt{t}$ is

$$
{(\sqrt{t})}^{′}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}.
$$

 
Since the derivative is not defined at $t=0,$ we conclude that  $\sqrt{t}$ is not differentiable at this point.

- The derivative of  $\frac{1}{t-4}$ is

$$
{(\frac{1}{t-4})}^{′}=-\frac{1}{(t-4)^{2}}.
$$

 
Since the derivative is defined for all the points on the interval $[0,4)\cup (4,\infty ),$ we conclude that  $\frac{1}{t-4}$ is differentiable on this interval.

- The derivative of  $-5{t}^{2}$ is

$$
{(-5{t}^{2})}^{′}=-10t.
$$

:question/problem "Which of the following vector-valued functions are differentiable with respect to $t$ on $t\in (\pi ,2\pi )?$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =⟨{sin}^{2}⁡t,\,\frac{1}{t},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ g(t) & =⟨t\sqrt{t},\,1-{t}^{2},\,t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩ \\ h(t) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,2t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "All of these vector-valued functions are defined for all  $t\in (\pi ,2\pi ).$ 

A function is differentiable on the interval $(\pi ,2\pi )$ if and only if each of its component functions is differentiable on that interval. 

Let's now consider the functions one-by-one.

- We differentiate $f(t)$ to find ${f}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({sin}^{2}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since each component of ${f}^{′}(t)$ is defined for all  $t\in (\pi ,2\pi )$, we conclude that $f(t)$ is differentiable on this interval.

- Next, we differentiate $g(t)$ to find ${g}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\sqrt{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3/2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2}{t}^{1/2},\,-2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{t},\,-2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since each component of  ${g}^{′}(t)$ is defined for all  $t\in (\pi ,2\pi )$, we have that $g(t)$ is differentiable on this interval.

- Finally, we differentiate $h(t)$ to find ${h}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,2,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since each component of  ${h}^{′}(t)$ is defined for all $t\in (\pi ,2\pi )$, we conclude that $h(t)$ is differentiable on this interval.

Therefore, the answer is: 

$\,$ All the functions are differentiable on $(\pi ,2\pi ).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-24c4782e-d988-5b6a-b328-68cc3dd0adb4"] :db/ensure $$" :question/worked-solution "The function $F(t)=f(t)\times g(t)$ is differentiable over the common domain where both $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are differentiable. A function is differentiable if and only if each component is differentiable.

Let's now find the intervals where each of the functions $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are differentiable.

For the function $f(t):$ 

- The first component $|t-1{|}^{3}$ is differentiable over $(-\infty ,1)\cup (1,\infty )$

- The second component $\operatorname{ln}⁡(t-1)$ is differentiable over $(1,\infty ).$

- The third component $t$ is differentiable for all values of $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

The intersection of the domains of all three components of $f(t)$ is $(1,\infty ).$ 

For the function $g(t):$ 

- The first component $\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}$ is differentiable over $(-2,2).$

- The second component ${e}^{\sqrt{t-1}}$ is differentiable for $(1,\infty ).$

- The third component ${t}^{3}$ is differentiable for all values of $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$

The intersection of the domains of all three components of $g(t)$ is $(1,2).$ 

Finally, the common domain of differentiability for both functions is

$$
(1,\infty )\cap (1,2)=(1,2).

A vector function $\mathbf f (t)$ is **continuous** at a point $t_0$ (in its domain) if

$$
\displaystyle \lim_{t \rightarrow t_0} \mathbf f (t) = \mathbf f (t_0).
$$

For example, the vector function 

$$
\mathbf f(t) = \left \langle e^t,  \dfrac{1}{t} \right \rangle
$$

is continuous at $t=1$ because

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}f(t) & =⟨{lim}_{t\to 1}({e}^{t}),\,{lim}_{t\to 1}(\frac{1}{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{1},\,\frac{1}{1}⟩ \\  & =⟨e,\,1⟩ \\  & =f(1)\end{aligned}
$$

Since the limit of a vector function is determined by the limits of the components, a vector function is continuous at a point $t_0$ *if and only if* each of its components is continuous at that point.

We say that a vector function is **continuous on the interval** $t\in[a,b]$ if it is continuous at every point of this interval." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186116444 :tutorial/content "Similar to scalar-valued functions, the vector function $\mathbf{f}(t)$ is **differentiable** at a point $t = t_0$ in the domain of the function if the following limit exists:

$$
\lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{\mathbf{f}(t_0+h) - \mathbf{f}(t_0)}{h}
$$

The value of the limit is then called the **derivative** of $\mathbf{f}(t)$ at $t = t_0$ and is denoted as $\mathbf{f}'(t_0)$. In general, a vector function is differentiable *if and only if* all of its components are differentiable.

For example, is the following vector function $\mathbf{g}(t)$ differentiable at $t=0$?

$$
\mathbf{g}(t) = \big\langle t, \: |\,t\,|, \: \sin t \big\rangle
$$

Notice that the second component, $|\,t\,|,$ is not differentiable at $t=0.$ Since one of the component functions is not differentiable at $t=0,$ we conclude that the overall vector function $\mathbf{g}(t)$ is not differentiable at $t=0.$ 

We say that a vector function is **differentiable on an open interval** $t \in (a,b)$ if it is differentiable at *every* point $t \in (a,b).$ This means that each component of the function must be differentiable at every point of $(a,b).$

Our function $\mathbf{g}(t)$, mentioned above, is differentiable on $(-\infty, 0) \cup (0, \infty)$ since all of its components are differentiable there.

Finally, a function is said to be **continuously differentiable** if it is differentiable and its derivative is continuous." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115484 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115282 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-a981d1c6-7401-5c05-a9ed-dfe4b1119a94"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115105 :question/problem "Plot the curve of $y=\log_7 (x+4).$" :question/worked-solution "To plot $y=\log_7 {(x+4)},$ we apply the following steps:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =k{log}_{5}⁡(b\cdot \frac{1}{b}) \\  & =k{log}_{5}⁡1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the point $\left(\dfrac1b, 0\right)$ lies on the curve. But from the diagram, we know that $(2,0)$ lies on the curve. Hence, 

$$
(2,0)  = \left(\dfrac1b,0\right)\quad\Rightarrow\quad b=\dfrac12.
$$

Now, we substitute coordinates of the point $(10,3)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}k{log}_{5}⁡(bx) & =y \\ k{log}_{5}⁡(\frac{1}{2}x) & =y \\ k{log}_{5}⁡(\frac{1}{2}\cdot 10) & =3 \\ k{log}_{5}⁡5 & =3 \\ k & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
b\cdot k = \dfrac12 \cdot 3 = \dfrac32.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-a981d1c6-7401-5c05-a9ed-dfe4b1119a94" :question/id #uuid "a981d1c6-7401-5c05-a9ed-dfe4b1119a94" :question/math-academy-id "q-28248" :question/problem "Which of the following is the graph of $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-4)?$" :question/worked-solution "To plot $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-4),$ we apply the following steps:

The diagram above shows the graph of $y=k{log}_{2}⁡(bx).$ Find the value of $k\cdot b.$" :question/worked-solution "Clearly, $b\ne 0.$ Substituting $x=\frac{1}{b}$ into the equation of the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =k{log}_{2}⁡(b\cdot \frac{1}{b}) \\  & =k{log}_{2}⁡1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the point $(\frac{1}{b},0)$ lies on the curve. But from the diagram, we know that $(3,0)$ lies on the curve. Hence

$$
(3,0)=(\frac{1}{b},0)\,⇒\,b=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Now, we substitute coordinates of the point $(6,2)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}k{log}_{2}⁡(bx) & =y \\ k{log}_{2}⁡(\frac{1}{3}x) & =y \\ k{log}_{2}⁡(\frac{1}{3}\cdot 6) & =2 \\ k{log}_{2}⁡2 & =2 \\ k & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
k\cdot b=2\cdot \frac{1}{3}=\frac{2}{3}.

The diagram above shows the graph of $y={log}_{4}⁡(x-d)+c.$ Find the value of $\frac{d}{c}.$" :question/worked-solution "In the given graph, the vertical asymptote is $x=4.$ So, the argument of the logarithm function should evaluate to zero at $x=4.$ Therefore,

$$
4-d=0\,⇒\,d=4.
$$

Now, we substitute coordinates of the point $(8,3)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{4}⁡(x-d)+c & =y \\ {log}_{4}⁡(x-4)+c & =y \\ {log}_{4}⁡(8-4)+c & =3 \\ {log}_{4}⁡(4)+c & =3 \\ 1+c & =3 \\ c & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\frac{d}{c}=\frac{4}{2}=2.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d0661678-c752-58dd-ae45-19a8a3ab5f43"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d0661678-c752-58dd-ae45-19a8a3ab5f43" :answer-field/id #uuid "d0661678-c752-58dd-ae45-19a8a3ab5f43" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-d728cb75-8aff-5441-a02b-d2123ed28dfa" :answer-field/choices ["answer-3fb69761-90da-5ef3-9336-c74c1cd1883c" "answer-3035fbac-63b9-5e92-a7af-7fae4221c58d" "answer-d728cb75-8aff-5441-a02b-d2123ed28dfa" "answer-1059a7c8-9a04-5280-9f29-30f8d8a20897" "answer-e7761c70-8716-56c9-a2cb-a35290fdff3f"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3fb69761-90da-5ef3-9336-c74c1cd1883c" :answer/id #uuid "3fb69761-90da-5ef3-9336-c74c1cd1883c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3035fbac-63b9-5e92-a7af-7fae4221c58d" :answer/id #uuid "3035fbac-63b9-5e92-a7af-7fae4221c58d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d728cb75-8aff-5441-a02b-d2123ed28dfa" :answer/id #uuid "d728cb75-8aff-5441-a02b-d2123ed28dfa" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1059a7c8-9a04-5280-9f29-30f8d8a20897" :answer/id #uuid "1059a7c8-9a04-5280-9f29-30f8d8a20897" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e7761c70-8716-56c9-a2cb-a35290fdff3f" :answer/id #uuid "e7761c70-8716-56c9-a2cb-a35290fdff3f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{4}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186116516 :tutorial/content "Suppose we are given the function

$$
y=5\log_6(x-2).
$$

How do we plot its graph?

As usual, we can do this by combining transformations of the curve $y=\log_6 x.$

- We start with the graph of $y=\log_6 x{:}$

- Translate it by $2$ units to the right to get the graph of $y=\log_6{(x-2)}.$
