Notice that points $(1,0)$ and $(6,1)$ on the graph of $y=\log_6 x$ map to the points $(3,0)$ and $(8,1)$ on the graph of $y=\log_6 (x-2),$ respectively.

- Then, stretch the result by a scale factor of $5$ parallel to the $y$-axis to get the graph of $y=5\log_6{(x-2)}.$

![](images/a6/a67b409068f67d81f0217aaeb30f76bd63c6501376d2adc567db7c4f319d7144.png)

So, to plot the curve of a transformed logarithmic function, we apply subsequent transformations presented in the given function, as usual." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115461 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186119808 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-c391d9c3-0c76-5e6f-b0c3-d6b4ee2c37cb" "question-a8427e64-b547-5ecb-a62e-824aa188b632" "question-ddfb229d-f01d-542c-8a6c-f2e9a5996154"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-c391d9c3-0c76-5e6f-b0c3-d6b4ee2c37cb" :question/id #uuid "c391d9c3-0c76-5e6f-b0c3-d6b4ee2c37cb" :question/math-academy-id "q-105199" :question/problem "The vectors ${a}_{1}$, ${a}_{2}$, and $b$ are given below. Determine if $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$ from the decomposition $b={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}.$

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 8\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "We know that $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ if there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} & =b \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=3 \\ 2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=8\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=3 \\ {x}_{2}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the system has a solution, we can conclude that $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}.$

Moreover, there is exactly one solution, so we have exactly one way to write $b$ as a linear combination of ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3{a}_{1}+2{a}_{2} & =b \\ 3\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+2\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=3\cdot 2=6.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7847d689-0e36-5ac4-b435-bd1cf0642bc0"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-7847d689-0e36-5ac4-b435-bd1cf0642bc0" :answer-field/id #uuid "7847d689-0e36-5ac4-b435-bd1cf0642bc0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-98c56786-6605-5401-b672-c63cb1cecd33" :answer-field/choices ["answer-976c158b-03de-5101-af86-c772a635e855" "answer-38fb4394-142f-596a-acba-652af141f7ea" "answer-1f1cbd99-3722-58a8-94e3-9b80df51c48b" "answer-1442cd36-01ab-57b5-b752-7b7131e887f9" "answer-98c56786-6605-5401-b672-c63cb1cecd33"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-976c158b-03de-5101-af86-c772a635e855" :answer/id #uuid "976c158b-03de-5101-af86-c772a635e855" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-38fb4394-142f-596a-acba-652af141f7ea" :answer/id #uuid "38fb4394-142f-596a-acba-652af141f7ea" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-9" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1f1cbd99-3722-58a8-94e3-9b80df51c48b" :answer/id #uuid "1f1cbd99-3722-58a8-94e3-9b80df51c48b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1442cd36-01ab-57b5-b752-7b7131e887f9" :answer/id #uuid "1442cd36-01ab-57b5-b752-7b7131e887f9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-98c56786-6605-5401-b672-c63cb1cecd33" :answer/id #uuid "98c56786-6605-5401-b672-c63cb1cecd33" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-a8427e64-b547-5ecb-a62e-824aa188b632" :question/id #uuid "a8427e64-b547-5ecb-a62e-824aa188b632" :question/math-academy-id "q-34114" :question/problem "The vectors ${a}_{1}$, ${a}_{2}$, and $b$ are given below. Determine if $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$ from the decomposition $b={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}.$

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ -7\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "We know that $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ if there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} & =b \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ -7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=2 \\ 2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0 \\ -3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-7\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & -7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 & -4 \\ -3 & 1 & -7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=2 \\ {x}_{2}=-1 \\ 0=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the system has a solution, we can conclude that $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}.$

Moreover, there is exactly one solution, so we have exactly one way to write $b$ as a linear combination of ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{a}_{1}+(-1){a}_{2} & =b \\ 2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+(-1)\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=2\cdot (-1)=-2.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-283164aa-73de-5dcd-8a69-e6c9e6374abc"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-283164aa-73de-5dcd-8a69-e6c9e6374abc" :answer-field/id #uuid "283164aa-73de-5dcd-8a69-e6c9e6374abc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-35881d2a-16d1-5e15-a12f-b325e9f8db16" :answer-field/choices ["answer-4d4a40a4-8887-524e-8b48-8a24128d12fd" "answer-35881d2a-16d1-5e15-a12f-b325e9f8db16" "answer-d639618d-a932-5b03-8225-fae8a0b21ef5" "answer-32966283-95f9-59c0-9da8-620246a44c9f" "answer-1e4a4287-0b4e-5134-b26d-e720107fbfce"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4d4a40a4-8887-524e-8b48-8a24128d12fd" :answer/id #uuid "4d4a40a4-8887-524e-8b48-8a24128d12fd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-35881d2a-16d1-5e15-a12f-b325e9f8db16" :answer/id #uuid "35881d2a-16d1-5e15-a12f-b325e9f8db16" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d639618d-a932-5b03-8225-fae8a0b21ef5" :answer/id #uuid "d639618d-a932-5b03-8225-fae8a0b21ef5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-32966283-95f9-59c0-9da8-620246a44c9f" :answer/id #uuid "32966283-95f9-59c0-9da8-620246a44c9f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1e4a4287-0b4e-5134-b26d-e720107fbfce" :answer/id #uuid "1e4a4287-0b4e-5134-b26d-e720107fbfce" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "b\notin \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-ddfb229d-f01d-542c-8a6c-f2e9a5996154" :question/id #uuid "ddfb229d-f01d-542c-8a6c-f2e9a5996154" :question/math-academy-id "q-34639" :question/problem "The vectors ${a}_{1}$, ${a}_{2}$, ${a}_{3}$, and $b$ are given below. Determine if $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}\cdot {x}_{3}$ from the decomposition $b={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}.$

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -8 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 18 \\ 9\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "We know that $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ if there exist ${x}_{1}$, ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3} & =b \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -8 \\ -3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 18 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{3}=3 \\ 4{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3}=18 \\ 2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{3}=9\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 4 & 1 & -8 & 18 \\ 2 & 0 & -3 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 6 \\ 2 & 0 & -3 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{3}=3 \\ {x}_{2}=6 \\ {x}_{3}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=3.$ Substituting into the first equation gives 

$$
{x}_{1}-2(3)=3\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=9.
$$

Since the system has a solution, we can conclude that $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}.$

Moreover, there is exactly one solution, so we have exactly one way to write $b$ as a linear combination of ${a}_{1}$, ${a}_{2}$ and ${a}_{3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}9{a}_{1}+6{a}_{2}+3{a}_{3} & =b \\ 9\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+6\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+3\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -8 \\ -3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 18 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}\cdot {x}_{3}=9\cdot 6\cdot 3=162.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0d94e257-45da-5352-bd7b-f0680253dc5b"] "Find the values of $k$ such that the vector $b$ lies in $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\},$ where

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "We know that $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ if there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} & =b \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -9 \\ 10\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4 \\ k\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=3 \\ -2{x}_{1}-9{x}_{2}=-4 \\ 2{x}_{1}+10{x}_{2}=k\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & 3 \\ -2 & -9 & -4 \\ 2 & 10 & k\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 10 & k\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & k-6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The third row of the augmented matrix now corresponds to the equation $0{x}_{1}+0{x}_{2}=k-6.$ Therefore, the system has a solution only if

$$
0=k-6\,⇒\,k=6.

17592186120304 :question/problem "Determine if the vector $u$ lies on the plane $Π:r=sb+tc,$ $t,s\in R$, where  $b=⟨1,5,8⟩$, $c=⟨-1,-1,-3⟩$, and  $u=⟨-3,5,-7⟩.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of $s\cdot t$ from the decomposition $u=sb+tc.$" :question/worked-solution "By definition, $u\in Π$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}sb+tc & =u \\ s[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5 \\ 8\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1 \\ -3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5 \\ -7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s-t=-3 \\ 5s-t=5 \\ 8s-3t=-7\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -3 \\ 5 & -1 & 5 \\ 8 & -3 & -7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-5{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 4 & 20 \\ 8 & -3 & -7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-8{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 4 & 20 \\ 0 & 5 & 17\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 5 & 17\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-5{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & -8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The third row of the augmented matrix now corresponds to the equation $0{x}_{1}+0{x}_{2}=-8,$ which has no solution.

So, there are no values of $s$ and $t$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}sb+tc=u.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $u$ does *not* lie on the plane $Π.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186117963 :answer-field/correct 17592186117964 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186121035 :tutorial/content "Given two vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2,$ the set of all possible linear combinations of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ is

$$
U = \left\{ x_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + x_2 \mathbf{a}_2 \: : \: x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R} \right\}.
$$

The set $U$ is also called the **linear span** of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2,$ and is denoted by $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}.$ We say that $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ are the **generators** of $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}.$

For example, let's find the linear span generated by the following vectors:
![](images/55/55c749dccc54c252b9120f148e383f395c09fb4cd4bec0e1cce8ed441ecb6199.svg)

From the definition of linear span, we know that if $\mathbf{b} \in \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ then $\mathbf{b}$ must take the form

$$
\mathbf{b} = x_1\mathbf{a_1} + x_2\mathbf{a_2}
$$

 for some $x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R}.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}b & ={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the linear span of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ is
![](images/21/2181b471f34906eeaea7889abbba37c797a2f9624cee455b43b00fc048247cd1.svg)

Geometrically, $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}$ can be viewed as the plane $\Pi$ that passes through the origin and is parallel to the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2,$ as shown below.

"7487be5e-d3cc-5ed9-9625-a2ce92482f7c" :question/math-academy-id "q-251806" :question/problem "Consider the two sets of $8$ paired observations in the table below.

- A set is *open* if it does not contain any of its boundary points. In other words, an open set consists only of the interior points of the set.

- A set is *closed* if it contains **all** of its boundary points. In other words, a closed set consists of all the interior and all the boundary points of the set.

The other sets are not open because:

- $[0,15]$ has two boundary points $0$, and $15$, and both of them lie in the set.

- $(-3,5]\cup [6,8)$ has four boundary points $-3$, $5$, $6$, and $8$, and the points $5$ and $6$ lie in the set.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only"." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9c9d3d2d-5c89-5028-8119-349ee1ac7225"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-9c9d3d2d-5c89-5028-8119-349ee1ac7225" :answer-field/id #uuid "9c9d3d2d-5c89-5028-8119-349ee1ac7225" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-df327c23-f0d8-51b7-8f66-04274266589e" :answer-field/choices ["answer-5ff4f3ba-42e5-570f-bca8-ed45b21cb1f7" "answer-1ed67d77-19b4-542e-9fbf-7d6adca9ad93" "answer-c0c57c73-2803-51dc-b2db-124289558110" "answer-e09f8edf-88de-5e68-86d0-9a2c8f07968e" "answer-df327c23-f0d8-51b7-8f66-04274266589e"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5ff4f3ba-42e5-570f-bca8-ed45b21cb1f7" :answer/id #uuid "5ff4f3ba-42e5-570f-bca8-ed45b21cb1f7" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1ed67d77-19b4-542e-9fbf-7d6adca9ad93" :answer/id #uuid "1ed67d77-19b4-542e-9fbf-7d6adca9ad93" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c0c57c73-2803-51dc-b2db-124289558110" :answer/id #uuid "c0c57c73-2803-51dc-b2db-124289558110" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e09f8edf-88de-5e68-86d0-9a2c8f07968e" :answer/id #uuid "e09f8edf-88de-5e68-86d0-9a2c8f07968e" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-df327c23-f0d8-51b7-8f66-04274266589e" :answer/id #uuid "df327c23-f0d8-51b7-8f66-04274266589e" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186193325 :question/problem "Which of the following sets are closed?

- Graphs II, III, and IV do not have rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin. So, it is **not** an odd function.

- On the other hand, graph I does have rotational symmetry about the origin. If we rotate the graph ${180}^{∘}$ around the origin, we get the same picture. This means that graph  I  show odd functions.

"question-d5075c32-f624-572f-a2d3-78616466d14e" :question/id #uuid "d5075c32-f624-572f-a2d3-78616466d14e" :question/math-academy-id "q-86430" :question/problem "Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=(2{x}^{2}-y)^{2}$ at the point $A(-1,1)$ in the direction towards the point $B(-2,2).$" :question/worked-solution "The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨-2,2⟩-⟨-1,1⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,1⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}}⟨-1,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-y)^{2},\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-y)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨16{x}^{3}-8xy,\,2y-4{x}^{2}⟩ \\ ∇f(-1,1) & =⟨16(-1)^{3}-8(-1)(1),\,2(1)-4(-1)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-8,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(-1,1) & =∇f(-1,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨-8,-2⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟩ \\  & =(-8)\cdot (-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})-2\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}) \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-aa2be9cd-8e25-5c22-a57c-dbf36efef798"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=2i+j.$" :question/worked-solution "The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{5} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(2i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\text{ }j \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡y+\frac{y}{x})\,i+(\frac{x}{y}+\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\,j \\ ∇\,f(1,1) & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡1+\frac{1}{1})\,i+(\frac{1}{1}+\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\,j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(1,1) & =∇\,f(1,1)\cdot u \\  & =(i+j)\cdot (\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}j) \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 2+1\cdot 1}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5f6b8a55-8b0f-5157-98ff-b7ec894bdaee"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-6xy+{y}^{2}$ at the point $(-1,3)$ in the direction of the vector $v=i+j.$" :question/worked-solution "The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{2} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(-1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-6xy+{y}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-6xy+{y}^{2})\text{ }j \\  & =(2x-6y)\,i+(2y-6x)j \\ ∇\,f(-1,3) & =(2(-1)-6(3))\,i+(2(3)-6(-1))j \\  & =-20\,i+12\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(-1,3) & =∇\,f(-1,3)\cdot u \\  & =(-20\,i+12\,j)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i+j) \\  & =\frac{-20(1)+12(1)}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =-\frac{8}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =-4\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-235850d9-4b74-5c62-9d1d-41026c4c9828"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id rapidly in the direction opposite to that of its gradient.

So, we compute $-∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}-∇f(x,y) & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{tan}⁡y+2{x}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\text{ }i-\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{tan}⁡y+2{x}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\text{ }j \\  & =-(\operatorname{tan}⁡y+4x-\frac{1}{x})i-x{sec}^{2}⁡y\text{ }j \\ -∇f(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-(\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+4\cdot 1-\frac{1}{1})i-1\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\text{ }j \\  & =-4\,i-2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

the direction of the vector $v=⟨4,-3⟩?$" :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(1,e)$ in the direction of $v$ is equal to the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(1,e).$ 

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+(-3)^{2}}=5 \\ u & =\frac{1}{5}⟨4,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the gradient $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{x}),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{x})⟩ \\  & =⟨{y}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,x{y}^{x-1}⟩ \\ ∇g(1,e) & =⟨{e}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡e,1{e}^{1-1}⟩ \\  & =⟨e,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(1,e)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{u}^{′}(1,e) & =∇g(1,e)\cdot u \\  & =⟨e,1⟩\cdot \frac{1}{5}⟨4,-3⟩ \\  & =\frac{e(4)+1(-3)}{5} \\  & =\frac{4e-3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-75da4e92-2341-5f89-a517-37e979e4303c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $g(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x).$ What is the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(\frac{\pi }{4},4)$ in the direction in which the function increases most rapidly?" :question/worked-solution "At a given point, a function $g(x,y)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

In our case, we compute $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(\frac{\pi }{4},4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x))⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{tan}⁡x,\,\frac{2}{y}⟩ \\ ∇\,g(\frac{\pi }{4},4) & =⟨-\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}),\,\frac{2}{4}⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(\frac{\pi }{4},4)$ in the direction of $∇g(\frac{\pi }{4},4)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}‖∇\,g(\frac{\pi }{4},4)‖ & =‖⟨-1,\frac{1}{2}⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{5}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-45ab83aa-a438-50c5-87d1-85ddbe0b15e9"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-45ab83aa-a438-50c5-87d1-85ddbe0b15e9" :answer-field/id #uuid "45ab83aa-a438-50c5-87d1-85ddbe0b15e9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-cd1cc6cd-5009-53a5-9550-f7f07275d8a5" :answer-field/choices ["answer-a937d5cd-9309-5b00-a446-cdfd649551b2" "answer-e69a9ba3-ccae-56d8-8e5f-5d06921f70e9" "answer-189ec891-a762-54dd-8e28-66f7d86f7621" "answer-cd1cc6cd-5009-53a5-9550-f7f07275d8a5" "answer-b2d80ddb-b0ea-50ab-81d2-6892d56e013c"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a937d5cd-9309-5b00-a446-cdfd649551b2" :answer/id #uuid "a937d5cd-9309-5b00-a446-cdfd649551b2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e69a9ba3-ccae-56d8-8e5f-5d06921f70e9" :answer/id #uuid "e69a9ba3-ccae-56d8-8e5f-5d06921f70e9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-189ec891-a762-54dd-8e28-66f7d86f7621" :answer/id #uuid "189ec891-a762-54dd-8e28-66f7d86f7621" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cd1cc6cd-5009-53a5-9550-f7f07275d8a5" :answer/id #uuid "cd1cc6cd-5009-53a5-9550-f7f07275d8a5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b2d80ddb-b0ea-50ab-81d2-6892d56e013c" :answer/id #uuid "b2d80ddb-b0ea-50ab-81d2-6892d56e013c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{5}}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]}]

$b=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "In part 1, we found that $p(15)=225a+15b.$ So, we need to solve the equation $225a+15b=4\,050$ for the parameter $b.$

We need to isolate the variable $b.$ To do this, we treat $a$ as though it were a constant and apply the addition and multiplication principles as usual.

First, we subtract $225a$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}225a+15b & =4\,050 \\ 225a+15b-225a & =4\,050-225a \\ 15b & =4\,050-225a\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide both sides of the equation by $15:$

$$
\begin{aligned}15b & =4\,050-225a \\ \frac{15b}{15} & =\frac{4\,050-225a}{15} \\ \frac{\cancel{15}b}{\cancel{15}} & =\frac{4\,050}{15}-\frac{225a}{15} \\ b & =270-15a\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $b=270-15a.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-187ca06a-34b2-52f2-bb4c-69c7613a1bfe"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-187ca06a-34b2-52f2-bb4c-69c7613a1bfe" :answer-field/id #uuid "187ca06a-34b2-52f2-bb4c-69c7613a1bfe" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-d436335e-8de5-5c08-ac68-22272df80bd8" :answer-field/choices ["answer-d436335e-8de5-5c08-ac68-22272df80bd8"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d436335e-8de5-5c08-ac68-22272df80bd8" :answer/id #uuid "d436335e-8de5-5c08-ac68-22272df80bd8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "270-15a" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186073752 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-b42bde79-43e7-5e0d-aa7f-ed2b4b36837d"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-b42bde79-43e7-5e0d-aa7f-ed2b4b36837d" :question/id #uuid "b42bde79-43e7-5e0d-aa7f-ed2b4b36837d" :question/math-academy-id "q-167218" :question/problem "The coefficients $a$ and $b$ also satisfy the equation $100a+15b=4\,800.$ Find the values of $a$ and $b.$

{{field-2}}" :question/worked-solution "We have the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}b=270-15a \\ 100a+15b=4\,800\end{aligned}
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. 

Notice that the first equation is already solved for $b:$

$$
b=270-15a
$$

So, we replace $b$ in the second equation and solve for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}100a+15b & =4\,800 \\ 100a+15(270-15a) & =4\,800 \\ 100a+4\,050-225a & =4\,800 \\ -125a+4\,050 & =4\,800 \\ -125a & =750 \\ a & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $a=-6$ into $b=270-15a,$ we can then find the value of $b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}b & =270-15(-6) \\ b & =360\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $a=-6,\,b=360.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-152e2f23-0e18-55aa-a6f1-c39bead952a2" "answer-field-ee0751b7-37b1-5581-b463-69aae210a148"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-152e2f23-0e18-55aa-a6f1-c39bead952a2" :answer-field/id #uuid "152e2f23-0e18-55aa-a6f1-c39bead952a2" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-283112f9-9ffe-5a11-bbfc-a5ba098b6d08" :answer-field/choices ["answer-283112f9-9ffe-5a11-bbfc-a5ba098b6d08"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-283112f9-9ffe-5a11-bbfc-a5ba098b6d08" :answer/id #uuid "283112f9-9ffe-5a11-bbfc-a5ba098b6d08" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-ee0751b7-37b1-5581-b463-69aae210a148" :answer-field/id #uuid "ee0751b7-37b1-5581-b463-69aae210a148" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-967fdc49-d3aa-54f3-af09-6a561f202139" :answer-field/choices ["answer-967fdc49-d3aa-54f3-af09-6a561f202139"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-967fdc49-d3aa-54f3-af09-6a561f202139" :answer/id #uuid "967fdc49-d3aa-54f3-af09-6a561f202139" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "360" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068701 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-527dba5f-2797-5f00-97de-509f725bd58d"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-527dba5f-2797-5f00-97de-509f725bd58d" :question/id #uuid "527dba5f-2797-5f00-97de-509f725bd58d" :question/math-academy-id "q-167219" :question/problem "Determine the weekly profit if the company produces $24$ wooden tables in a week.

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The explicit formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}+(n-1)d,\,n\ge 1,
$$

so we need to determine the first term ${a}_{1}$ and the common difference $d.$

We are given that the first term is ${a}_{1}=12,$ and we can use the recursive rule to compute the second term as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & ={a}_{1}+4 \\  & =12+4 \\  & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Using the first and second terms, we can compute the common difference:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={a}_{2}-{a}_{1} \\  & =16-12 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now we substitute ${a}_{1}=12$ and $d=4$ into the formula for the $n$th term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =12+(n-1)(4) \\  & =12+4n-4 \\  & =4n+8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is

$$
{a}_{n}=4n+8,\,n\ge 1.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c3549239-369c-5dc5-b97f-5b91a23e416d"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-c3549239-369c-5dc5-b97f-5b91a23e416d" :answer-field/id #uuid "c3549239-369c-5dc5-b97f-5b91a23e416d" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-d7608f3d-23f5-549b-a860-02910a5e6580" :answer-field/choices ["answer-d7608f3d-23f5-549b-a860-02910a5e6580"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d7608f3d-23f5-549b-a860-02910a5e6580" :answer/id #uuid "d7608f3d-23f5-549b-a860-02910a5e6580" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4n+8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "multistep-bb1bcb11-dd3e-5ef2-acf5-2bd2feb4ce5d" :multistep/id #uuid "bb1bcb11-dd3e-5ef2-acf5-2bd2feb4ce5d" :multistep/context "The sales manager of a company that produces wooden furniture analyses the weekly profit made by creating $x$ wooden tables per week. In this case, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{4}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{4},$ as follows:

$$

$$
f(x)=\frac{7{x}^{2}+4}{3{x}^{3}+12x}
$$

To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{3}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{3},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{7{x}^{2}+4}{3{x}^{3}+12x} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{7{x}^{2}}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{4}{{x}^{3}})}{(\frac{3{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{12x}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{7}{x}+\frac{4}{{x}^{3}})}{(3+\frac{12}{{x}^{2}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Knowing that the average rate of change of the function $f(x)$ on the interval $[3p,5]$ is $-2,$ find the value of $p.$ 

| $x$ | $\,-10\,$ | $\,-7\,$ | $\,3p\,$ | $\,-2\,$ | $\,0\,$ | $\,1\,$ | $\,5\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{Δf}{Δx} & =\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a} \\  & =\frac{f(5)-f(3p)}{5-3p} \\  & =\frac{-8-11}{5-3p} \\  & =\frac{-19}{5-3p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we know that $\frac{Δf}{Δx}=-2$ on the interval $[3p,5].$ Thus, 

$$
\frac{-19}{5-3p}=-2.
$$

Solving for $p,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-19}{5-3p} & =-2 \\ -19 & =-2\cdot (5-3p) \\ -19 & =-10+6p \\ -19+10 & =6p \\ -9 & =6p \\ \frac{-9}{6} & =\frac{6p}{6} \\ -\frac{3}{2} & =p.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $p=-\frac{3}{2}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ffb11692-b94a-52a8-a712-f1575499549c"] :db/ensure :question/problem "Calculate ${lim}_{t\to 2}f(t),$ if $f(t)=⟨{e}^{t-2},\,\sqrt{6-t},\,\frac{3}{t+2}⟩.$" :question/worked-solution "First, recall that

$$
{lim}_{t\to 2}f(t)=⟨{lim}_{t\to 2}{e}^{t-2},\,{lim}_{t\to 2}\sqrt{6-t},\,{lim}_{t\to 2}\frac{3}{t+2}⟩.
$$

Now, we find the limits one by one.

- For the first component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 2}{e}^{t-2} & ={e}^{2-2} \\  & ={e}^{0} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 2}\sqrt{6-t} & =\sqrt{6-2} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the third component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 2}\frac{3}{t+2} & =\frac{3}{2+2} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{t\to 2}f(t)=⟨1,2,\frac{3}{4}⟩.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8fb29db3-ac82-5b56-ae72-c2f44640f27f"] :db/ensure (1+5s)^{1-s}\end{aligned}].$" :question/worked-solution "First, recall that

$$
{lim}_{s\to 1}f(s)=[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 1}\sqrt{5-s} \\ {lim}_{s\to 1}\frac{{e}^{1-s}}{s} \\ {lim}_{s\to 1}\,(1+5s)^{1/(2s)}.\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we find the limits one by one.

- For the first component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 1}\sqrt{5-s} & =\sqrt{5-1} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 1}\frac{{e}^{1-s}}{s}=\frac{{e}^{1-1}}{1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the third component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 1}\,(1+5s)^{1-s} & =(1+5\cdot 1)^{1-1} \\  & ={6}^{0} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{s\to 1}f(s)=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-934d475b-f1bc-5ebd-a7fa-3293dabf3b69"] $$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 2}\frac{5}{{e}^{s-2}} & =\frac{5}{{e}^{2-2}}=5.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 2}\,({s}^{3}-5) & ={2}^{3}-5=3.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{arcsin}⁡s}{s} & ={lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{{(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡s)}^{′}}{{s}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{s}^{2}}}}{1} \\  & ={lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{s}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{0}^{2}}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- The third component can be found using a special limit:

$$

$$

$f(s)=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5-s} \\ \frac{{e}^{1-s}}{s} \\ (1+5s)^{1-s}\end{aligned}].$" :question/worked-solution "First, recall that

$$
{lim}_{s\to 1}f(s)=[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 1}\sqrt{5-s} \\ {lim}_{s\to 1}\frac{{e}^{1-s}}{1-s} \\ {lim}_{s\to 1}\,(1+5s)^{1/(2s)}\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we find the limits one by one.

- For the first component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 1}\sqrt{5-s} & =\sqrt{5-1} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 1}\frac{{e}^{1-s}}{s}=\frac{1}{1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the third component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 1}\,(1+5s)^{1-s} & =(1+5\cdot 1)^{1-1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{s\to 1}f(s)=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Finally, the limit of $‖f(s)‖$ as $s$ approaches $1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 1}‖f(s)‖ & =‖{lim}_{s\to 1}f(s)‖ \\  & =‖[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8dbde469-aa7e-5bcb-a66c-2dae3c6fa5e6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $f(s)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{s}{(s+1)^{2}} \\ \frac{{sin}^{2}⁡s}{{s}^{2}} \\ \frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡s}{2{s}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\,.$" :question/worked-solution "First, recall that:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 0}f(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{s}{(s+1)^{2}} \\ {lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡s}{{s}^{2}} \\ {lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡s}{2{s}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the limits one-by-one.

- For the first component, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{s}{(s+1)^{2}} & =\frac{0}{(0+1)^{2}}=0\end{aligned}
$$

- The second component can be found using a special limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡s}{{s}^{2}} & ={lim}_{s\to 0}{(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡s}{s})}^{2} \\  & ={({lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡s}{s})}^{2} \\  & ={1}^{2} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- The third component can be found using L'Hopital's Rule twice:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡s}{2{s}^{2}} & ={lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡s)}^{″}}{{(2{s}^{2})}^{″}} \\  & ={lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡s}{4} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡0}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{s\to 0}f(s)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1/4\end{aligned}]\,.$

Finally, the limit of $‖f(s)‖$ as $s$ approaches $0$ is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 0}‖f(s)‖ & =‖{lim}_{s\to 0}f(s)‖ \\  & =‖[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1/4\end{aligned}]‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{4})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{17}{16}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{17}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a738fbe9-b746-555f-a431-6ff37c754328"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

$$

Now, we find the limits one-by-one.

- For the first component, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}\frac{4+t}{5} & =\frac{4+1}{5}=1\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-1)}{{t}^{2}-1} & ={lim}_{t\to 1}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-1)}{(t-1)(t+1)} \\  & =({lim}_{t\to 1}\frac{1}{t+1})\cdot ({lim}_{t\to 1}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-1)}{t-1}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{1+1})\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- For the third component, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}\sqrt{9t} & =\sqrt{9(1)}=3\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{t\to 1}f(t)=i+\frac{1}{2}\,j+3\,k.$

Finally, the limit of $‖f(t)‖$ as $t$ approaches $1$ is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}‖f(t)‖ & =‖{lim}_{t\to 1}f(t)‖ \\  & =‖i+\frac{1}{2}\,j+3\,k‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4}+9} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{41}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{41}}{2}\end{aligned}

$$

Now, we find the limits one-by-one.

- For the first component, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 3}({t}^{2}-3t) & ={3}^{2}-3(3)=0\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 3}\frac{1}{{t}^{2}-8} & =\frac{1}{{3}^{2}-8}=1\end{aligned}
$$

- For the third component, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 3}(5-2t) & =5-2(3)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{t\to 3}f(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

Finally, the limit of $‖f(t)‖$ as $t$ approaches $3$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 3}‖f(t)‖ & =‖{lim}_{t\to 3}f(t)‖ \\  & =‖[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c84f65d5-7aae-5814-8581-c9fd5f811b31"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "Find ${lim}_{t\to \infty }[g(t)+2f(t)]$ given that $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are defined as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =\frac{{t}^{2}}{1-{t}^{2}}\,i+(1+\frac{1}{t})\,j+{t}^{-2}\,k \\ g(t) & =2\,i+{e}^{-t}\,j+{(1+\frac{1}{t})}^{t}\,k\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \infty }f(t) & =({lim}_{t\to \infty }\frac{{t}^{2}}{1-{t}^{2}})\,i+({lim}_{t\to \infty }(1+\frac{1}{t}))\,j-({lim}_{t\to \infty }{t}^{-2})\,k, \\ {lim}_{t\to \infty }g(t) & =({lim}_{t\to \infty }2)\,i-({lim}_{t\to \infty }{e}^{-t})\,j+({lim}_{t\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{t})}^{t})\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's find the limits one-by-one.

$$
\begin{aligned} & {lim}_{t\to \infty }\frac{{t}^{2}}{1-{t}^{2}}={lim}_{t\to \infty }\frac{1}{\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}-1}=-1 \\  & {lim}_{t\to \infty }(1+\frac{1}{t})=1+{lim}_{t\to \infty }\frac{1}{t}=1 \\  & {lim}_{t\to \infty }{t}^{-2}={lim}_{t\to \infty }\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}=0 \\  & {lim}_{t\to \infty }2=2 \\  & {lim}_{t\to \infty }{e}^{-t}=0 \\  & {lim}_{t\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{t})}^{t}=e\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \infty }f(t) & =-1\,i+1\,j+0\,k \\  & =-i+j, \\ {lim}_{t\to \infty }g(t) & =2\,i+0\,j+e\,k \\  & =2\,i+e\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \infty }[g(t)+2f(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to \infty }g(t)+2{lim}_{t\to \infty }f(t) \\  & =(2\,i+e\,k)+2(-i+j) \\  & =2j+e\,k\end{aligned}

$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the limit of each function:

$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}f(t) & =⟨{lim}_{t\to 1}({t}^{2}),\,{lim}_{t\to 1}({t}^{3}),\,{lim}_{t\to 1}(\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})⟩ \\  & =⟨{1}^{2},{1}^{3},\frac{1}{{1}^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,1,1⟩ \\ {lim}_{t\to 1}g(t) & =⟨{lim}_{t\to 1}(5-{t}^{3}),\,{lim}_{t\to 1}({t}^{2}-t+2),\,{lim}_{t\to 1}(4)⟩ \\  & =⟨5-{1}^{3},{1}^{2}-1+2,4⟩ \\  & =⟨4,2,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

"Find ${lim}_{t\to 2}[f(t)\times g(t)]$ given that $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =⟨6-{t}^{3},\,{t}^{2}-6,\,\frac{16}{{t}^{3}}⟩, \\ g(t) & =⟨5-\operatorname{ln}⁡(3-t),\,\sqrt{6-t},\,2t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 2}f(t) & =⟨{lim}_{t\to 2}\,(6-{t}^{3}),\,{lim}_{t\to 2}\,({t}^{2}-6),\,{lim}_{t\to 2}\frac{16}{{t}^{3}}⟩ \\  & =⟨6-{2}^{3},{2}^{2}-6,\frac{16}{{2}^{3}}⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,-2,2⟩ \\ {lim}_{t\to 2}g(t) & =⟨{lim}_{t\to 2}\,(5-\operatorname{ln}⁡(3-t)),\,{lim}_{t\to 2}\,\sqrt{6-t},\,{lim}_{t\to 2}\,2t⟩ \\  & =⟨5-\operatorname{ln}⁡(3-2),\sqrt{6-2},2(2)⟩ \\  & =⟨5,2,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 2}[f(t)\times g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to 2}f(t)\times {lim}_{t\to 2}g(t) \\  & =⟨-2,-2,2⟩\times ⟨5,2,4⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -2 & -2 & 2 \\ 5 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 5 & 4\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}|k \\  & =((-2)\cdot 4-2\cdot 2)\,i-((-2)\cdot 4-5\cdot 2)\,j+((-2)\cdot 2-5\cdot (-2))\,k \\  & =-12\,i+18\,j+6\,k \\  & =⟨-12,18,6⟩\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4a9c7ac2-4c78-5bd6-ac32-375910d4abbb"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-4a9c7ac2-4c78-5bd6-ac32-375910d4abbb" :answer-field/id #uuid "4a9c7ac2-4c78-5bd6-ac32-375910d4abbb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-7eacfd82-115e-5369-9ea0-e0661e38dc5a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-7eacfd82-115e-5369-9ea0-e0661e38dc5a" "answer-37a1710a-45e4-557c-9442-1e74ba9112ce" "answer-e9e869f0-043f-53a7-9d36-e47ddd23102f" "answer-3f8fd679-95eb-5199-ba6a-a1cfb67ca9ca" "answer-bbc42210-6e93-5e95-b495-30f65a2b1ba3"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7eacfd82-115e-5369-9ea0-e0661e38dc5a" :answer/id #uuid "7eacfd82-115e-5369-9ea0-e0661e38dc5a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "⟨-12,18,6⟩" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-37a1710a-45e4-557c-9442-1e74ba9112ce" :answer/id #uuid "37a1710a-45e4-557c-9442-1e74ba9112ce" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "⟨-18,12,6⟩" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e9e869f0-043f-53a7-9d36-e47ddd23102f" :answer/id #uuid "e9e869f0-043f-53a7-9d36-e47ddd23102f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "⟨-2,8,6⟩" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3f8fd679-95eb-5199-ba6a-a1cfb67ca9ca" :answer/id #uuid "3f8fd679-95eb-5199-ba6a-a1cfb67ca9ca" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "⟨12,8,9⟩" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bbc42210-6e93-5e95-b495-30f65a2b1ba3" :answer/id #uuid "bbc42210-6e93-5e95-b495-30f65a2b1ba3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "⟨5,2,4⟩" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-33768c70-a4a8-56c5-b929-58df88c6ba1b" :question/id #uuid "33768c70-a4a8-56c5-b929-58df88c6ba1b" :question/math-academy-id "q-78268" :question/problem "Find the limit ${lim}_{t\to 1}[f(t)\cdot g(t)]$ given that $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are defined as:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{t-1} \\ \frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t}{t} \\ \frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t}{t}\end{aligned}],\,g(t)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{t}^{2}-2t+1}{t+1} \\ \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t}{t+1} \\ \frac{{e}^{t+1}}{t+1}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}\,(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{t-1}) \\ {lim}_{t\to 1}\,(\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t}{t}) \\ {lim}_{t\to 1}\,(\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t}{t})\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}\,(\frac{(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)^{′}}{(t-1)^{′}}) \\ {lim}_{t\to 1}\,(\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t}{t}) \\ {lim}_{t\to 1}\,(\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t}{t})\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}\,(\frac{1}{t}) \\ \frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi }{1} \\ \frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi }{1}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Note that for the first component of ${lim}_{t\to 1}f(t)$ we used L'Hopital's Rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}g(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}\,\frac{{t}^{2}-2t+1}{t+1} \\ {lim}_{t\to 1}\,\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t}{t+1} \\ {lim}_{t\to 1}\,\frac{{e}^{t+1}}{t+1}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{1}^{2}-2\cdot 1+1}{1+1} \\ \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡1+1}{1+1} \\ \frac{{e}^{1+1}}{1+1}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{{e}^{2}}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}[f(t)\cdot g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to 1}f(t)\cdot {lim}_{t\to 1}g(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{{e}^{2}}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =1\cdot 0+(-2)\cdot \frac{1}{2}+0\cdot \frac{{e}^{2}}{2} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b24006f7-dcb6-5a3e-962f-d3babb6d995e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b24006f7-dcb6-5a3e-962f-d3babb6d995e" :answer-field/id #uuid "b24006f7-dcb6-5a3e-962f-d3babb6d995e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-873d5f29-f5c3-5d96-8997-2e96d20efdab" :answer-field/choices ["answer-873d5f29-f5c3-5d96-8997-2e96d20efdab" "answer-8ccbdb14-9c0c-5f46-a3d4-ae2fd1da959c" "answer-920aaecc-64b5-5927-be63-43fbf263f51a" "answer-5f6847e3-eb2c-5cc6-9cd0-83733cfef02d" "answer-4e7082bf-94bc-5f95-a646-926615cd1b1a"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-873d5f29-f5c3-5d96-8997-2e96d20efdab" :answer/id #uuid "873d5f29-f5c3-5d96-8997-2e96d20efdab" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8ccbdb14-9c0c-5f46-a3d4-ae2fd1da959c" :answer/id #uuid "8ccbdb14-9c0c-5f46-a3d4-ae2fd1da959c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-{e}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-920aaecc-64b5-5927-be63-43fbf263f51a" :answer/id #uuid "920aaecc-64b5-5927-be63-43fbf263f51a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5f6847e3-eb2c-5cc6-9cd0-83733cfef02d" :answer/id #uuid "5f6847e3-eb2c-5cc6-9cd0-83733cfef02d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1-\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4e7082bf-94bc-5f95-a646-926615cd1b1a" :answer/id #uuid "4e7082bf-94bc-5f95-a646-926615cd1b1a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1-{e}^{2}}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-0e9c7e83-813e-5902-881b-22d16eab32e5" :question/id #uuid "0e9c7e83-813e-5902-881b-22d16eab32e5" :question/math-academy-id "q-78269" :question/problem "Find the limit ${lim}_{t\to 0}[f(t)\cdot g(t)]$ given that $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are defined as:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =⟨\frac{{t}^{2}-2t+2}{t+1},\,\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{t},\,t\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ g(t) & =⟨\frac{{e}^{2t}-1}{t},\,1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t+1⟩\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}f(t) & =⟨{lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{{t}^{2}-2t+2}{t+1},\,{lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{t},\,{lim}_{t\to 0}t\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =⟨{lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{{t}^{2}-2t+2}{t+1},\,2{lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{(2t)},\,{lim}_{t\to 0}t\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{0}^{2}-2\cdot 0+2}{0+1},\,2\cdot 1,\,0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡0⟩ \\  & =⟨2,2,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Note that for the second component of ${lim}_{t\to 0}f(t)$ we used a special limit ${lim}_{u\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡u}{u}=1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}g(t) & =⟨{lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{{e}^{2t}-1}{t},\,{lim}_{t\to 0}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,{lim}_{t\to 0}(t+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨{lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{({e}^{2t}-1)^{′}}{(t)^{′}},\,{lim}_{t\to 0}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,{lim}_{t\to 0}(t+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨{lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{2{e}^{2t}}{1},\,{lim}_{t\to 0}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,{lim}_{t\to 0}(t+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{e}^{0},\,1-\operatorname{cos}⁡0,\,0+1⟩ \\  & =⟨2,0,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Note that for the first component of ${lim}_{t\to 0}g(t)$ we used L'Hopital's Rule.

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}[f(t)\cdot g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to 0}f(t)\cdot {lim}_{t\to 0}g(t) \\  & =⟨2,\,2,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨2,0,1⟩ \\  & =2\cdot 2+2\cdot 0+0\cdot 1 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-fa331f7b-2a1a-5cc2-9b0b-49206016e7e3"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-fa331f7b-2a1a-5cc2-9b0b-49206016e7e3" :answer-field/id #uuid "fa331f7b-2a1a-5cc2-9b0b-49206016e7e3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-dfc4555a-8d25-52bb-84f7-9a18b8237849" :answer-field/choices ["answer-0e7b3ee8-302c-5bb1-a016-50116576c2f2" "answer-7f679746-4683-54bf-906e-e3418d6fd20d" "answer-dfc4555a-8d25-52bb-84f7-9a18b8237849" "answer-a18cb561-1016-5b60-a141-a208ee290e53" "answer-9a621fae-e013-5531-ad51-a186fffabdb1"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0e7b3ee8-302c-5bb1-a016-50116576c2f2" :answer/id #uuid "0e7b3ee8-302c-5bb1-a016-50116576c2f2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7f679746-4683-54bf-906e-e3418d6fd20d" :answer/id #uuid "7f679746-4683-54bf-906e-e3418d6fd20d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-dfc4555a-8d25-52bb-84f7-9a18b8237849" :answer/id #uuid "dfc4555a-8d25-52bb-84f7-9a18b8237849" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a18cb561-1016-5b60-a141-a208ee290e53" :answer/id #uuid "a18cb561-1016-5b60-a141-a208ee290e53" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9a621fae-e013-5531-ad51-a186fffabdb1" :answer/id #uuid "9a621fae-e013-5531-ad51-a186fffabdb1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-e00ec48a-b851-58e1-a999-f80b28436a4f" :question/id #uuid "e00ec48a-b851-58e1-a999-f80b28436a4f" :question/math-academy-id "q-130317" :question/problem "Find the limit ${lim}_{t\to 0}[f(t)\cdot g(t)]$ given that $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)=[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{t} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{{t}^{2}+9}{t+3}\end{aligned}],\,g(t)=[\begin{aligned}t-2 \\ \frac{3t-2}{{t}^{2}-1} \\ {2}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}3{e}^{t} \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{{t}^{2}+9}{t+3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{0} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡0 \\ \frac{{0}^{2}+9}{0+3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}g(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}\,(t-2) \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{3t-2}{{t}^{2}-1} \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}{2}^{t}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0-2 \\ \frac{3(0)-2}{{0}^{2}-1} \\ {2}^{0}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 1+\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \frac{4t}{\pi }\end{aligned}],\,g(t)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 2+\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \pi }f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \pi }\,(\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\ {lim}_{t\to \pi }\,(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\ {lim}_{t\to \pi }\,(\frac{4t}{\pi })\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi  \\ 1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\ \frac{4\pi }{\pi }\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ {lim}_{t\to \pi }g(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \pi }\,(\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\ {lim}_{t\to \pi }\,(2+\operatorname{tan}⁡t) \\ {lim}_{t\to \pi }\,(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\ (2+\operatorname{tan}⁡\pi ) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \pi }[f(t)\cdot g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to \pi }f(t)\cdot {lim}_{t\to \pi }g(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =0\cdot (-1)+0\cdot 2+4\cdot (-1) \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186113520 :answer-field/correct 17592186113523 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186116437 :tutorial/content "To find the limit of a vector function, we compute the limit of each component individually. So, if $\mathbf f (t) = x(t) \ \mathbf {i} + y(t) \ \mathbf {j} +z(t) \ \mathbf {k}$ is our vector function, then the limit is computed as follows:

$$
\displaystyle \lim_{t\to a} \mathbf f (t) = \bigg[ \lim_{t \to a} x(t) \bigg] \mathbf {i} + \bigg[ \lim_{t \to a}y(t) \bigg] \mathbf {j} +\bigg[ \lim_{t \to a}z(t) \bigg] \mathbf {k}
$$

The limit on the left exists *if and only if* all the limits on the right exist too.

For example, suppose we are given the vector function

$$
\mathbf f (t) = \left( 5+t \right) \ \mathbf {i} +  (t^{2}-1) \ \mathbf {j} + \sin{t} \ \mathbf {k},
$$

and we want to compute the limit $\lim\limits_{t \to 0} \mathbf f (t).$ To do this, we find the limit of each component function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}f(t) & =[\,{{{lim}_{t\to 0}(5+t)}_{⏟}}_{=\,5}\,]i+[\,{{{lim}_{t\to 0}({t}^{2}-1)\,}_{⏟}}_{=\,-1}]j+[\,{{{lim}_{t\to 0}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,}_{⏟}}_{=\,0}]k \\  & =5\text{ }i+(-1)\text{ }j+0\text{ }k \\  & =⟨5,\,-1,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186116438 :tutorial/content "Many properties of limits of scalar functions extend naturally to limits of vector functions. For instance, if $\mathbf f(t)$ and $\mathbf g(t)$ are vector functions and $p,q$ are constants, then

$$
\lim_{t \to a}\left[p \ \mathbf f(t) + q \ \mathbf g(t)\right] =  p \ \lim_{t \to a}\mathbf f(t) + q \ \lim_{t \to a}\mathbf g(t).
$$

We also have the following property for the magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to a}‖f(t)‖ & =‖{lim}_{t\to a}f(t)‖,\end{aligned}
$$

where $\left\| \mathbf f(t) \right\|$ denotes the magnitude of the vector $\mathbf f(t)$." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186116439 :tutorial/content "For two vector functions, the limit of a product is equal to the product of the limits:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to a}[f(t)\cdot g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to a}f(t)\cdot {lim}_{t\to a}g(t) \\ {lim}_{t\to a}[f(t)\times g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to a}f(t)\times {lim}_{t\to a}g(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Here, $\mathbf f(t)\cdot \mathbf g(t)$ and $\mathbf f(t) \times \mathbf g(t)$ are the dot product and the cross product of $\mathbf f(t)$ and $\mathbf g(t),$ respectively." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115485 :activity/expected-seconds 840.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124437 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-4e141666-84d5-5edd-9a4e-a7cb3e788f33"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-4e141666-84d5-5edd-9a4e-a7cb3e788f33" :question/id #uuid "4e141666-84d5-5edd-9a4e-a7cb3e788f33" :question/math-academy-id "q-132581" :question/problem "A surface $S$ is defined by $z=f(x,y).$ The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $x=2.$ Given that the point $P$ with $y$-coordinate $\frac{\pi }{4}$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy-\frac{\pi }{3})$, find the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$" :question/worked-solution "The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point where $y=\frac{\pi }{4}$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(2,\frac{\pi }{4}).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(2,\frac{\pi }{4}):$

${f}_{x}=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-x\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$" :question/worked-solution "The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,\frac{\pi }{2})}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(1,\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,\frac{\pi }{2})} & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(1\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})-1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =2\cdot 1-1\cdot 0 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,\frac{\pi }{2})} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,\frac{\pi }{2})}(x-1) \\ z-0 & =2(x-1) \\ z & =2x-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=\frac{\pi }{2} \\ z=2x-2\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d2ed29c1-ef21-57a0-9839-78668465edfc"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "19ce6755-ce5c-5344-86b9-dca6271615dd" :question/math-academy-id "q-132608" :question/problem "The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=0.$ Given that the point $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=(y+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$" :question/worked-solution "The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=0.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(\frac{1}{2},0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(\frac{1}{2},0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(\frac{1}{2},0) & =(0+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2})+2(\frac{1}{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(\frac{1}{2},0) & ={f}_{x}(\frac{1}{2},0)(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =1(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =x-\frac{1}{2} \\ z & =x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=0 \\ z=x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=x+\frac{1}{2}$ (or $x-z+\frac{1}{2}=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $-i-k$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-(-i-k)=i+k$ is also parallel to it." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields :question/worked-solution "We can solve this equation by isolating the $(x+4)^{3}$ term and then taking the $3$rd root of each side.

First, let's isolate the $(x+4)^{3}$ term on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2(x+4)^{3} & =686 \\ (x+4)^{3} & =343\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we take the $3$rd root of each side and solve for $x.$ Since $n=3$ is odd, there is only one real solution to this equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+4)^{3} & =343 \\ \sqrt[3]{(x+4)^{3}} & =\sqrt[3]{343} \\ x+4 & =\sqrt[3]{{7}^{3}} \\ x+4 & =7 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=3.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179320 :answer-field/correct 17592186179321 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179681 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-ee997e26-088f-52b1-8913-d296b8992e92"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-ee997e26-088f-52b1-8913-d296b8992e92" :question/id #uuid "ee997e26-088f-52b1-8913-d296b8992e92" :question/math-academy-id "q-91348" :question/problem "Find the real solution to the equation ${x}^{7}=-\frac{1}{128}.$" :question/worked-solution "We can solve this equation by taking the $7$th root of each side and solving for $x.$ Since $n=7$ is odd, there is only one real solution to this equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{7} & =-\frac{1}{128} \\ \sqrt[7]{{x}^{7}} & =\sqrt[7]{(-\frac{1}{128})} \\ x & =\sqrt[7]{{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{7}} \\ x & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-\frac{1}{2}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-76b0b8d7-ead0-5e0b-96f7-c011cf47b3ce"] :db/ensure :question/problem "Find the real solution to the equation $(x-3)^{7}=-128.$" :question/worked-solution "We can solve this equation by taking the $7$th root of each side and solving for $x.$
Since $n=7$ is odd, there is only one real solution to this equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-3)^{7} & =-128 \\ \sqrt[7]{(x-3)^{7}} & =\sqrt[7]{-128} \\ x-3 & =\sqrt[7]{(-2)^{7}} \\ x-3 & =-2 \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=1.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8dda18e4-efa2-53cb-b386-72e8b9f7b0ad"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} "a95ee677-1642-5975-8b50-8432d56de160" :question/math-academy-id "q-97770" :question/problem "$\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-4x}}\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}-4x & =-({x}^{2}+4x) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}) \\  & =-((x+2)^{2}-4) \\  & =4-(x+2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-4x}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{4-(x+2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{2(x+2)\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x+2}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x+2}{2})\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x+2}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\frac{x+2}{2}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-4x}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x+2}{2})\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x+2}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(\frac{x+2}{2})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0526b46b-564d-561d-a9aa-fedc41539160"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "$\int \frac{3}{(x+3)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-6x}}\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}-6x & =-({x}^{2}+6x) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}) \\  & =-((x+3)^{2}-9) \\  & =9-(x+3)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{(x+3)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-6x}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{3}{(x+3)\sqrt{9-{(x+3)}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x+3}{3})\sqrt{9-9{(\frac{x+3}{3})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x+3}{3})\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x+3}{3})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\frac{x+3}{3}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{(x+3)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-6x}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x+3}{3})\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x+3}{3})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot 3\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡(\frac{x+3}{3})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a1d9e3fb-7750-5a4b-a417-c4a5e9cfd326"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "$\int \frac{\sqrt{2}}{|x-5|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-10x+27}}\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-10x+27 & ={x}^{2}-2\cdot 5x+{5}^{2}-{5}^{2}+27 \\  & =(x-5)^{2}+2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\sqrt{2}}{|x-5|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-10x+27}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{\sqrt{2}}{|x-5|\sqrt{2+(x-5)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{2}}|\sqrt{2+2{(\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{2}}|\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{2}}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{2}}|\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{2}})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0b36eef3-f0c2-5b45-97f7-a2607c73a159"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id \frac{1}{16-(3x+2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that

$$
\int \frac{1}{16-(3x+2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{16-16(\frac{1}{16}(3x+2)^{2})}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{16}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{4}(3x+2))}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{4}(3x+2).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3}{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{4}{3}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{16}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{4}(3x+2))}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{16}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\cdot \frac{4}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{3x+2}{4})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{3x+2}{4}|>1.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4fbff315-ecc9-5c1a-aaa6-d1781060ca7f"] "$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-2x(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].$*" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8ea9a430-3071-50b8-b617-7ec74f7a4ddc"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}].$*

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-1)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-1)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-1)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-1))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-1))\, \\ \,3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-1))\,\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0f7c85fb-7d21-5d48-8f24-4c37d6bc47ea" "answer-field-9ff392b1-754b-5f5c-ad8a-af1f4c91dfa9"] :db/ensure So, we can just plot the exponential function and reflect it over the line $y=x.$

For example, suppose that we wish to plot the graph of 

$$
y=\log_2 x.
$$

The corresponding inverse function is $y=2^x,$ and since $y=2^x$ is a one-to-one function defined for all real $x,$ we can obtain the graph of $y=\log_2{x}$ by reflecting $y=2^x$ over the line $y=x.$ The result is shown below:

![](images/0c/0c614201798324262429f080d8e8a31bfefe58c4008bfe82e6da1b91dc158b7a.png)

Here are some key points to note about $y=\log_2(x)\mathbin{:}$

- The domain is $x>0$, and the range is $-\infty <   y <   \infty.$

- The graph has the vertical asymptote $x=0.$

- The function is an increasing function.

- The graph passes through the point $(1,0).$

- For $x>1$, the graph is positive and grows very slowly as we increase $x.$ We say that $y\rightarrow \infty$ (slowly) as $x\rightarrow \infty.$

In general, for any base $n>1,$ the graph of $y=\log_n{x}$ always has the same shape, and all of the above points are valid. We can verify that this is true by inspecting some possible graphs shown below:

![](images/91/91567f282acbc3b8390da1e4147b445018ae649d913205e59867d58ea980ff7b.png)

**Note:** The important points covered above also apply to two familiar logarithms.

- $y = \ln x = \log_e x$ is the natural logarithm. Since the base is $n=e>1,$ all of the important points covered above apply.

- $y = \log x = \log_{10} x$ is the logarithm with base $10.$ Since the base is $n=10>1,$ all the important points covered above apply." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110877 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054604 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d591e3b7-0993-5fb9-b7f0-ff97c33bf559" "question-2b9acb7e-8235-5df0-907d-863119079541"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-d591e3b7-0993-5fb9-b7f0-ff97c33bf559" :question/id #uuid "d591e3b7-0993-5fb9-b7f0-ff97c33bf559" :question/math-academy-id "q-100250" :question/problem "Find ${lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{3x}{\sqrt[3]{2{x}^{4}-5}}.$" :question/worked-solution "Applying the quotient rule, we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{3x}{\sqrt[3]{2{x}^{4}-5}}=\frac{{lim}_{x\to 2}3x}{{lim}_{x\to 2}\sqrt[3]{2{x}^{4}-5}}
$$

We calculate the limits of the numerator and denominator, separately.

For the numerator, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}3x & =3{lim}_{x\to 2}x \\  & =3\cdot 2 \\  & =6\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the root rule in the denominator, we have
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\sqrt[3]{2{x}^{4}-5} & =\sqrt[3]{{lim}_{x\to 2}(2{x}^{4}-5)} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{2(2)^{4}-5)} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{27} \\  & =3\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{3x}{\sqrt[3]{2{x}^{4}-5}} & =\frac{6}{3}=2\,.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ddff0f96-aeb7-5490-8d56-4c8b9d0de231"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id If the figure above shows the graph of the function $f(x),$ then

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "From the graph, we get that ${lim}_{x\to \,2}f(x)=3.$

From the product rule, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,2}(x-1)^{2}\,(f(x)-2)^{3}={lim}_{x\to \,2}(x-1)^{2}\cdot {lim}_{x\to \,2}(f(x)-2)^{3}.
$$

We calculate the limits of each factor, separately.

Applying the power rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,2}(x-1)^{2} & ={({lim}_{x\to \,2}(x-1))}^{2} \\  & =(2-1)^{2} \\  & ={1}^{2} \\  & =1\,,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,2}(f(x)-2)^{3} & ={({lim}_{x\to \,2}(f(x)-2))}^{3} \\  & =(3-2)^{3} \\  & ={1}^{3} \\  & =1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,2}(x-1)^{2}\,(f(x)-2)^{3} & =(1)\cdot (1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-817fc64f-fe17-5ab1-8ab5-8f8ebfd722a2"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-817fc64f-fe17-5ab1-8ab5-8f8ebfd722a2" :answer-field/id #uuid "817fc64f-fe17-5ab1-8ab5-8f8ebfd722a2" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-066cb984-e17a-5fea-af4c-48188475d862" :answer-field/choices ["answer-066cb984-e17a-5fea-af4c-48188475d862"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-066cb984-e17a-5fea-af4c-48188475d862" :answer/id #uuid "066cb984-e17a-5fea-af4c-48188475d862" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-2b9acb7e-8235-5df0-907d-863119079541" :question/id #uuid "2b9acb7e-8235-5df0-907d-863119079541" :question/math-academy-id "q-338390" :question/problem "Find the **exact** value of the limit.

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-32d33a71-45d3-5a70-b6f2-f587f0b3ec0b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id
