$$
\begin{aligned}3\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{27}+3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}-\sqrt{{x}^{5}} & = \\ 3\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{9\cdot 3}+3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}-\sqrt{{x}^{4}\cdot x} & = \\ 3\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{9}\cdot \sqrt{3}+3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}-\sqrt{{x}^{4}}\cdot \sqrt{x} & = \\ 3\sqrt{3}-3\sqrt{3}+3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}-{x}^{2}\sqrt{x} & \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we combine the like terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\sqrt{3}-3\sqrt{3}+3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}-{x}^{2}\sqrt{x} & = \\ (3-3)\sqrt{3}+3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}-{x}^{2}\sqrt{x} & = \\ 0\cdot \sqrt{3}+3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}-{x}^{2}\sqrt{x} & = \\ 3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}-{x}^{2}\sqrt{x} & \end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c61d8497-db30-5312-b6cc-cc9f8eeed283"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id terms using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x\sqrt{54}+2x\sqrt{x}-5x\sqrt{6} & = \\ 2x\sqrt{9\cdot 6}+2x\sqrt{x}-5x\sqrt{6} & = \\ 2x\sqrt{9}\cdot \sqrt{6}+2x\sqrt{x}-5x\sqrt{6} & = \\ 2x\cdot 3\cdot \sqrt{6}+2x\sqrt{x}-5x\sqrt{6} & = \\ 6x\sqrt{6}+2x\sqrt{x}-5x\sqrt{6} & \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we combine the like terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}6x\sqrt{6}+2x\sqrt{x}-5x\sqrt{6} & = \\ (6x-5x)\sqrt{6}+2x\sqrt{x} & = \\ x\sqrt{6}+2x\sqrt{x}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2edd54bc-8785-50e5-9005-f3528fdfbcbc"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Find the cosine of $∠Y.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall the definition of cosine: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡Y=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{XY}{YZ}=\frac{XY}{5}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $XY.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}XY & =\sqrt{Y{Z}^{2}-X{Z}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}-(\sqrt{7})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25-7} \\  & =\sqrt{18} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡Y & =\frac{XY}{5}=\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186075298 :answer-field/correct 17592186075301 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-b2b55850-322e-5b17-9a94-b2696bd083f6" :question/id #uuid "b2b55850-322e-5b17-9a94-b2696bd083f6" :question/math-academy-id "q-122050" :question/problem "In the right triangle $△JKL,$ $∠J$ is a right angle, $JL=8$ and $KL=12.$ Find $\operatorname{tan}⁡K.$" :question/worked-solution "The following triangle illustrates the information given.

![](images/cc/cc33327cc6d071cb6ec9ac0c10d58e57bc35f8d81b326731120cf04c18f58ec1.png)

Recall the definition of tangent: 

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡K=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}=\frac{JL}{JK}=\frac{8}{JK}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $JK.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}JK & =\sqrt{K{L}^{2}-J{L}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{12}^{2}-{8}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{144-64} \\  & =\sqrt{80} \\  & =4\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡K & =\frac{8}{4\sqrt{5}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f15bdbe8-d486-594d-b02d-d29460c4afc4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Find the tangent of $∠P.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall the definition of tangent: 

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡P=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}=\frac{QR}{PQ}=\frac{QR}{3.5}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing length $QR.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}QR & =\sqrt{P{R}^{2}-P{Q}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{12.5}^{2}-{3.5}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{156.25-12.25} \\  & =\sqrt{144} \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡P & =\frac{QR}{3.5} \\  & =\frac{12}{3.5} \\  & =\frac{120}{35} \\  & =\frac{24}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-518b1e5c-6389-594b-b333-90ba109eabdc"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id t+3\end{aligned}]$  is continuous." :question/worked-solution "A vector-valued function is continuous on an interval if and only if each of its components is continuous on that interval.

Let's now consider the components of $f(t)$ one by one.

- The function $\frac{1}{{t}^{2}-1}$ is continuous everywhere except the excluded points $t=\pm 1.$

- The function $\sqrt{t}$ is continuous for $t\ge 0.$

- The function $t+3$ is continuous for all real numbers.

Therefore, the vector-valued function $f(t)$ is continuous for all $t\ge 0$ except the point $t=1.$ So the interval of continuity is $[0,1)\cup (1,\infty ).$" :question/difficulty "Determine the interval on which the function $f(t)=\frac{{t}^{2}+4t}{t}\,i+({t}^{2}-1)\,j+\frac{1}{t-2}\,k$ is continuous." :question/worked-solution "A vector-valued function is continuous on an interval if and only if each of its components is continuous on that interval.

Let's now consider the components of $f(t)$ one-by-one.

- The function $\frac{{t}^{2}+4t}{t}$ is continuous everywhere except the excluded point $t=0.$

- The function ${t}^{2}-1$ is continuous for all real numbers.

- The function $\frac{1}{t-2}$ is continuous everywhere except the point $t=2.$

Therefore, the vector-valued function $f(t)$ is continuous everywhere except the points $t=0$ and $t=2.$ So the interval of continuity is $(-\infty ,0)\cup (0,2)\cup (2,\infty ).$" "question-48e5a226-dec1-538c-a739-b2da6b892931" :question/id #uuid "48e5a226-dec1-538c-a739-b2da6b892931" :question/math-academy-id "q-127807" :question/problem "Which of the following vector-valued $$
\begin{aligned}p(s) & =|{s}^{2}-1|\,i+\frac{s+1}{s}\,j+2{s}^{2}\,k \\ q(s) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(s-1)\,i+({s}^{2}+1)\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡s\,k \\ r(s) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡s\,i-2\operatorname{tan}⁡s\,j+\operatorname{csc}⁡s\,k\end{aligned}

its second component, $\frac{s+1}{s},$ is undefined at $s=0$ and hence discontinuous on $[-1,1].$

- The function $q(s)$ is **not** continuous on $[-1,1]$ because 
its first component, $\operatorname{ln}⁡(s-1)$, is undefined at $s=1$ and hence discontinuous on $[-1,1].$

- The function $r(s)$ is **not** continuous on $[-1,1]$ because 
its third component, $\operatorname{csc}⁡s$, is undefined at $s=0$ and hence discontinuous on $[-1,1].$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the functions are continuous on $[-1,1].$"" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e733f8a2-e030-5a6d-ae1a-9d5ff92e104f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-e733f8a2-e030-5a6d-ae1a-9d5ff92e104f" :answer-field/id #uuid "e733f8a2-e030-5a6d-ae1a-9d5ff92e104f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-897e666e-5017-5c68-b94e-f2a61cddac86" :answer-field/choices ["answer-98a35e8c-50cb-52af-93af-e4c92463935b" "answer-8d44025a-769b-53ed-8380-a28de619549a" "answer-5f216b60-e388-51f5-ba21-e8378f9d2558" "answer-ea628c3b-5f80-5519-9722-358822a7671c" "answer-897e666e-5017-5c68-b94e-f2a61cddac86"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-98a35e8c-50cb-52af-93af-e4c92463935b" :answer/id #uuid "98a35e8c-50cb-52af-93af-e4c92463935b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "r(s)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8d44025a-769b-53ed-8380-a28de619549a" :answer/id #uuid "8d44025a-769b-53ed-8380-a28de619549a" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$p(s)$  and $q(s)$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5f216b60-e388-51f5-ba21-e8378f9d2558" :answer/id #uuid "5f216b60-e388-51f5-ba21-e8378f9d2558" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$p(s)$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ea628c3b-5f80-5519-9722-358822a7671c" :answer/id #uuid "ea628c3b-5f80-5519-9722-358822a7671c" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$q(s)$ only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-897e666e-5017-5c68-b94e-f2a61cddac86" :answer/id #uuid "897e666e-5017-5c68-b94e-f2a61cddac86" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "None of the functions are continuous on $[-1,1]$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115761 :question/problem "Which of the following vector-valued functions are continuous at $t=0?$

$$
{lim}_{t\to 5}[f(t)+3g(t)]=⟨1,3,1⟩\,.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Using the  addition rule for limits, and the fact that both functions are continuous, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 5}[f(t)+3g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to 5}f(t)+{lim}_{t\to 5}[3g(t)] \\  & ={lim}_{t\to 5}f(t)+3{lim}_{t\to 5}g(t) \\  & =f(5)+3g(5) \\  & =f(5)+3{{⟨-1,1,-2⟩}_{⏟}}_{g(5)} \\  & =f(5)+⟨-3,3,-6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, we are told that

$$
{lim}_{t\to 5}[f(t)+3g(t)]=⟨1,3,1⟩.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 5}[f(t)+3g(t)] & =⟨1,3,1⟩ \\ f(5)+⟨-3,3,-6⟩ & =⟨1,3,1⟩ \\ f(5) & =⟨1,3,1⟩-⟨-3,3,-6⟩ \\ f(5) & =⟨4,0,7⟩\end{aligned}

"question-5dae5e77-95b3-5116-bdbb-e15146f075a1" :question/id #uuid "5dae5e77-95b3-5116-bdbb-e15146f075a1" :question/math-academy-id "q-71006" :question/problem "Find $f(0)$ given that $f(t)$ is a continuous vector-valued function and $u(t)$ is continuous real-valued function for which $u(0)=3$ and 

$$
{lim}_{t\to 0}[u(t)f(t)]=⟨-18,-21,6⟩\,.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Using the scalar function multiple rule for limits, and the fact that both functions are continuous, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}[u(t)f(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to 0}u(t)\cdot {lim}_{t\to 0}f(t) \\  & =u(0)f(0) \\  & =3f(0)\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, we are told that

$$
{lim}_{t\to 0}[u(t)f(t)]=⟨-18,-21,6⟩\,.
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following equation which we can solve for $f(0):$

:question/problem "Which of the following vector-valued functions are differentiable with respect to $t$ on $t\in (\pi ,2\pi )?$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =⟨{sin}^{2}⁡t,\,\frac{1}{t},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ g(t) & =⟨t\sqrt{t},\,1-{t}^{2},\,t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩ \\ h(t) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,2t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "All of these vector-valued functions are defined for all  $t\in (\pi ,2\pi ).$ 

A function is differentiable on the interval $(\pi ,2\pi )$ if and only if each of its component functions is differentiable on that interval. 

Let's now consider the functions one-by-one.

- We differentiate $f(t)$ to find ${f}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({sin}^{2}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since each component of ${f}^{′}(t)$ is defined for all  $t\in (\pi ,2\pi )$, we conclude that $f(t)$ is differentiable on this interval.

- Next, we differentiate $g(t)$ to find ${g}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\sqrt{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3/2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2}{t}^{1/2},\,-2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{t},\,-2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since each component of  ${g}^{′}(t)$ is defined for all  $t\in (\pi ,2\pi )$, we have that $g(t)$ is differentiable on this interval.

- Finally, we differentiate $h(t)$ to find ${h}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,2,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since each component of  ${h}^{′}(t)$ is defined for all $t\in (\pi ,2\pi )$, we conclude that $h(t)$ is differentiable on this interval.

Therefore, the answer is: 

$\,$ All the functions are differentiable on $(\pi ,2\pi ).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-24c4782e-d988-5b6a-b328-68cc3dd0adb4"] :db/ensure :answer.type/math :answer/value "[1,\infty )" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115771 :question/problem "Which of the following vector-valued functions are differentiable with respect to $t$ on $t\in (0,1)?$

$$
\begin{aligned}p(t) & =⟨2t-1,\,{t}^{2}+4,\,-{e}^{t}⟩ \\ q(t) & =⟨(t+1)^{4},\,\sqrt[3]{t},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡t⟩ \\ r(t) & =⟨3t+2,\,\operatorname{arctan}⁡t,\,{t}^{2}-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "All of these vector-valued functions are defined on $t\in (0,1).$ 

A function is differentiable on the interval $t\in (0,1)$ if and only if each component is differentiable on that interval.

Let's now consider the functions one-by-one.

- We differentiate $p(t)$ to find ${p}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{p}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+4),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{e}^{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,2t,\,-{e}^{t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since each component of ${p}^{′}(t)$ is defined on $t\in (0,1)$, we conclude that $p(t)$ is differentiable on this interval.

- Next, we differentiate $q(t)$ to find ${q}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}((t+1)^{4}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt[3]{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨4(t+1)^{3},\,\frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{t}^{2}}},\,\frac{1}{t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since each component of ${q}^{′}(t)$ is defined on $t\in (0,1)$, we have that $q(t)$ is differentiable on this interval.

- Finally, we differentiate $r(t)$ to find ${r}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+2),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-2)⟩ \\  & =⟨3,\,\frac{1}{1+{t}^{2}},\,2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since each component of ${r}^{′}(t)$ is defined on $t\in (0,1)$, we conclude that $r(t)$ is differentiable on this interval.

Therefore, the answer is:

$\,$ All the functions are differentiable on $(0,1).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186113592 :answer-field/correct "answer-9f0eae6e-708e-5574-aa53-37eb5b37b2c4" :answer-field/choices ["answer-9f0eae6e-708e-5574-aa53-37eb5b37b2c4" "answer-2bc1a731-b484-519e-93a3-569ae5979606"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9f0eae6e-708e-5574-aa53-37eb5b37b2c4" :answer/id #uuid "9f0eae6e-708e-5574-aa53-37eb5b37b2c4" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "All the functions are differentiable on $t\in (0,1)$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2bc1a731-b484-519e-93a3-569ae5979606" :answer/id #uuid "2bc1a731-b484-519e-93a3-569ae5979606" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "None of the functions are differentiable on $t\in (0,1)$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-cff5ef5d-ae0d-5005-af50-0efa2caca50a" :question/id #uuid "cff5ef5d-ae0d-5005-af50-0efa2caca50a" :question/math-academy-id "q-71094" :question/problem "Find the interval where the function $f(t)=u(t)g(t)$ is differentiable, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =|t-1|\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+\sqrt{1-t}\,k \\ g(t) & ={t}^{2}\,i+\sqrt{{t}^{2}-9}\,j+\operatorname{ln}⁡(3-t)\,k\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "The function $F(t)=f(t)\times g(t)$ is differentiable over the common domain where both $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are differentiable. A function is differentiable if and only if each component is differentiable.

Let's now find the intervals where each of the functions $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are differentiable.

For the function $f(t):$ 

- The first component $|t-1|$ is differentiable over $(-\infty ,1)\cup (1,\infty )$, as its derivative is not defined at $t=1.$

- The second component $\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is differentiable for all values of $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

- The third component $\sqrt{1-t}$ is differentiable on $(-\infty ,1)$, as its derivative is not defined at $t=1$ and the function is not defined for $t>1.$

The intersection of the domains of all three components of $f(t)$ is $(-\infty ,1).$ 

For the function $g(t):$ 

- The first component ${t}^{2}$ is differentiable for all values of $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

- The second component $\sqrt{{t}^{2}-9}$ is differentiable for $(-\infty ,-3)\cup (3,\infty ).$

- The third component $\operatorname{ln}⁡(3-t)$ is differentiable only on $(-\infty ,3).$

The intersection of the domains of all three components of $g(t)$ is $(-\infty ,-3).$ 

Finally, the common domain of differentiability for both functions is $(-\infty ,1)\cap (-\infty ,-3)=(-\infty ,-3).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186113767 :answer-field/correct "answer-9f18fad1-1cd0-5b00-bdc0-9f0c14dfa40b" :answer-field/choices ["answer-aa5c267b-63e8-5dd0-bb3a-f4eac717c321" "answer-9f18fad1-1cd0-5b00-bdc0-9f0c14dfa40b" "answer-eafc1913-afb8-5c4d-969b-a557a69f332f" "answer-c838c1be-6f79-573c-844f-4ea6d6563720"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-aa5c267b-63e8-5dd0-bb3a-f4eac717c321" :answer/id #uuid "aa5c267b-63e8-5dd0-bb3a-f4eac717c321" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(-3,3)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9f18fad1-1cd0-5b00-bdc0-9f0c14dfa40b" :answer/id #uuid "9f18fad1-1cd0-5b00-bdc0-9f0c14dfa40b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(-\infty ,-3)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-eafc1913-afb8-5c4d-969b-a557a69f332f" :answer/id #uuid "eafc1913-afb8-5c4d-969b-a557a69f332f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(-\infty ,3)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c838c1be-6f79-573c-844f-4ea6d6563720" :answer/id #uuid "c838c1be-6f79-573c-844f-4ea6d6563720" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(3,\infty )" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186116443 :tutorial/content "Determining the continuity of a vector function is very similar to determining the continuity of a scalar function.  A vector function $\mathbf f (t)$ is **continuous** at a point $t_0$ (in its domain) if

$$
\displaystyle \lim_{t \rightarrow t_0} \mathbf f (t) = \mathbf f (t_0).
$$

For example, the vector function 

$$
\mathbf f(t) = \left \langle e^t,  \dfrac{1}{t} \right \rangle
$$

is continuous at $t=1$ because

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}f(t) & =⟨{lim}_{t\to 1}({e}^{t}),\,{lim}_{t\to 1}(\frac{1}{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{1},\,\frac{1}{1}⟩ \\  & =⟨e,\,1⟩ \\  & =f(1)\end{aligned}
$$

Since the limit of a vector function is determined by the limits of the components, a vector function is continuous at a point $t_0$ *if and only if* each of its components is continuous at that point.

We say that a vector function is **continuous on the interval** $t\in[a,b]$ if it is continuous at every point of this interval." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186116444 :tutorial/content "Similar to scalar-valued functions, the vector function $\mathbf{f}(t)$ is **differentiable** at a point $t = t_0$ in the domain of the function if the following limit exists:

$$
\lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{\mathbf{f}(t_0+h) - \mathbf{f}(t_0)}{h}
$$

The value of the limit is then called the **derivative** of $\mathbf{f}(t)$ at $t = t_0$ and is denoted as $\mathbf{f}'(t_0)$. In general, a vector function is differentiable *if and only if* all of its components are differentiable.

For example, is the following vector function $\mathbf{g}(t)$ differentiable at $t=0$?

$$
\mathbf{g}(t) = \big\langle t, \: |\,t\,|, \: \sin t \big\rangle
$$

Notice that the second component, $|\,t\,|,$ is not differentiable at $t=0.$ Since one of the component functions is not differentiable at $t=0,$ we conclude that the overall vector function $\mathbf{g}(t)$ is not differentiable at $t=0.$ 

We say that a vector function is **differentiable on an open interval** $t \in (a,b)$ if it is differentiable at *every* point $t \in (a,b).$ This means that each component of the function must be differentiable at every point of $(a,b).$

Our function $\mathbf{g}(t)$, mentioned above, is differentiable on $(-\infty, 0) \cup (0, \infty)$ since all of its components are differentiable there.

Finally, a function is said to be **continuously differentiable** if it is differentiable and its derivative is continuous." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115484 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115282 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-a981d1c6-7401-5c05-a9ed-dfe4b1119a94"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115105 :question/problem "Plot the curve of $y=\log_7 (x+4).$" :question/worked-solution "To plot $y=\log_7 {(x+4)},$ we apply the following steps:

![](images/36/3698fc49edb443517ed0ee2cfa81c586c428f402df7028a8ec4b47702d8a4fad.png)" :question/worked-solution "Clearly, $b \neq 0.$ Substituting $x=\dfrac1b$ into the equation of the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =k{log}_{5}⁡(b\cdot \frac{1}{b}) \\  & =k{log}_{5}⁡1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the point $\left(\dfrac1b, 0\right)$ lies on the curve. But from the diagram, we know that $(2,0)$ lies on the curve. Hence, 

$$
(2,0)  = \left(\dfrac1b,0\right)\quad\Rightarrow\quad b=\dfrac12.
$$

Now, we substitute coordinates of the point $(10,3)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}k{log}_{5}⁡(bx) & =y \\ k{log}_{5}⁡(\frac{1}{2}x) & =y \\ k{log}_{5}⁡(\frac{1}{2}\cdot 10) & =3 \\ k{log}_{5}⁡5 & =3 \\ k & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
b\cdot k = \dfrac12 \cdot 3 = \dfrac32.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-a981d1c6-7401-5c05-a9ed-dfe4b1119a94" :question/id #uuid "a981d1c6-7401-5c05-a9ed-dfe4b1119a94" :question/math-academy-id "q-28248" :question/problem "Which of the following is the graph of $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-4)?$" :question/worked-solution "To plot $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-4),$ we apply the following steps:

The diagram above shows the graph of $y=k{log}_{2}⁡(bx).$ Find the value of $k\cdot b.$" :question/worked-solution "Clearly, $b\ne 0.$ Substituting $x=\frac{1}{b}$ into the equation of the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =k{log}_{2}⁡(b\cdot \frac{1}{b}) \\  & =k{log}_{2}⁡1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the point $(\frac{1}{b},0)$ lies on the curve. But from the diagram, we know that $(3,0)$ lies on the curve. Hence

$$
(3,0)=(\frac{1}{b},0)\,⇒\,b=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Now, we substitute coordinates of the point $(6,2)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}k{log}_{2}⁡(bx) & =y \\ k{log}_{2}⁡(\frac{1}{3}x) & =y \\ k{log}_{2}⁡(\frac{1}{3}\cdot 6) & =2 \\ k{log}_{2}⁡2 & =2 \\ k & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
k\cdot b=2\cdot \frac{1}{3}=\frac{2}{3}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-27ae073a-5203-5077-b949-ae499f36c0ca"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-27ae073a-5203-5077-b949-ae499f36c0ca" :answer-field/id #uuid "27ae073a-5203-5077-b949-ae499f36c0ca" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-c139792e-bada-5b41-886d-9250900c5b59" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ac31a6ee-2e8d-52cd-b56a-12f4039e5b52" "answer-ab9acb21-3d7e-5418-97ba-19ff056536c8" "answer-75c99027-a990-59e8-84c8-d409c6f5f2c8" "answer-c139792e-bada-5b41-886d-9250900c5b59" "answer-8a753746-656b-5851-961e-7895d0368ce1"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ac31a6ee-2e8d-52cd-b56a-12f4039e5b52" :answer/id #uuid "ac31a6ee-2e8d-52cd-b56a-12f4039e5b52" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ab9acb21-3d7e-5418-97ba-19ff056536c8" :answer/id #uuid "ab9acb21-3d7e-5418-97ba-19ff056536c8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{1}{6}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-75c99027-a990-59e8-84c8-d409c6f5f2c8" :answer/id #uuid "75c99027-a990-59e8-84c8-d409c6f5f2c8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c139792e-bada-5b41-886d-9250900c5b59" :answer/id #uuid "c139792e-bada-5b41-886d-9250900c5b59" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8a753746-656b-5851-961e-7895d0368ce1" :answer/id #uuid "8a753746-656b-5851-961e-7895d0368ce1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-7ee0988d-03dd-5330-89a0-142478096881" :question/id #uuid "7ee0988d-03dd-5330-89a0-142478096881" :question/math-academy-id "q-33465" :question/problem "![](images/0c/0c09cf7f047cb341d3e2e2337ac41847d9cf5ff9435d075414a7db092aec3be2.png)

The diagram above shows the graph of $y={log}_{4}⁡(x-d)+c.$ Find the value of $\frac{d}{c}.$" :question/worked-solution "In the given graph, the vertical asymptote is $x=4.$ So, the argument of the logarithm function should evaluate to zero at $x=4.$ Therefore,

$$
4-d=0\,⇒\,d=4.
$$

Now, we substitute coordinates of the point $(8,3)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{4}⁡(x-d)+c & =y \\ {log}_{4}⁡(x-4)+c & =y \\ {log}_{4}⁡(8-4)+c & =3 \\ {log}_{4}⁡(4)+c & =3 \\ 1+c & =3 \\ c & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\frac{d}{c}=\frac{4}{2}=2.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d0661678-c752-58dd-ae45-19a8a3ab5f43"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d0661678-c752-58dd-ae45-19a8a3ab5f43" :answer-field/id #uuid "d0661678-c752-58dd-ae45-19a8a3ab5f43" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-d728cb75-8aff-5441-a02b-d2123ed28dfa" :answer-field/choices ["answer-3fb69761-90da-5ef3-9336-c74c1cd1883c" "answer-3035fbac-63b9-5e92-a7af-7fae4221c58d" "answer-d728cb75-8aff-5441-a02b-d2123ed28dfa" "answer-1059a7c8-9a04-5280-9f29-30f8d8a20897" "answer-e7761c70-8716-56c9-a2cb-a35290fdff3f"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3fb69761-90da-5ef3-9336-c74c1cd1883c" :answer/id #uuid "3fb69761-90da-5ef3-9336-c74c1cd1883c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3035fbac-63b9-5e92-a7af-7fae4221c58d" :answer/id #uuid "3035fbac-63b9-5e92-a7af-7fae4221c58d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d728cb75-8aff-5441-a02b-d2123ed28dfa" :answer/id #uuid "d728cb75-8aff-5441-a02b-d2123ed28dfa" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1059a7c8-9a04-5280-9f29-30f8d8a20897" :answer/id #uuid "1059a7c8-9a04-5280-9f29-30f8d8a20897" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e7761c70-8716-56c9-a2cb-a35290fdff3f" :answer/id #uuid "e7761c70-8716-56c9-a2cb-a35290fdff3f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{4}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186116516 :tutorial/content "Suppose we are given the function

$$
y=5\log_6(x-2).
$$

How do we plot its graph?

As usual, we can do this by combining transformations of the curve $y=\log_6 x.$

- We start with the graph of $y=\log_6 x{:}$

![](images/a8/a85eb96e169e43568da76e33ee7f997af9196d26e867d7e7db1b2ddea0725d2a.png)

- Translate it by $2$ units to the right to get the graph of $y=\log_6{(x-2)}.$

![](images/24/248a60c13ac422aeace5ba19f9f25716b188c19dbe04f5970287c587adb44c85.png)

Notice that points $(1,0)$ and $(6,1)$ on the graph of $y=\log_6 x$ map to the points $(3,0)$ and $(8,1)$ on the graph of $y=\log_6 (x-2),$ respectively.

- Then, stretch the result by a scale factor of $5$ parallel to the $y$-axis to get the graph of $y=5\log_6{(x-2)}.$

![](images/a6/a67b409068f67d81f0217aaeb30f76bd63c6501376d2adc567db7c4f319d7144.png)

So, to plot the curve of a transformed logarithmic function, we apply subsequent transformations presented in the given function, as usual." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115461 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186119808 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-c391d9c3-0c76-5e6f-b0c3-d6b4ee2c37cb" "question-a8427e64-b547-5ecb-a62e-824aa188b632" "question-ddfb229d-f01d-542c-8a6c-f2e9a5996154"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-c391d9c3-0c76-5e6f-b0c3-d6b4ee2c37cb" :question/id #uuid "c391d9c3-0c76-5e6f-b0c3-d6b4ee2c37cb" :question/math-academy-id "q-105199" :question/problem "The vectors ${a}_{1}$, ${a}_{2}$, and $b$ are given below. Determine if $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$ from the decomposition $b={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}.$

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 8\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "We know that $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ if there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} & =b \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=3 \\ 2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=8\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=3 \\ {x}_{2}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the system has a solution, we can conclude that $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}.$

Moreover, there is exactly one solution, so we have exactly one way to write $b$ as a linear combination of ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3{a}_{1}+2{a}_{2} & =b \\ 3\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+2\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Determine if $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$ from the decomposition $b={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}.$

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ -7\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "We know that $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ if there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} & =b \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ -7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=2 \\ 2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0 \\ -3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-7\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & -7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 & -4 \\ -3 & 1 & -7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=2 \\ {x}_{2}=-1 \\ 0=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the system has a solution, we can conclude that $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}.$

Moreover, there is exactly one solution, so we have exactly one way to write $b$ as a linear combination of ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{a}_{1}+(-1){a}_{2} & =b \\ 2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+(-1)\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=2\cdot (-1)=-2.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-283164aa-73de-5dcd-8a69-e6c9e6374abc"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-283164aa-73de-5dcd-8a69-e6c9e6374abc" :answer-field/id #uuid "283164aa-73de-5dcd-8a69-e6c9e6374abc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-35881d2a-16d1-5e15-a12f-b325e9f8db16" :answer-field/choices ["answer-4d4a40a4-8887-524e-8b48-8a24128d12fd" "answer-35881d2a-16d1-5e15-a12f-b325e9f8db16" "answer-d639618d-a932-5b03-8225-fae8a0b21ef5" "answer-32966283-95f9-59c0-9da8-620246a44c9f" "answer-1e4a4287-0b4e-5134-b26d-e720107fbfce"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4d4a40a4-8887-524e-8b48-8a24128d12fd" :answer/id #uuid "4d4a40a4-8887-524e-8b48-8a24128d12fd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-35881d2a-16d1-5e15-a12f-b325e9f8db16" :answer/id #uuid "35881d2a-16d1-5e15-a12f-b325e9f8db16" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d639618d-a932-5b03-8225-fae8a0b21ef5" :answer/id #uuid "d639618d-a932-5b03-8225-fae8a0b21ef5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-32966283-95f9-59c0-9da8-620246a44c9f" :answer/id #uuid "32966283-95f9-59c0-9da8-620246a44c9f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1e4a4287-0b4e-5134-b26d-e720107fbfce" :answer/id #uuid "1e4a4287-0b4e-5134-b26d-e720107fbfce" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "b\notin \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-ddfb229d-f01d-542c-8a6c-f2e9a5996154" :question/id #uuid "ddfb229d-f01d-542c-8a6c-f2e9a5996154" :question/math-academy-id "q-34639" :question/problem "The vectors ${a}_{1}$, ${a}_{2}$, ${a}_{3}$, and $b$ are given below. Determine if $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}\cdot {x}_{3}$ from the decomposition $b={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}.$

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -8 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 18 \\ 9\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "We know that $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ if there exist ${x}_{1}$, ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3} & =b \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -8 \\ -3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 18 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{3}=3 \\ 4{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3}=18 \\ 2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{3}=9\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 4 & 1 & -8 & 18 \\ 2 & 0 & -3 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 6 \\ 2 & 0 & -3 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{3}=3 \\ {x}_{2}=6 \\ {x}_{3}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=3.$ Substituting into the first equation gives 

$$
{x}_{1}-2(3)=3\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=9.
$$

Since the system has a solution, we can conclude that $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}.$

Moreover, there is exactly one solution, so we have exactly one way to write $b$ as a linear combination of ${a}_{1}$, ${a}_{2}$ and ${a}_{3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}9{a}_{1}+6{a}_{2}+3{a}_{3} & =b \\ 9\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+6\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+3\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -8 \\ -3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 18 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}\cdot {x}_{3}=9\cdot 6\cdot 3=162.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0d94e257-45da-5352-bd7b-f0680253dc5b"] "Find the values of $k$ such that the vector $b$ lies in $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -9 \\ 10\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4 \\ k\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "We know that $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ if there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that

$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=3 \\ -2{x}_{1}-9{x}_{2}=-4 \\ 2{x}_{1}+10{x}_{2}=k\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & 3 \\ -2 & -9 & -4 \\ 2 & 10 & k\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 10 & k\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & k-6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The third row of the augmented matrix now corresponds to the equation $0{x}_{1}+0{x}_{2}=k-6.$ Therefore, the system has a solution only if

$$

17592186120304 :question/problem "Determine if the vector $u$ lies on the plane $Π:r=sb+tc,$ $t,s\in R$, where  $b=⟨1,5,8⟩$, $c=⟨-1,-1,-3⟩$, and  $u=⟨-3,5,-7⟩.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of $s\cdot t$ from the decomposition $u=sb+tc.$" :question/worked-solution "By definition, $u\in Π$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}sb+tc & =u \\ s[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5 \\ 8\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1 \\ -3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5 \\ -7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s-t=-3 \\ 5s-t=5 \\ 8s-3t=-7\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -3 \\ 5 & -1 & 5 \\ 8 & -3 & -7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-5{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 4 & 20 \\ 8 & -3 & -7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-8{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 4 & 20 \\ 0 & 5 & 17\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 5 & 17\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-5{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & -8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The third row of the augmented matrix now corresponds to the equation $0{x}_{1}+0{x}_{2}=-8,$ which has no solution.

So, there are no values of $s$ and $t$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}sb+tc=u.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $u$ does *not* lie on the plane $Π.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186117963 :answer-field/correct 17592186117964 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186121035 :tutorial/content "Given two vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2,$ the set of all possible linear combinations of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ is

$$
U = \left\{ x_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + x_2 \mathbf{a}_2 \: : \: x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R} \right\}.
$$

The set $U$ is also called the **linear span** of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2,$ and is denoted by $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}.$ We say that $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ are the **generators** of $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}.$

For example, let's find the linear span generated by the following vectors:
![](images/55/55c749dccc54c252b9120f148e383f395c09fb4cd4bec0e1cce8ed441ecb6199.svg)

From the definition of linear span, we know that if $\mathbf{b} \in \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ then $\mathbf{b}$ must take the form

$$
\mathbf{b} = x_1\mathbf{a_1} + x_2\mathbf{a_2}
$$

 for some $x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R}.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}b & ={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the linear span of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ is
![](images/21/2181b471f34906eeaea7889abbba37c797a2f9624cee455b43b00fc048247cd1.svg)

Geometrically, $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}$ can be viewed as the plane $\Pi$ that passes through the origin and is parallel to the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2,$ as shown below.

![](images/d5/d5b202475e0bc3ebb07df1f07bab72e9e74b13a99196c2a8a5adb624a7534a03.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id "activity-1c9dbcb8-61c8-5cf9-96d4-e96bf0a4fe24" :activity/id #uuid "7487be5e-d3cc-5ed9-9625-a2ce92482f7c" :question/math-academy-id "q-251806" :question/problem "Consider the two sets of $8$ paired observations in the table below.

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

Given that ${\sum }_{i=1}^{8}{x}_{i}{y}_{i}=695,$ calculate ${S}_{xy}.$" :question/worked-solution "Given a set of $n$ paired observations ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ and ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n},$ the sum of products of deviations from the means can be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i}{x}_{i}{y}_{i}-\frac{1}{n}({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i})({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i})\end{aligned}
$$

First, we calculate the sum of the ${x}_{i}$ and ${y}_{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} & =16+9+12+10+11+11+6+9=84, \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i} & =10+14+8+10+7+8+2+4=63\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that ${\sum }_{i=1}^{8}{x}_{i}{y}_{i}=695.$

Finally, by substituting in the above formula, we get

$$
{S}_{xy}=695-\frac{1}{8}(84)(63)=695-661.5=33.5.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-71771a9c-6d44-5ba0-b159-1c1d1cb21717"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "c7bf2d22-67db-5bfb-9d76-d999020db50d" :question/math-academy-id "q-105190" :question/problem "Which of the following sets are open?

I. $[0,15]$

II. $(-3,5]\cup [6,8)$

III. $(1,6)$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that:

- A set is *open* if it does not contain any of its boundary points. In other words, an open set consists only of the interior points of the set.

- A set is *closed* if it contains **all** of its boundary points. In other words, a closed set consists of all the interior and all the boundary points of the set.

Among the given sets, only $(1,6)$ is open. The boundary points are $1$, and $6.$ None of them lie in the set.

The other sets are not open because:

- $[0,15]$ has two boundary points $0$, and $15$, and both of them lie in the set.

- a function is odd if $f(-x)=-f(x)$ for all $x$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)^{3}+8(-x) \\  & =-{x}^{3}-8x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(-x)\ne f(x),$ the function is not even.

Lastly, we compute $-f(x)$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}-f(x) & =-({x}^{3}+8x) \\  & =-{x}^{3}-8x.\end{aligned}
$$

function $f(x,y)=(2{x}^{2}-y)^{2}$ at the point $A(-1,1)$ in the direction towards the point $B(-2,2).$" :question/worked-solution "The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨-2,2⟩-⟨-1,1⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,1⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}}⟨-1,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-y)^{2},\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-y)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨16{x}^{3}-8xy,\,2y-4{x}^{2}⟩ \\ ∇f(-1,1) & =⟨16(-1)^{3}-8(-1)(1),\,2(1)-4(-1)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-8,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(-1,1) & =∇f(-1,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨-8,-2⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟩ \\  & =(-8)\cdot (-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})-2\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}) \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}∇\,g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x))⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{tan}⁡x,\,\frac{2}{y}⟩ \\ ∇\,g(\frac{\pi }{4},4) & =⟨-\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}),\,\frac{2}{4}⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(\frac{\pi }{4},4)$ in the direction of $∇g(\frac{\pi }{4},4)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}‖∇\,g(\frac{\pi }{4},4)‖ & =‖⟨-1,\frac{1}{2}⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{5}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}.\end{aligned}

{{field-1}}"] ["question-354145f6-5e93-540e-9ff9-3f90c1a259ed" :question/worked-solution "In part 1, we found that $p(15)=225a+15b.$ So, we need to solve the equation $225a+15b=4\,050$ for the parameter $b.$

We need to isolate the variable $b.$ To do this, we treat $a$ as though it were a constant and apply the addition and multiplication principles as usual.

First, we subtract $225a$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}225a+15b & =4\,050 \\ 225a+15b-225a & =4\,050-225a \\ 15b & =4\,050-225a\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide both sides of the equation by $15:$

$$
\begin{aligned}15b & =4\,050-225a \\ \frac{15b}{15} & =\frac{4\,050-225a}{15} \\ \frac{\cancel{15}b}{\cancel{15}} & =\frac{4\,050}{15}-\frac{225a}{15} \\ b & =270-15a\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the GCF, we get

$$

$$

Then, we rewrite each term in the original expression as a product with the $\text{GCF}:$

$$

$$

Finally, we write the $\text{GCF}$ outside the parentheses and keep the remaining terms inside:

$$
\begin{aligned}6\cdot ({x}^{2})+6\cdot (-60x)+6\cdot (800) & = \\ 6({x}^{2}-60x+800)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing expression is ${x}^{2}-60x+800.$"] ["question-497dcd2a-064b-5508-ade6-dffd4f30752c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-56c69cd5-07d2-598b-b43c-0e186d6e3185" :answer-field/id #uuid "56c69cd5-07d2-598b-b43c-0e186d6e3185"] ["answer-820e6076-fcaa-5c6f-b5f8-e29610fe3682" :answer/id #uuid "820e6076-fcaa-5c6f-b5f8-e29610fe3682"] ["answer-820e6076-fcaa-5c6f-b5f8-e29610fe3682" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-820e6076-fcaa-5c6f-b5f8-e29610fe3682" :answer/value "(x-20)(x-40)"] ["answer-field-56c69cd5-07d2-598b-b43c-0e186d6e3185" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-56c69cd5-07d2-598b-b43c-0e186d6e3185" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-56c69cd5-07d2-598b-b43c-0e186d6e3185" :answer-field/correct "answer-820e6076-fcaa-5c6f-b5f8-e29610fe3682"] ["answer-field-56c69cd5-07d2-598b-b43c-0e186d6e3185" :answer-field/choices "answer-820e6076-fcaa-5c6f-b5f8-e29610fe3682"] ["question-497dcd2a-064b-5508-ade6-dffd4f30752c" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-56c69cd5-07d2-598b-b43c-0e186d6e3185"] [17592186064323 :knowledge-point/questions "question-497dcd2a-064b-5508-ade6-dffd4f30752c"] ["question-f01f8f3f-d44f-517a-a672-79bef06856d4" :question/id #uuid "f01f8f3f-d44f-517a-a672-79bef06856d4"] ["question-f01f8f3f-d44f-517a-a672-79bef06856d4" :question/math-academy-id "q-167221"] ["question-f01f8f3f-d44f-517a-a672-79bef06856d4" :question/problem "Find the minimum number of wooden tables the company needs to produce per week to make a weekly profit of $\$4\,800.$

The company needs to produce$\,$
{{field-1}}$\,$ wooden tables per week."] ["question-f01f8f3f-d44f-517a-a672-79bef06856d4" :question/worked-solution "From part 5, the required number of wooden tables $x$ is the solution to the equation

$$
6\cdot ({x}^{2}-60x+800)=0.
$$

Dividing this equation by $6,$ we have

$$
{x}^{2}-60x+800=0.
$$

To solve this equation, we want to find a factor pair of the constant term $(800)$ that also adds up to the coefficient of the linear term $(-60).$ The required factors are $(-20)$ and $(-40).$

Using this factor pair, we write the linear term as $-60x=-20x-40x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-60x+800 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-20x-40x+800 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately and then factor the expression completely:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-20x-40x+800 & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}-20x)+(-40x+800) & =0 \\ x(x-20)-40(x-20) & =0 \\ (x-20)(x-40)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the solutions are $x=20$ or $x=40.$ Since we require the minimum solution, we conclude that the company needs to produce $20$ wooden tables per week to make a profit of $$4\,800.$"] ["question-f01f8f3f-d44f-517a-a672-79bef06856d4" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-69bddd2d-4ab6-5d13-b5cd-247cb058b864" :answer-field/id #uuid "69bddd2d-4ab6-5d13-b5cd-247cb058b864"] ["answer-81d6fadc-c6fc-54df-85f4-906ea6060968" :answer/id #uuid "81d6fadc-c6fc-54df-85f4-906ea6060968"] ["answer-81d6fadc-c6fc-54df-85f4-906ea6060968" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-81d6fadc-c6fc-54df-85f4-906ea6060968" :answer/value "20"] ["answer-field-69bddd2d-4ab6-5d13-b5cd-247cb058b864" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-69bddd2d-4ab6-5d13-b5cd-247cb058b864" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-69bddd2d-4ab6-5d13-b5cd-247cb058b864" :answer-field/correct "answer-81d6fadc-c6fc-54df-85f4-906ea6060968"] ["answer-field-69bddd2d-4ab6-5d13-b5cd-247cb058b864" :answer-field/choices "answer-81d6fadc-c6fc-54df-85f4-906ea6060968"] ["question-f01f8f3f-d44f-517a-a672-79bef06856d4" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-69bddd2d-4ab6-5d13-b5cd-247cb058b864"] [17592186054658 :knowledge-point/questions "question-f01f8f3f-d44f-517a-a672-79bef06856d4"] ["question-f85c7e50-3cac-5133-ab86-e4e54ecc65fa" :question/id #uuid "f85c7e50-3cac-5133-ab86-e4e54ecc65fa"] ["question-f85c7e50-3cac-5133-ab86-e4e54ecc65fa" :question/math-academy-id "q-167222"] ["question-f85c7e50-3cac-5133-ab86-e4e54ecc65fa" :question/problem "The company wants to increase its output by implementing a new production model. The number of wooden tables ${a}_{n}$ produced in the $n$th week since the implementation of the new model is given by the arithmetic sequence

$$
{a}_{n+1}={a}_{n}+4,\,{a}_{1}=12,\,n\ge 1
$$

What is the explicit formula for the $n$th term of this arithmetic sequence?

${a}_{n}=$
{{field-1}}"] ["question-f85c7e50-3cac-5133-ab86-e4e54ecc65fa" :question/worked-solution "The explicit formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}+(n-1)d,\,n\ge 1,
$$

so we need to determine the first term ${a}_{1}$ and the common difference $d.$

We are given that the first term is ${a}_{1}=12,$ and we can use the recursive rule to compute the second term as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & ={a}_{1}+4 \\  & =12+4 \\  & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Using the first and second terms, we can compute the common difference:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={a}_{2}-{a}_{1} \\  & =16-12 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now we substitute ${a}_{1}=12$ and $d=4$ into the formula for the $n$th term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =12+(n-1)(4) \\  & =12+4n-4 \\  & =4n+8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is

$$
{a}_{n}=4n+8,\,n\ge 1.
$$"] ["question-f85c7e50-3cac-5133-ab86-e4e54ecc65fa" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-c3549239-369c-5dc5-b97f-5b91a23e416d" :answer-field/id #uuid {{field-1}}"] ["question-4c9070fc-7290-592a-a3f4-9617ce57a8a0" :question/worked-solution "First, we will calculate the axis of symmetry in terms of $k.$ Then, since we know that the axis of symmetry is $x=\frac{5}{4},$ we will set our result equal to $\frac{5}{4}.$ 

From the equation $y=(2x+3)(x-k),$ we find that the roots of the parabola are ${x}_{1}=-\frac{3}{2}$ and ${x}_{2}=k.$ 

To find the axis of symmetry, we take the average of the roots, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2} \\  & =\frac{(-\frac{3}{2}+k)}{2} \\  & =\frac{(-\frac{3}{2}+\frac{2k}{2})}{2} \\  & =\frac{2k-3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

We know that the axis of symmetry is $x=\frac{5}{4}.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2k-3}{4} & =\frac{5}{4} \\ 2k-3 & =5 \\ 2k & =8 \\ k & =4.\end{aligned}

{{field-1}}"] [17592186110978 :question/worked-solution "First, we will calculate the axis of symmetry in terms of $k.$ Then, since we know that the axis of symmetry is $x=-\frac{1}{8},$ we will set our result equal to $\frac{1}{8}.$ 

From the equation $y=-(x+5k)(3x-4k),$ we find that the roots of the parabola are ${x}_{1}=-5k$ and ${x}_{2}=\frac{4k}{3}.$ 

To find the axis of symmetry, we take the average of the roots, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2} \\  & =\frac{(-5k+\frac{4k}{3})}{2} \\  & =-\frac{(-\frac{11k}{3})}{2} \\  & =-\frac{11k}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

We know that the axis of symmetry is $x=-\frac{1}{8}.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{11k}{6} & =-\frac{1}{8} \\ -11k & =-\frac{6}{8} \\ -11k & =-\frac{3}{4} \\ k & =\frac{3}{44}.\end{aligned}

$$

Therefore, the parabola's axis of symmetry must be equidistant from the lines $x=22$ and $x=25.$ We can find this by taking the average of these two values.

\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(\frac{9}{{x}^{3}}-1)}{(2+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & \to \frac{0-1}{2+0} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{4}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{4},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2{x}^{4}+3{x}^{3}}{16{x}^{4}-1} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2{x}^{4}}{{x}^{4}}+\frac{3{x}^{3}}{{x}^{4}})}{(\frac{16{x}^{4}}{{x}^{4}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{4}})} \\  & =\frac{(2+\frac{3}{x})}{(16-\frac{1}{{x}^{4}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{3}{x}$ and $\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(2+\frac{3}{x})}{(16-\frac{1}{{x}^{4}})} \\  & \to \frac{2+0}{16-0} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the horizontal asymptote is $y=\frac{1}{8}.$"] ["question-69e4acc7-7029-59de-a5d6-0ccfcee72b69" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-87a9e411-8f65-5124-9c8e-cea45774f41c" $$
f(x)=\frac{7{x}^{2}+4}{3{x}^{3}+12x}
$$

To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{3}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{3},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{7{x}^{2}+4}{3{x}^{3}+12x} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{7{x}^{2}}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{4}{{x}^{3}})}{(\frac{3{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{12x}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{7}{x}+\frac{4}{{x}^{3}})}{(3+\frac{12}{{x}^{2}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{7}{x},\frac{4}{{x}^{3}}$ and $\frac{12}{{x}^{2}}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(\frac{7}{x}+\frac{4}{{x}^{3}})}{(3+\frac{12}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & \to \frac{0+0}{3+0} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the horizontal asymptote is $y=0.$"] [17592186088279 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-4d5db833-4c7c-5ecf-873d-e9c31e077feb" :answer/id #uuid ["question-648c2e1a-c875-5372-ad66-c0b63e6cb405" :question/math-academy-id "q-18760"] ["question-648c2e1a-c875-5372-ad66-c0b63e6cb405" :question/problem "Let $(a,b)$ be the solution of the following system. What is the value of $a+b?$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0.05a-0.2b=0.04 \\ 0.12a-1.2b=0.24\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-648c2e1a-c875-5372-ad66-c0b63e6cb405" :question/worked-solution "To get rid of the decimals, we multiply both equations by $100,$ as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0.05a-0.2b=0.04 & |\times 100 \\ 0.12a-1.2b=0.24 & |\times 100\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}5a-20b=4 \\ 12a-120b=24\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that if we multiply the first equation by $-2$ and divide the second equation by $3,$ we will get a $40b$ term in the first equation that can cancel with the $-40b$ term in the second equation:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}5a-20b=4 & |\,\times (-2) \\ 12a-120b=24 & |\,÷3\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}-10a+40b=-8 \\ 4a-40b=8\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $b$-variable and allows us to solve for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-10a+\cancel{40b} & =-8 \\ 4a-\cancel{40b} & =8 \\ (-10a+4a) & =(-8+8) \\ -6a & =0 \\ a & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $a=0$ into the equation $5a-20b=4$ to solve for $b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5a-20b & =4 \\ 5(0)-20b & =4 \\ -20b & =4 \\ b & =-\frac{4}{20} \\ b & =-0.2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $a=0,\,b=-0.2.$ So,

$$
a+b=0+(-0.2)=-0.2.
$$"] ["question-648c2e1a-c875-5372-ad66-c0b63e6cb405" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-a297791d-ebee-5b0c-89e6-af072a20920b" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-c6acc05f-c544-5e0c-918b-0d7218132aa6" :question/math-academy-id "q-101729"] ["question-c6acc05f-c544-5e0c-918b-0d7218132aa6" :question/problem "The table below lists values of $f(x)$ at distinct $x$-values. Knowing that the average rate of change of the function $f(x)$ on the interval $[3p,5]$ is $-2,$ find the value of $p.$ 

| $x$ | $\,-10\,$ | $\,-7\,$ | $\,3p\,$ | $\,-2\,$ | $\,0\,$ | $\,1\,$ | $\,5\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $\,12\,$ | $\,8\,$ | $\,11\,$ | $\,-2\,$ | $\,3\,$ | $\,-16\,$ | $\,-8\,$ |"] ["question-c6acc05f-c544-5e0c-918b-0d7218132aa6" :question/worked-solution "Using the formula for the average rate of change, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{Δf}{Δx} & =\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a} \\  & =\frac{f(5)-f(3p)}{5-3p} \\  & =\frac{-8-11}{5-3p} \\  & =\frac{-19}{5-3p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we know that $\frac{Δf}{Δx}=-2$ on the interval $[3p,5].$ Thus, 

$$
\frac{-19}{5-3p}=-2.
$$

Solving for $p,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-19}{5-3p} & =-2 \\ -19 & =-2\cdot (5-3p) \\ -19 & =-10+6p \\ -19+10 & =6p \\ -9 & =6p \\ \frac{-9}{6} & =\frac{6p}{6} \\ -\frac{3}{2} & =p.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $p=-\frac{3}{2}.$"] ["question-c6acc05f-c544-5e0c-918b-0d7218132aa6" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["question-2c409cd1-fe1f-5e01-a403-dbc5d06f9573" :question/problem "Calculate ${lim}_{t\to 2}f(t),$ if $f(t)=⟨{e}^{t-2},\,\sqrt{6-t},\,\frac{3}{t+2}⟩.$"] ["question-2c409cd1-fe1f-5e01-a403-dbc5d06f9573" :question/worked-solution "First, recall that

$$
{lim}_{t\to 2}f(t)=⟨{lim}_{t\to 2}{e}^{t-2},\,{lim}_{t\to 2}\sqrt{6-t},\,{lim}_{t\to 2}\frac{3}{t+2}⟩.
$$

Now, we find the limits one by one.

- For the first component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 2}{e}^{t-2} & ={e}^{2-2} \\  & ={e}^{0} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 2}\sqrt{6-t} & =\sqrt{6-2} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the third component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 2}\frac{3}{t+2} & =\frac{3}{2+2} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{t\to 2}f(t)=⟨1,2,\frac{3}{4}⟩.$"] ["question-2c409cd1-fe1f-5e01-a403-dbc5d06f9573" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-8fb29db3-ac82-5b56-ae72-c2f44640f27f" $f(s)=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5-s} \\ \frac{{e}^{1-s}}{s} \\ (1+5s)^{1-s}\end{aligned}].$"] ["question-e7a9644a-6597-5c1c-8581-2dcd08c08372" :question/worked-solution "First, recall that

$$
{lim}_{s\to 1}f(s)=[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 1}\sqrt{5-s} \\ {lim}_{s\to 1}\frac{{e}^{1-s}}{s} \\ {lim}_{s\to 1}\,(1+5s)^{1/(2s)}.\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we find the limits one by one.

- For the first component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 1}\sqrt{5-s} & =\sqrt{5-1} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 1}\frac{{e}^{1-s}}{s}=\frac{{e}^{1-1}}{1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the third component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 1}\,(1+5s)^{1-s} & =(1+5\cdot 1)^{1-1} \\  & ={6}^{0} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{s\to 1}f(s)=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$"] ["question-e7a9644a-6597-5c1c-8581-2dcd08c08372" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] $f(s)=⟨\frac{5}{{e}^{s-2}},\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4-2s),\,{s}^{3}-5⟩.$"] ["question-d22af4f5-52e4-5523-b72f-519be01c5f87" :question/worked-solution "First, recall that

$$
{lim}_{s\to 2}f(s)=⟨{lim}_{s\to 2}\frac{5}{{e}^{s-2}},\,{lim}_{s\to 2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4-2s),\,{lim}_{s\to 2}\,({s}^{3}-5)⟩.
$$

Now, we find the limits one by one.

- For the first component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 2}\frac{5}{{e}^{s-2}} & =\frac{5}{{e}^{2-2}}=5.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the first component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4-2s) & =3{lim}_{s\to 2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4-2s) \\  & =3\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(4-2\cdot 2) \\  & =3\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the third component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 2}\,({s}^{3}-5) & ={2}^{3}-5=3.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{s\to 2}f(s)=⟨5,3,3⟩.$"] ["question-d22af4f5-52e4-5523-b72f-519be01c5f87" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-84e8b7b2-23ed-5a0a-99f0-5172dcf54f18" ["question-37a31447-f0c5-5a53-afc7-a1edb4864b07" :question/worked-solution "First, recall that:

$$
{lim}_{s\to 0}f(s)=[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 0}\sqrt{s+8} \\ {lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{arcsin}⁡s}{s} \\ {lim}_{s\to 0}(1+2s)^{1/(2s)}\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we find the limits one-by-one.

- For the first component, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 0}\sqrt{s+8} & =\sqrt{0+8} \\  & =\sqrt{8} \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{3}} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- The second component can be found using L'Hopital's Rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{arcsin}⁡s}{s} & ={lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{{(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡s)}^{′}}{{s}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{s}^{2}}}}{1} \\  & ={lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{s}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{0}^{2}}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- The third component can be found using a special limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 0}(1+2s)^{1/(2s)} & ={lim}_{u\to 0}(1+u)^{1/u}=e\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{s\to 0}f(s)=[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{2} \\ 1 \\ e\end{aligned}].$"] ["question-37a31447-f0c5-5a53-afc7-a1edb4864b07" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] $f(s)=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5-s} \\ \frac{{e}^{1-s}}{s} \\ (1+5s)^{1-s}\end{aligned}].$"] ["question-6199f517-7214-5d4f-b510-e7e4d600a748" :question/worked-solution "First, recall that

$$
{lim}_{s\to 1}f(s)=[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 1}\sqrt{5-s} \\ {lim}_{s\to 1}\frac{{e}^{1-s}}{1-s} \\ {lim}_{s\to 1}\,(1+5s)^{1/(2s)}\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we find the limits one by one.

- For the first component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 1}\sqrt{5-s} & =\sqrt{5-1} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 1}\frac{{e}^{1-s}}{s}=\frac{1}{1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the third component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 1}\,(1+5s)^{1-s} & =(1+5\cdot 1)^{1-1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{s\to 1}f(s)=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Finally, the limit of $‖f(s)‖$ as $s$ approaches $1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 1}‖f(s)‖ & =‖{lim}_{s\to 1}f(s)‖ \\  & =‖[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-6199f517-7214-5d4f-b510-e7e4d600a748" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-8dbde469-aa7e-5bcb-a66c-2dae3c6fa5e6" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "First, recall that:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 0}f(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{s}{(s+1)^{2}} \\ {lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡s}{{s}^{2}} \\ {lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡s}{2{s}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the limits one-by-one.

- For the first component, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{s}{(s+1)^{2}} & =\frac{0}{(0+1)^{2}}=0\end{aligned}
$$

- The second component can be found using a special limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡s}{{s}^{2}} & ={lim}_{s\to 0}{(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡s}{s})}^{2} \\  & ={({lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡s}{s})}^{2} \\  & ={1}^{2} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- The third component can be found using L'Hopital's Rule twice:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡s}{2{s}^{2}} & ={lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡s)}^{″}}{{(2{s}^{2})}^{″}} \\  & ={lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡s}{4} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡0}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{s\to 0}f(s)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1/4\end{aligned}]\,.$

Finally, the limit of $‖f(s)‖$ as $s$ approaches $0$ is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 0}‖f(s)‖ & =‖{lim}_{s\to 0}f(s)‖ \\  & =‖[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1/4\end{aligned}]‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{4})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{17}{16}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{17}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-9a567a48-e070-587a-94df-8a2d7148a763" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-a738fbe9-b746-555f-a431-6ff37c754328" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "First, recall that:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}f(t) & =({lim}_{t\to 1}\frac{4+t}{5})\,i+({lim}_{t\to 1}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-1)}{{t}^{2}-1})\,j+({lim}_{t\to 1}\sqrt{9t})\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the limits one-by-one.

- For the first component, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}\frac{4+t}{5} & =\frac{4+1}{5}=1\end{aligned}
$$

- The second component can be found using a special limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-1)}{{t}^{2}-1} & ={lim}_{t\to 1}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-1)}{(t-1)(t+1)} \\  & =({lim}_{t\to 1}\frac{1}{t+1})\cdot ({lim}_{t\to 1}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-1)}{t-1}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{1+1})\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- For the third component, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}\sqrt{9t} & =\sqrt{9(1)}=3\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{t\to 1}f(t)=i+\frac{1}{2}\,j+3\,k.$

Finally, the limit of $‖f(t)‖$ as $t$ approaches $1$ is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}‖f(t)‖ & =‖{lim}_{t\to 1}f(t)‖ \\  & =‖i+\frac{1}{2}\,j+3\,k‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4}+9} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{41}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{41}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-2cd66931-0513-5d1c-9823-4729248ee301" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-d1f9bfc4-206c-5615-9e86-3cd20425df2f" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
{lim}_{t\to 3}f(t)=[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 3}({t}^{2}-3t) \\ {lim}_{t\to 3}\frac{1}{{t}^{2}-8} \\ {lim}_{t\to 3}(5-2t)\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we find the limits one-by-one.

- For the first component, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 3}({t}^{2}-3t) & ={3}^{2}-3(3)=0\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 3}\frac{1}{{t}^{2}-8} & =\frac{1}{{3}^{2}-8}=1\end{aligned}
$$

- For the third component, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 3}(5-2t) & =5-2(3)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{t\to 3}f(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

Finally, the limit of $‖f(t)‖$ as $t$ approaches $3$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 3}‖f(t)‖ & =‖{lim}_{t\to 3}f(t)‖ \\  & =‖[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-86cd099b-e0a6-5dec-b63e-d3e60dda2214" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-c84f65d5-7aae-5814-8581-c9fd5f811b31" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
{lim}_{t\to 0}f(t)=({lim}_{t\to 0}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)i+({lim}_{t\to 0}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)j+({lim}_{t\to 0}(t+2)^{2})k.
$$

Now, we find the limits one by one.

- For the first component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}\operatorname{sin}⁡t & =\operatorname{sin}⁡0=0.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}\operatorname{cos}⁡0=1.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the third component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}\,(t+2)^{2} & =(0+2)^{2}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{t\to 0}f(t)=j+4\,k.$

Finally, the limit of $‖f(t)‖$ as $t$ approaches $0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}‖f(t)‖ & =‖{lim}_{t\to 0}f(t)‖ \\  & =‖j+4\,k‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{17}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-e2503fc5-32a5-54fb-be4e-1b9923b33c22" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-1e315895-d72c-57a7-afdc-8b9e80c82011" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-33768c70-a4a8-56c5-b929-58df88c6ba1b" :question/math-academy-id "q-78268"] ["question-33768c70-a4a8-56c5-b929-58df88c6ba1b" :question/problem "Find the limit ${lim}_{t\to 1}[f(t)\cdot g(t)]$ given that $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are defined as:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{t-1} \\ \frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t}{t} \\ \frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t}{t}\end{aligned}],\,g(t)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{t}^{2}-2t+1}{t+1} \\ \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t}{t+1} \\ \frac{{e}^{t+1}}{t+1}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-33768c70-a4a8-56c5-b929-58df88c6ba1b" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}\,(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{t-1}) \\ {lim}_{t\to 1}\,(\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t}{t}) \\ {lim}_{t\to 1}\,(\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t}{t})\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}\,(\frac{(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)^{′}}{(t-1)^{′}}) \\ {lim}_{t\to 1}\,(\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t}{t}) \\ {lim}_{t\to 1}\,(\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t}{t})\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}\,(\frac{1}{t}) \\ \frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi }{1} \\ \frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi }{1}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Note that for the first component of ${lim}_{t\to 1}f(t)$ we used L'Hopital's Rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}g(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}\,\frac{{t}^{2}-2t+1}{t+1} \\ {lim}_{t\to 1}\,\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t}{t+1} \\ {lim}_{t\to 1}\,\frac{{e}^{t+1}}{t+1}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{1}^{2}-2\cdot 1+1}{1+1} \\ \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡1+1}{1+1} \\ \frac{{e}^{1+1}}{1+1}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{{e}^{2}}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}[f(t)\cdot g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to 1}f(t)\cdot {lim}_{t\to 1}g(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{{e}^{2}}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =1\cdot 0+(-2)\cdot \frac{1}{2}+0\cdot \frac{{e}^{2}}{2} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-33768c70-a4a8-56c5-b929-58df88c6ba1b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-b24006f7-dcb6-5a3e-962f-d3babb6d995e" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

Note that for the second component of ${lim}_{t\to 0}f(t)$ we used a special limit ${lim}_{u\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡u}{u}=1.$

$$

$$

Note that for the first component of ${lim}_{t\to 0}g(t)$ we used L'Hopital's Rule.

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}[f(t)\cdot g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to 0}f(t)\cdot {lim}_{t\to 0}g(t) \\  & =⟨2,\,2,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨2,0,1⟩ \\  & =2\cdot 2+2\cdot 0+0\cdot 1 \\  & =4\end{aligned}

$C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,\frac{\pi }{2})}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(1,\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,\frac{\pi }{2})} & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(1\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})-1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =2\cdot 1-1\cdot 0 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,\frac{\pi }{2})} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,\frac{\pi }{2})}(x-1) \\ z-0 & =2(x-1) \\ z & =2x-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=\frac{\pi }{2} \\ z=2x-2\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-bd4791a4-a5ea-5e12-b1c8-f45a53372bd0" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-d2ed29c1-ef21-57a0-9839-78668465edfc" :answer-field/id #uuid Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(\frac{1}{2},0) & ={f}_{x}(\frac{1}{2},0)(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =1(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =x-\frac{1}{2} \\ z & =x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=0 \\ z=x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=x+\frac{1}{2}$ (or $x-z+\frac{1}{2}=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $-i-k$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-(-i-k)=i+k$ is also parallel to it."] ["question-19ce6755-ce5c-5344-86b9-dca6271615dd" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] "First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}-4x & =-({x}^{2}+4x) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}) \\  & =-((x+2)^{2}-4) \\  & =4-(x+2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-4x}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{4-(x+2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{2(x+2)\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x+2}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x+2}{2})\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x+2}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\frac{x+2}{2}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-4x}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x+2}{2})\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x+2}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(\frac{x+2}{2})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-a95ee677-1642-5975-8b50-8432d56de160" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-0526b46b-564d-561d-a9aa-fedc41539160" :answer-field/id #uuid in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-10x+27 & ={x}^{2}-2\cdot 5x+{5}^{2}-{5}^{2}+27 \\  & =(x-5)^{2}+2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\sqrt{2}}{|x-5|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-10x+27}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{\sqrt{2}}{|x-5|\sqrt{2+(x-5)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{2}}|\sqrt{2+2{(\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{2}}|\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{2}}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{2}}|\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{2}})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-38a6fd7f-85a4-5b9d-9914-3bd5a2ab420c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-0b36eef3-f0c2-5b45-97f7-a2607c73a159" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-6a55ffae-eeb7-54cf-a5ce-c644ed8a6a5a" :question/math-academy-id "q-97905"] ["question-6a55ffae-eeb7-54cf-a5ce-c644ed8a6a5a" :question/problem "$\int -\frac{15}{|5x+10|\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4x+5}}\text{d}x=$"] ["question-6a55ffae-eeb7-54cf-a5ce-c644ed8a6a5a" :question/worked-solution "First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+4x+5 & ={x}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}+5 \\  & =(x+2)^{2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int -\frac{15}{|5x-10|\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4x+5}}\,\text{d}x=-\int \frac{15}{5|x+2|\sqrt{1+(x+2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x=-3\int \frac{1}{|x+2|\sqrt{1+(x+2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x+2.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}-3\int \frac{1}{|x+2|\sqrt{1+(x+2)^{2}}}\text{d}x & =-3\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =3\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(x+2)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-6a55ffae-eeb7-54cf-a5ce-c644ed8a6a5a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-96a55f92-f39f-5881-94c0-2f84b4c3471a" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Calculate $\int \frac{1}{16-(3x+2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x=$"] ["question-1369cbfd-a46c-5064-baa1-cbe5720fb540" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that

$$
\int \frac{1}{16-(3x+2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{16-16(\frac{1}{16}(3x+2)^{2})}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{16}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{4}(3x+2))}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{4}(3x+2).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3}{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{4}{3}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{16}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{4}(3x+2))}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{16}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\cdot \frac{4}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{3x+2}{4})+C.\end{aligned}
$$
