["question-eaac4ca3-6936-5237-9e98-3d7aa72b5385" :question/problem "$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-2x(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].$*"] ["question-eaac4ca3-6936-5237-9e98-3d7aa72b5385" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.$"] ["question-eaac4ca3-6936-5237-9e98-3d7aa72b5385" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-8ea9a430-3071-50b8-b617-7ec74f7a4ddc" :answer-field/id Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}].$*

</tbody></table>"] ["question-701145a1-1f00-509b-9c1b-60626233c2a4" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-1)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-1)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-1)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-1))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-1))\, \\ \,3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-1))\,\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-701145a1-1f00-509b-9c1b-60626233c2a4" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-0f7c85fb-7d21-5d48-8f24-4c37d6bc47ea" :answer-field/id #uuid "answer-field-c42bbbe5-1f49-507b-a85b-15a0a5e80a99"] [17592186110678 :knowledge-point/questions "question-96d6c320-22a1-578b-bc1b-575bf1a1c004"] [17592186111907 :tutorial/content "To plot the graph of a logarithmic function, it helps to remember that the inverse of a logarithmic function is an exponential function. So, we can just plot the exponential function and reflect it over the line $y=x.$

For example, suppose that we wish to plot the graph of 

$$
y=\log_2 x.
$$

The corresponding inverse function is $y=2^x,$ and since $y=2^x$ is a one-to-one function defined for all real $x,$ we can obtain the graph of $y=\log_2{x}$ by reflecting $y=2^x$ over the line $y=x.$ The result is shown below:

![](images/0c/0c614201798324262429f080d8e8a31bfefe58c4008bfe82e6da1b91dc158b7a.png)

Here are some key points to note about $y=\log_2(x)\mathbin{:}$

- The domain is $x>0$, and the range is $-\infty <   y <   \infty.$

- The graph has the vertical asymptote $x=0.$

- The function is an increasing function.

- The graph passes through the point $(1,0).$

- For $x>1$, the graph is positive and grows very slowly as we increase $x.$ We say that $y\rightarrow \infty$ (slowly) as $x\rightarrow \infty.$

In general, for any base $n>1,$ the graph of $y=\log_n{x}$ always has the same shape, and all of the above points are valid. We can verify that this is true by inspecting some possible graphs shown below:

![](images/91/91567f282acbc3b8390da1e4147b445018ae649d913205e59867d58ea980ff7b.png)

**Note:** The important points covered above also apply to two familiar logarithms.

- $y = \ln x = \log_e x$ is the natural logarithm. Since the base is $n=e>1,$ all of the important points covered above apply.

- $y = \log x = \log_{10} x$ is the logarithm with base $10.$ Since the base is $n=10>1,$ all the important points covered above apply."] [17592186110877 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] ["question-d591e3b7-0993-5fb9-b7f0-ff97c33bf559" :question/id #uuid "d591e3b7-0993-5fb9-b7f0-ff97c33bf559"] ["question-d591e3b7-0993-5fb9-b7f0-ff97c33bf559" :question/math-academy-id "q-100250"] ["question-d591e3b7-0993-5fb9-b7f0-ff97c33bf559" :question/problem "Find ${lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{3x}{\sqrt[3]{2{x}^{4}-5}}.$"] ["question-d591e3b7-0993-5fb9-b7f0-ff97c33bf559" :question/worked-solution "Applying the quotient rule, we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{3x}{\sqrt[3]{2{x}^{4}-5}}=\frac{{lim}_{x\to 2}3x}{{lim}_{x\to 2}\sqrt[3]{2{x}^{4}-5}}
$$

We calculate the limits of the numerator and denominator, separately.

For the numerator, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}3x & =3{lim}_{x\to 2}x \\  & =3\cdot 2 \\  & =6\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the root rule in the denominator, we have
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\sqrt[3]{2{x}^{4}-5} & =\sqrt[3]{{lim}_{x\to 2}(2{x}^{4}-5)} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{2(2)^{4}-5)} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{27} \\  & =3\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{3x}{\sqrt[3]{2{x}^{4}-5}} & =\frac{6}{3}=2\,.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-d591e3b7-0993-5fb9-b7f0-ff97c33bf559" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-ddff0f96-aeb7-5490-8d56-4c8b9d0de231" :answer-field/id #uuid From the product rule, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,2}(x-1)^{2}\,(f(x)-2)^{3}={lim}_{x\to \,2}(x-1)^{2}\cdot {lim}_{x\to \,2}(f(x)-2)^{3}.
$$

We calculate the limits of each factor, separately.

Applying the power rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,2}(x-1)^{2} & ={({lim}_{x\to \,2}(x-1))}^{2} \\  & =(2-1)^{2} \\  & ={1}^{2} \\  & =1\,,\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,2}(f(x)-2)^{3} & ={({lim}_{x\to \,2}(f(x)-2))}^{3} \\  & =(3-2)^{3} \\  & ={1}^{3} \\  & =1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,2}(x-1)^{2}\,(f(x)-2)^{3} & =(1)\cdot (1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-41ad1c03-af11-5517-b3f9-c73f27dc13ff" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-817fc64f-fe17-5ab1-8ab5-8f8ebfd722a2" :answer-field/id #uuid "817fc64f-fe17-5ab1-8ab5-8f8ebfd722a2"] ["answer-066cb984-e17a-5fea-af4c-48188475d862" :answer/id #uuid "066cb984-e17a-5fea-af4c-48188475d862"] ["answer-066cb984-e17a-5fea-af4c-48188475d862" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-066cb984-e17a-5fea-af4c-48188475d862" :answer/value "1"] ["answer-field-817fc64f-fe17-5ab1-8ab5-8f8ebfd722a2" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-817fc64f-fe17-5ab1-8ab5-8f8ebfd722a2" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-817fc64f-fe17-5ab1-8ab5-8f8ebfd722a2" :answer-field/correct "answer-066cb984-e17a-5fea-af4c-48188475d862"] ["answer-field-817fc64f-fe17-5ab1-8ab5-8f8ebfd722a2" :answer-field/choices "answer-066cb984-e17a-5fea-af4c-48188475d862"] ["question-41ad1c03-af11-5517-b3f9-c73f27dc13ff" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-817fc64f-fe17-5ab1-8ab5-8f8ebfd722a2"] [17592186054703 :knowledge-point/questions "question-41ad1c03-af11-5517-b3f9-c73f27dc13ff"] ["question-2b9acb7e-8235-5df0-907d-863119079541" :question/id #uuid "2b9acb7e-8235-5df0-907d-863119079541"] ["question-2b9acb7e-8235-5df0-907d-863119079541" :question/math-academy-id "q-338390"] ["question-2b9acb7e-8235-5df0-907d-863119079541" :question/problem "Find the **exact** value of the limit.

$$
\begin{aligned}2x\sqrt{54}+2x\sqrt{x}-5x\sqrt{6} & = \\ 2x\sqrt{9\cdot 6}+2x\sqrt{x}-5x\sqrt{6} & = \\ 2x\sqrt{9}\cdot \sqrt{6}+2x\sqrt{x}-5x\sqrt{6} & = \\ 2x\cdot 3\cdot \sqrt{6}+2x\sqrt{x}-5x\sqrt{6} & = \\ 6x\sqrt{6}+2x\sqrt{x}-5x\sqrt{6} & \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we combine the like terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}6x\sqrt{6}+2x\sqrt{x}-5x\sqrt{6} & = \\ (6x-5x)\sqrt{6}+2x\sqrt{x} & = \\ x\sqrt{6}+2x\sqrt{x}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-aceecb75-92cf-58b4-997d-d31ecad9d81f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-2edd54bc-8785-50e5-9005-f3528fdfbcbc" :answer-field/id #uuid Find the cosine of $∠Y.$"] [17592186078737 :question/worked-solution "Recall the definition of cosine: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡Y=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{XY}{YZ}=\frac{XY}{5}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $XY.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}XY & =\sqrt{Y{Z}^{2}-X{Z}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}-(\sqrt{7})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25-7} \\  & =\sqrt{18} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡Y & =\frac{XY}{5}=\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186078737 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] [17592186075298 :answer-field/correct 17592186075301] ["question-b2b55850-322e-5b17-9a94-b2696bd083f6" :question/id #uuid "b2b55850-322e-5b17-9a94-b2696bd083f6"] ["question-b2b55850-322e-5b17-9a94-b2696bd083f6" :question/math-academy-id "q-122050"] ["question-b2b55850-322e-5b17-9a94-b2696bd083f6" :question/problem "In the right triangle $△JKL,$ $∠J$ is a right angle, $JL=8$ and $KL=12.$ Find $\operatorname{tan}⁡K.$"] ["question-b2b55850-322e-5b17-9a94-b2696bd083f6" :question/worked-solution "The following triangle illustrates the information given.

![](images/cc/cc33327cc6d071cb6ec9ac0c10d58e57bc35f8d81b326731120cf04c18f58ec1.png)

Recall the definition of tangent: 

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡K=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}=\frac{JL}{JK}=\frac{8}{JK}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $JK.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}JK & =\sqrt{K{L}^{2}-J{L}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{12}^{2}-{8}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{144-64} \\  & =\sqrt{80} \\  & =4\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡K & =\frac{8}{4\sqrt{5}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-b2b55850-322e-5b17-9a94-b2696bd083f6" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-f15bdbe8-d486-594d-b02d-d29460c4afc4" :answer-field/id #uuid \operatorname{tan}⁡P=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}=\frac{QR}{PQ}=\frac{QR}{3.5}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}QR & =\sqrt{P{R}^{2}-P{Q}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{12.5}^{2}-{3.5}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{156.25-12.25} \\  & =\sqrt{144} \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡P & =\frac{QR}{3.5} \\  & =\frac{12}{3.5} \\  & =\frac{120}{35} \\  & =\frac{24}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-44ffb250-1ebe-5832-a06b-038dd7ff73b2" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-518b1e5c-6389-594b-b333-90ba109eabdc" :answer-field/id #uuid "Determine the interval on which the function $f(t)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{t}^{2}-1} \\ \sqrt{t} \\ t+3\end{aligned}]$  is continuous."] ["question-0b1d012f-068b-5ef8-8288-effe2d51246e" :question/worked-solution "A vector-valued function is continuous on an interval if and only if each of its components is continuous on that interval.

Let's now consider the components of $f(t)$ one by one.

- The function $\frac{1}{{t}^{2}-1}$ is continuous everywhere except the excluded points $t=\pm 1.$

- The function $\sqrt{t}$ is continuous for $t\ge 0.$

- The function $t+3$ is continuous for all real numbers.

Therefore, the vector-valued function $f(t)$ is continuous for all $t\ge 0$ except the point $t=1.$ So the interval of continuity is $[0,1)\cup (1,\infty ).$"] $$

Let's consider the functions one by one. 

- The function $p(s)$ is **not** continuous on $[-1,1]$ because 
its second component, $\frac{s+1}{s},$ is undefined at $s=0$ and hence discontinuous on $[-1,1].$

- The function $q(s)$ is **not** continuous on $[-1,1]$ because 
its first component, $\operatorname{ln}⁡(s-1)$, is undefined at $s=1$ and hence discontinuous on $[-1,1].$

- The function $r(s)$ is **not** continuous on $[-1,1]$ because 
its third component, $\operatorname{csc}⁡s$, is undefined at $s=0$ and hence discontinuous on $[-1,1].$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the functions are continuous on $[-1,1].$""] ["question-48e5a226-dec1-538c-a739-b2da6b892931" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] "question-48e5a226-dec1-538c-a739-b2da6b892931"] [17592186115761 :question/problem "Which of the following vector-valued functions are continuous at $t=0?$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =\operatorname{cot}⁡t\,i+3{t}^{3}\,j+(2t+1)\,k \\ g(t) & =\frac{2}{t}\,i+{t}^{3}\,j+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k \\ h(t) & =2t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+{t}^{4}\,k\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186115761 :question/worked-solution "A vector-valued function is continuous at a point if and only if each of its components is continuous at that point.

Let's now consider the functions one-by-one.

- Function $f(t)$ is **not** continuous at $t=0$ since its first component $\operatorname{cot}⁡t$ is not continuous at $t=0.$ Indeed, the left and right limits are not equal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to +0}\operatorname{cot}⁡t=+\infty  \\ {lim}_{t\to -0}\operatorname{cot}⁡t=-\infty \end{aligned}
$$

 
Hence, ${lim}_{t\to 0}\operatorname{cot}⁡t$ doesn’t exist.

- Function $g(t)$ is **not** continuous at $t=0$ since its first component $\frac{2}{t}$ is not continuous at $t=0.$

$$

$$

On the other hand, we are told that

$$
{lim}_{t\to 5}[f(t)+3g(t)]=⟨1,3,1⟩.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 5}[f(t)+3g(t)] & =⟨1,3,1⟩ \\ f(5)+⟨-3,3,-6⟩ & =⟨1,3,1⟩ \\ f(5) & =⟨1,3,1⟩-⟨-3,3,-6⟩ \\ f(5) & =⟨4,0,7⟩\end{aligned}

$$

$$

On the other hand, we are told that:

$$
{lim}_{t\to 0}[f(t)-g(t)]=⟨-2,-3,0⟩
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}[f(t)-g(t)] & =⟨-2,-3,0⟩ \\ ⟨-2,-3,0⟩ & =f(0)-⟨-1,0,1⟩ \\ ⟨-2,-3,0⟩+⟨-1,0,1⟩ & =f(0) \\ f(0) & =⟨-3,-3,1⟩\end{aligned}

- The derivative of  $\frac{1}{t-4}$ is

$$
{(\frac{1}{t-4})}^{′}=-\frac{1}{(t-4)^{2}}.
$$

 
Since the derivative is defined for all the points on the interval $[0,4)\cup (4,\infty ),$ we conclude that  $\frac{1}{t-4}$ is differentiable on this interval.

- The derivative of  $-5{t}^{2}$ is

$$
{(-5{t}^{2})}^{′}=-10t.
$$

 
Since the derivative is defined for all the points on the interval $[0,4)\cup (4,\infty ),$ we conclude that  $-5{t}^{2}$ is differentiable on this interval.

:question/problem "Which of the following vector-valued functions are differentiable with respect to $t$ on $t\in (\pi ,2\pi )?$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =⟨{sin}^{2}⁡t,\,\frac{1}{t},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ g(t) & =⟨t\sqrt{t},\,1-{t}^{2},\,t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩ \\ h(t) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,2t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-d69b9419-ecda-5adb-b076-9a4d08de1698" :question/worked-solution "All of these vector-valued functions are defined for all  $t\in (\pi ,2\pi ).$ 

A function is differentiable on the interval $(\pi ,2\pi )$ if and only if each of its component functions is differentiable on that interval. 

Let's now consider the functions one-by-one.

- We differentiate $f(t)$ to find ${f}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({sin}^{2}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since each component of ${f}^{′}(t)$ is defined for all  $t\in (\pi ,2\pi )$, we conclude that $f(t)$ is differentiable on this interval.

- Next, we differentiate $g(t)$ to find ${g}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\sqrt{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3/2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2}{t}^{1/2},\,-2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{t},\,-2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since each component of  ${g}^{′}(t)$ is defined for all  $t\in (\pi ,2\pi )$, we have that $g(t)$ is differentiable on this interval.

- Finally, we differentiate $h(t)$ to find ${h}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,2,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since each component of  ${h}^{′}(t)$ is defined for all $t\in (\pi ,2\pi )$, we conclude that $h(t)$ is differentiable on this interval.

Therefore, the answer is: 

$\,$ All the functions are differentiable on $(\pi ,2\pi ).$"] ["question-d69b9419-ecda-5adb-b076-9a4d08de1698" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] $$
{(\sqrt{{t}^{2}-1})}^{′}=\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}-1}}.
$$

 
Since the derivative is not defined at $t=\pm 1,$ we conclude that  $\sqrt{{t}^{2}-1}$ is not differentiable at this points.

- The derivative of  $-\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is

$$
{(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 
Since the derivative is defined for all the points on the interval $(-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ),$ we conclude that  $-\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is differentiable on this interval.

For the function $g(t):$ 

- The first component, $\sqrt[3]{t-3}$, is differentiable over $(-\infty ,3)\cup (3,\infty )$ as its derivative is not defined at $t=3.$

- The second and third components, ${cos}^{2}⁡t$ and $\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}},$ are differentiable for all values of $t.$

Let's now find the intervals where each of the functions $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are differentiable.

For the function $f(t):$ 

- The first component $|t-1{|}^{3}$ is differentiable over $(-\infty ,1)\cup (1,\infty )$

- The second component $\operatorname{ln}⁡(t-1)$ is differentiable over $(1,\infty ).$

- The third component $t$ is differentiable for all values of $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

The intersection of the domains of all three components of $f(t)$ is $(1,\infty ).$ 

For the function $g(t):$ 

- The first component $\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}$ is differentiable over $(-2,2).$

- The second component ${e}^{\sqrt{t-1}}$ is differentiable for $(1,\infty ).$

- The third component ${t}^{3}$ is differentiable for all values of $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$

The intersection of the domains of all three components of $g(t)$ is $(1,2).$ 

Finally, the common domain of differentiability for both functions is

$$
(1,\infty )\cap (1,2)=(1,2).
$$"] ["question-ef76f5ac-70f5-5f95-86dd-2e2b577b8988" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-816ea349-9124-5703-a18d-858815a67291" :answer-field/id #uuid Let's now find the intervals where each of the functions $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are differentiable.

- The third component $(5+t)$ is differentiable for all values of $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

For the function $g(t):$ 

- The first component $\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ is differentiable for all values of $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

- The second component $\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is differentiable for all values of $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

- The third component $\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)$ is differentiable on $(-1,\infty ).$

The intersection of the domains of all three components of $g(t)$ is $(-1,\infty ).$

$$

A vector function $\mathbf f (t)$ is **continuous** at a point $t_0$ (in its domain) if

$$
\displaystyle \lim_{t \rightarrow t_0} \mathbf f (t) = \mathbf f (t_0).
$$

For example, the vector function 

$$
\mathbf f(t) = \left \langle e^t,  \dfrac{1}{t} \right \rangle
$$

is continuous at $t=1$ because

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}f(t) & =⟨{lim}_{t\to 1}({e}^{t}),\,{lim}_{t\to 1}(\frac{1}{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{1},\,\frac{1}{1}⟩ \\  & =⟨e,\,1⟩ \\  & =f(1)\end{aligned}
$$

Since the limit of a vector function is determined by the limits of the components, a vector function is continuous at a point $t_0$ *if and only if* each of its components is continuous at that point.

We say that a vector function is **continuous on the interval** $t\in[a,b]$ if it is continuous at every point of this interval."] [17592186116444 :tutorial/content "Similar to scalar-valued functions, the vector function $\mathbf{f}(t)$ is **differentiable** at a point $t = t_0$ in the domain of the function if the following limit exists:

$$
\lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{\mathbf{f}(t_0+h) - \mathbf{f}(t_0)}{h}
$$

The value of the limit is then called the **derivative** of $\mathbf{f}(t)$ at $t = t_0$ and is denoted as $\mathbf{f}'(t_0)$. In general, a vector function is differentiable *if and only if* all of its components are differentiable.

For example, is the following vector function $\mathbf{g}(t)$ differentiable at $t=0$?

$$
\mathbf{g}(t) = \big\langle t, \: |\,t\,|, \: \sin t \big\rangle
$$

Notice that the second component, $|\,t\,|,$ is not differentiable at $t=0.$ Since one of the component functions is not differentiable at $t=0,$ we conclude that the overall vector function $\mathbf{g}(t)$ is not differentiable at $t=0.$ 

We say that a vector function is **differentiable on an open interval** $t \in (a,b)$ if it is differentiable at *every* point $t \in (a,b).$ This means that each component of the function must be differentiable at every point of $(a,b).$

Our function $\mathbf{g}(t)$, mentioned above, is differentiable on $(-\infty, 0) \cup (0, \infty)$ since all of its components are differentiable there.

Finally, a function is said to be **continuously differentiable** if it is differentiable and its derivative is continuous."] [17592186115484 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0] [17592186115105 :question/problem "Plot the curve of $y=\log_7 (x+4).$"] [17592186115105 :question/worked-solution "To plot $y=\log_7 {(x+4)},$ we apply the following steps:

The diagram above shows the graph of $y=k{log}_{2}⁡(bx).$ Find the value of $k\cdot b.$"] ["question-736b21cf-cbb6-5fc6-8626-c4e49709882d" :question/worked-solution "Clearly, $b\ne 0.$ Substituting $x=\frac{1}{b}$ into the equation of the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =k{log}_{2}⁡(b\cdot \frac{1}{b}) \\  & =k{log}_{2}⁡1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the point $(\frac{1}{b},0)$ lies on the curve. But from the diagram, we know that $(3,0)$ lies on the curve. Hence

$$
(3,0)=(\frac{1}{b},0)\,⇒\,b=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Now, we substitute coordinates of the point $(6,2)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}k{log}_{2}⁡(bx) & =y \\ k{log}_{2}⁡(\frac{1}{3}x) & =y \\ k{log}_{2}⁡(\frac{1}{3}\cdot 6) & =2 \\ k{log}_{2}⁡2 & =2 \\ k & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
k\cdot b=2\cdot \frac{1}{3}=\frac{2}{3}.
$$"] ["question-736b21cf-cbb6-5fc6-8626-c4e49709882d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-27ae073a-5203-5077-b949-ae499f36c0ca" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
4-d=0\,⇒\,d=4.
$$

Now, we substitute coordinates of the point $(8,3)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{4}⁡(x-d)+c & =y \\ {log}_{4}⁡(x-4)+c & =y \\ {log}_{4}⁡(8-4)+c & =3 \\ {log}_{4}⁡(4)+c & =3 \\ 1+c & =3 \\ c & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\frac{d}{c}=\frac{4}{2}=2.
$$"] ["question-7ee0988d-03dd-5330-89a0-142478096881" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-d0661678-c752-58dd-ae45-19a8a3ab5f43" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{3}=3 \\ 4{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3}=18 \\ 2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{3}=9\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 4 & 1 & -8 & 18 \\ 2 & 0 & -3 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 6 \\ 2 & 0 & -3 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{3}=3 \\ {x}_{2}=6 \\ {x}_{3}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=3.$ Substituting into the first equation gives 

$$
{x}_{1}-2(3)=3\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=9.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}9{a}_{1}+6{a}_{2}+3{a}_{3} & =b \\ 9\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+6\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+3\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -8 \\ -3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 18 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}\cdot {x}_{3}=9\cdot 6\cdot 3=162.$"] ["question-ddfb229d-f01d-542c-8a6c-f2e9a5996154" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] $$
U = \left\{ x_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + x_2 \mathbf{a}_2 \: : \: x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R} \right\}.
$$

The set $U$ is also called the **linear span** of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2,$ and is denoted by $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}.$ We say that $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ are the **generators** of $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}.$

For example, let's find the linear span generated by the following vectors:
![](images/55/55c749dccc54c252b9120f148e383f395c09fb4cd4bec0e1cce8ed441ecb6199.svg)

$$
\mathbf{b} = x_1\mathbf{a_1} + x_2\mathbf{a_2}
$$

 for some $x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R}.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}b & ={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the linear span of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ is

Given that ${\sum }_{i=1}^{8}{x}_{i}{y}_{i}=695,$ calculate ${S}_{xy}.$"] ["question-7487be5e-d3cc-5ed9-9625-a2ce92482f7c" :question/worked-solution "Given a set of $n$ paired observations ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ and ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n},$ the sum of products of deviations from the means can be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i}{x}_{i}{y}_{i}-\frac{1}{n}({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i})({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i})\end{aligned}
$$

First, we calculate the sum of the ${x}_{i}$ and ${y}_{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} & =16+9+12+10+11+11+6+9=84, \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i} & =10+14+8+10+7+8+2+4=63\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that ${\sum }_{i=1}^{8}{x}_{i}{y}_{i}=695.$

Finally, by substituting in the above formula, we get

$$
{S}_{xy}=695-\frac{1}{8}(84)(63)=695-661.5=33.5.
$$"] ["question-7487be5e-d3cc-5ed9-9625-a2ce92482f7c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-71771a9c-6d44-5ba0-b159-1c1d1cb21717" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{y}^{2} & =\frac{{S}_{yy}}{n},\end{aligned}

- A set is *open* if it does not contain any of its boundary points. In other words, an open set consists only of the interior points of the set.

- A set is *closed* if it contains **all** of its boundary points. In other words, a closed set consists of all the interior and all the boundary points of the set.

Among the given sets, only $(1,6)$ is open. The boundary points are $1$, and $6.$ None of them lie in the set.

The other sets are not open because:

- $[0,15]$ has two boundary points $0$, and $15$, and both of them lie in the set.

- $(-3,5]\cup [6,8)$ has four boundary points $-3$, $5$, $6$, and $8$, and the points $5$ and $6$ lie in the set.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only"."] ["question-c7bf2d22-67db-5bfb-9d76-d999020db50d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-9c9d3d2d-5c89-5028-8119-349ee1ac7225" :question/problem "Is the function $f(x)={x}^{3}+8x$ even, odd, or neither?"] ["question-81602105-d969-550d-9191-b0d8d8e1aacf" :question/worked-solution "Recall that

- a function is even if $f(-x)=f(x)$ for all $x$

- a function is odd if $f(-x)=-f(x)$ for all $x$

Computing $f(-x)$ for the given function and comparing it to $f(x),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)^{3}+8(-x) \\  & =-{x}^{3}-8x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(-x)\ne f(x),$ the function is not even.

Lastly, we compute $-f(x)$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}-f(x) & =-({x}^{3}+8x) \\  & =-{x}^{3}-8x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(-x)=-f(x),$ the function is odd."] ["question-81602105-d969-550d-9191-b0d8d8e1aacf" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-94f1e14e-2d96-586a-93e5-1ee8371fd0d7" :question/worked-solution "The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨-2,2⟩-⟨-1,1⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,1⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}}⟨-1,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-y)^{2},\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-y)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨16{x}^{3}-8xy,\,2y-4{x}^{2}⟩ \\ ∇f(-1,1) & =⟨16(-1)^{3}-8(-1)(1),\,2(1)-4(-1)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-8,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(-1,1) & =∇f(-1,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨-8,-2⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟩ \\  & =(-8)\cdot (-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})-2\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}) \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-d5075c32-f624-572f-a2d3-78616466d14e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-aa2be9cd-8e25-5c22-a57c-dbf36efef798" :answer-field/id #uuid "The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{5} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(2i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\text{ }j \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡y+\frac{y}{x})\,i+(\frac{x}{y}+\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\,j \\ ∇\,f(1,1) & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡1+\frac{1}{1})\,i+(\frac{1}{1}+\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\,j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(1,1) & =∇\,f(1,1)\cdot u \\  & =(i+j)\cdot (\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}j) \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 2+1\cdot 1}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-f7872fd6-9c54-5e48-b08b-71d8ca0a2063" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-5f6b8a55-8b0f-5157-98ff-b7ec894bdaee" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{2} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

$g(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xyz$ increase most rapidly at the point $(1,0,-2)?$"] ["question-8889b56a-bb69-56d7-b6a6-42f214a1a3f7" :question/worked-solution "At a given point, a function $g(x,y,z)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute $∇g(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,0,-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y,z) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xyz),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xyz),\,\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xyz)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x-yz,\,2y-xz,\,2z-xy⟩ \\ ∇g(1,0,-2) & =⟨2(1)-0(-2),2(0)-1(-2),2(-2)-1(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,2,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of $⟨2,2,-4⟩.$"] ["question-8889b56a-bb69-56d7-b6a6-42f214a1a3f7" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] :question/problem "Consider the function $g(x,y)={y}^{x}.$ What is the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(1,e)$ in the direction of the vector $v=⟨4,-3⟩?$"] ["question-0fb365d6-3918-560a-af36-ae398310b595" :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(1,e)$ in the direction of $v$ is equal to the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(1,e).$ 

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+(-3)^{2}}=5 \\ u & =\frac{1}{5}⟨4,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the gradient $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{x}),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{x})⟩ \\  & =⟨{y}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,x{y}^{x-1}⟩ \\ ∇g(1,e) & =⟨{e}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡e,1{e}^{1-1}⟩ \\  & =⟨e,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(1,e)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{u}^{′}(1,e) & =∇g(1,e)\cdot u \\  & =⟨e,1⟩\cdot \frac{1}{5}⟨4,-3⟩ \\  & =\frac{e(4)+1(-3)}{5} \\  & =\frac{4e-3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-0fb365d6-3918-560a-af36-ae398310b595" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-75da4e92-2341-5f89-a517-37e979e4303c" :answer-field/id #uuid gradient at that point.

In our case, we compute $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(\frac{\pi }{4},4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x))⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{tan}⁡x,\,\frac{2}{y}⟩ \\ ∇\,g(\frac{\pi }{4},4) & =⟨-\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}),\,\frac{2}{4}⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(\frac{\pi }{4},4)$ in the direction of $∇g(\frac{\pi }{4},4)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}‖∇\,g(\frac{\pi }{4},4)‖ & =‖⟨-1,\frac{1}{2}⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{5}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-56172e38-6320-5f34-8b75-aab1067f37e6" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-45ab83aa-a438-50c5-87d1-85ddbe0b15e9" :answer-field/id #uuid A vector function $\mathbf f (t)$ is **continuous** at a point $t_0$ (in its domain) if

$$\displaystyle \lim_{t \rightarrow t_0} \mathbf f (t) = \mathbf f (t_0).$$

For example, the vector function

$$\mathbf f(t) = \left \langle e^t, \dfrac{1}{t} \right \rangle$$

is continuous at $t=1$ because

$$\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}f(t) & =⟨{lim}_{t\to 1}({e}^{t}),\,{lim}_{t\to 1}(\frac{1}{t})⟩ \\ & =⟨{e}^{1},\,\frac{1}{1}⟩ \\ & =⟨e,\,1⟩ \\ & =f(1)\end{aligned}$$

Since the limit of a vector function is determined by the limits of the components, a vector function is continuous at a point $t_0$ *if and only if* each of its components is continuous at that point.

We say that a vector function is **continuous on the interval** $t\in[a,b]$ if it is continuous at every point of this interval."] [17592186116444 :tutorial/content "Similar to scalar-valued functions, the vector function $\mathbf{f}(t)$ is **differentiable** at a point $t = t_0$ in the domain of the function if the following limit exists: $$\lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{\mathbf{f}(t_0+h) - \mathbf{f}(t_0)}{h}$$ The value of the limit is then called the **derivative** of $\mathbf{f}(t)$ at $t = t_0$ and is denoted as $\mathbf{f}'(t_0)$. In general, a vector function is differentiable *if and only if* all of its components are differentiable.

For example, is the following vector function $\mathbf{g}(t)$ differentiable at $t=0$? $$\mathbf{g}(t) = \big\langle t, \: |\,t\,|, \: \sin t \big\rangle$$

Notice that the second component, $|\,t\,|,$ is not differentiable at $t=0.$ Since one of the component functions is not differentiable at $t=0,$ we conclude that the overall vector function $\mathbf{g}(t)$ is not differentiable at $t=0.$

We say that a vector function is **differentiable on an open interval** $t \in (a,b)$ if it is differentiable at *every* point $t \in (a,b).$ This means that each component of the function must be differentiable at every point of $(a,b).$

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "The mass, in metric tons, of a meteor is modeled by the function $m(t)=20\cdot (0.4)^{t},$ where To calculate this, we find the meteor's mass after $2$ minutes, and we subtract its mass after $3$ minutes. So we need to evaluate

$$
m(2)-m(3).
$$

The mass of the meteor after $t=2$ minutes is equal to

$$
\begin{aligned}m(2) & =20\cdot (0.4)^{2} \\  & =20\cdot 0.16 \\  & =3.2.\end{aligned}
$$

The mass of the meteor after $t=3$ minutes is equal to

$$
\begin{aligned}m(3) & =20\cdot (0.4)^{3} \\  & =20\cdot 0.064 \\  & =1.28.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the total mass lost between the second and third minute is

$$
m(2)-m(3)=3.2-1.28=1.92.
$$

Therefore, the meteor's mass decreased by $1.92$ metric tons between the second and third minutes."} {:db/id 17592186115869 :question/id #uuid "977226b8-4490-5f1a-950f-1ae37c9b67f0" - $a=30\,000$ represents the initial value of the car (in dollars).

- $1-r=0.85,$ where $r$ is the decay rate.

- $t$ is the time since the start of the observations, in years.

Solving for $r,$ we get

$$
1-r=0.85\,⟹\,r=0.15.
$$

exponential decay expression or function.

For example, suppose that, due to overfishing, a fish population decays exponentially. The population $y(t)$ is given by

$$
y(t) = 5\,000 \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^t,
$$

where $t$ is the time, in months, since the overfishing began. What can we deduce about the population of fish from this model?

The first thing to notice is that the function above is an exponential decay function of the form

$$
y(t) = a \cdot b^t.
$$

So, we can deduce the following:

- $a=5\,000$ represents the initial value. So this tells us that there were $5\,000$ fish when the overfishing began.

- $b = \dfrac 1 2$ is the decay factor. Since $0 < b < 1,$ this tells us that we're dealing with exponential decay, *not* exponential growth (for exponential growth we need $b > 1$).

- $t$ is the time, in months, since the overfishing began." :tutorial/id #uuid "adec391e-8573-55bf-b53b-d5d15177f633" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1970 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "If $\frac{z}{3}-2y=1$ then $z=$" :question/worked-solution "We need to isolate the variable $z.$ To do this, we treat $y$ as though it were a constant and apply the addition and multiplication principles as usual.

First, we add $2y$ to both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{z}{3}-2y & =1 \\ \frac{z}{3}-2y+2y & =1+2y \\ \frac{z}{3} & =1+2y\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we multiply both sides of the equation by $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{z}{3} & =1+2y \\ 3\cdot \frac{z}{3} & =3\cdot (1+2y) \\ \cancel{3}\cdot \frac{z}{\cancel{3}} & =3\cdot (1+2y) \\ z & =3\cdot (1+2y) \\ z & =3\cdot 1+3\cdot 2y \\ z & =3+6y\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064349 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186063938 :question/id #uuid "3237ac51-d473-548d-b316-9425717c22bb" :question/math-academy-id "e-12907"} :knowledge-point/id First, we add $4b$ to both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}b-5c & =c-4b \\ b-5c+4b & =c-4b+4b \\ b+4b-5c & =c-4b+4b \\ 5b-5c & =c\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we add $5c$ to both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}5b-5c & =c \\ 5b-5c+5c & =c+5c \\ 5b & =6c\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides of the equation by $5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5b & =6c \\ \frac{5b}{5} & =\frac{6c}{5} \\ \frac{\cancel{5}b}{\cancel{5}} & =\frac{6c}{5} \\ b & =\frac{6c}{5}\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}2x-y & =y-x \\ 2x-y+y & =y-x+y \\ 2x & =-x+2y\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & =-x+2y \\ 2x+x & =-x+2y+x \\ 3x & =2y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides of the equation by $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3x & =2y \\ \frac{3x}{3} & =\frac{2y}{3} \\ \frac{\cancel{3}x}{\cancel{3}} & =\frac{2y}{3} \\ x & =\frac{2y}{3}\end{aligned}

17592186045487} :question/problem "Given the system of equations below, what is the value of $p-q?$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3p=15 \\ p+2q=9.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It doesn't matter which equation we pick first, so we choose the easiest one. In this case, the first equation looks like the easiest.

Using the first equation, we can isolate $p$ by dividing both sides of the equation by $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3p & =15 \\ p & =5\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $p=5$ into $p+2q=9,$ then we can find the value of $q:$

$$
\begin{aligned}p+2q & =9 \\ (5)+2q & =9 \\ 2q & =4 \\ q & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $p=5,\,q=2.$ So,

$$
p-q=5-2=3.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186233560 :question/id #uuid "ba03c851-f080-5b98-bcba-fc2174ffc663" :question/math-academy-id "q-167194"} {:db/id 17592186233567 :question/id #uuid :question/problem "Given the system of equations below, what is the value of $a-b?$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}a=7 \\ 3a+6b=15\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It so happens that the first equation is already solved for $a:$

$$
a=7
$$

If we now substitute $a=7$ into $3a+6b=15,$ then we can find the value of $b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3a+6b & =15 \\ 3(7)+6b & =15 \\ 6b & =-6 \\ b & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $a=7,\,b=-1.$ So,

$$
a-b=7-(-1)=7+1=8.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186558573 :question/id #uuid "f2633cd2-d747-5eed-ad0b-333971ef5a97" :question/math-academy-id "q-181154"} {:db/id 17592186562396 :question/id #uuid :db/id 17592186546940}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Given the system of equations below, what is the value of $a+b?$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2b=6a+14 \\ 5b+25=0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "We number the equations so that we can refer to them more easily:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2b=6a+14 & \,\,(1) \\ 5b+25=0. & \,\,(2)\end{aligned}
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $(2),$ we can solve for $b$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5b+25 & =0 \\ 5b & =-25 \\ b & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $b=-5$ into equation $(1)$ and solve for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(-5) & =6a+14 \\ -10 & =6a+14 \\ -10-14 & =6a \\ 6a & =-24 \\ a & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content {:db/id 17592186070022 :tutorial/content "A **function** is a rule that takes a number as **input** and then **outputs** another number.

For instance, let's look at the following function: 

$$
f(x) = 3x+1
$$

In this example,

- $f$ is the **name** of the function,

- the number $x$ is the **input**,

- the number $3x+1$ is the **output**.

If we **substitute** a number into our function in place of $x$, we get another number as output. 

For example, by substituting $x={\color{blue}{2}},$ we get

$$
f({\color{blue}{2}}) = 3\cdot {\color{blue}{2}}+1 = 7.
$$

So, the input $x={\color{blue}{2}}$ results in an output of $7.$

We can substitute any number we like into this function! For example, if we substitute $x={\color{red}{-2}},$ we get

$$
f({\color{red}{-2}}) = 3\cdot ({\color{red}{-2}})+1 = -5.
$$

So, the input $x={\color{red}{-2}}$ results in an output of $-5.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "902a3802-7423-5fa0-9cf1-43856055c65c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8783 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "726a2782-726c-5f7e-b8e5-138b8563ebff" :step/math-academy-id 138156 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069579}} {:db/id 17592186069579 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068701 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068486 :question/id #uuid "38228952-21ef-5caf-9805-76e42ebf0caa" :question/math-academy-id "e-14148"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4e5366dd-a374-5abd-bdf6-77f378f97145" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048594} {:db/id 17592186049299} {:db/id 17592186050127}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069041} {:db/id 17592186069115} {:db/id 17592186069123} {:db/id 17592186233385} {:db/id 17592186233396} {:db/id 17592186233405} {:db/id 17592186233561} {:db/id 17592186233568} {:db/id 17592186233575} {:db/id 17592186482561} {:db/id 17592186482574} {:db/id 17592186492831} {:db/id 17592186492850} {:db/id 17592186492901} {:db/id 17592186522723}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Function"} :step/id #uuid "8af30817-9be7-537a-9bfb-2ce31b525422" :step/math-academy-id 138157 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069580}} {:db/id 17592186069580 :step/content {:db/id 17592186070023 :tutorial/content "Functions with more than one input are called **multivariable functions**. 

For example, the multivariable function 

$$
f(x,y)=x-y
$$

takes in two numbers, $x$ and $y$, and returns their difference. 

For multivariable functions, the order of the inputs matters. For example, if we substitute $x={\color{blue}{3}}$ and $y={\color{red}{2}},$ we get

$$
f({\color{blue}{3}},{\color{red}{2}}) = {\color{blue}{3}}-{\color{red}{2}}=1,
$$

whereas if we substitute $x={\color{red}{2}}$ and $y={\color{blue}{3}},$ we get a different output:

$$
f({\color{red}{2}},{\color{blue}{3}})={\color{red}{2}}-{\color{blue}{3}}=-1
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "0bef6d6f-bda2-56dd-badb-0001ca2e4329" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8784 :tutorial/title "Evaluating Functions of More Than One Variable"} :step/id #uuid "004a3461-1ea4-5e28-807b-fea6c51ae3d4" :step/math-academy-id 138161 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069581}} {:db/id 17592186069581 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068702 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068487 :question/id #uuid "4e06fa0b-f3f0-5e60-9a83-67a393b4cc07" :question/math-academy-id "e-14150"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2b5f42de-fad6-54b6-90e1-205fdbe8a456" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069042} {:db/id 17592186069116} {:db/id 17592186069124} {:db/id 17592186482526} {:db/id 17592186482569} {:db/id 17592186492852} {:db/id 17592186544826} {:db/id 17592186544830} {:db/id 17592186544841}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Multivariable Function"} :step/id #uuid "e7679093-39bc-5822-a013-8ae88e7f542e" :step/math-academy-id 138162}] :activity/title "Introduction to Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186068995} {:db/id 17592186069578 :step/content {:db/id 17592186070022 :tutorial/content "A **function** is a rule that takes a number as **input** and then **outputs** another number.

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186074657 :step/content {:db/id 17592186075033 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to solve, *without* using graphs, the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y &=4 \\ x-2 &=y\,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

In order to solve the system without a graph, we will need to combine the equations into a single equation that can be solved using algebraic manipulation.

One way to combine the equations is called the **substitution method.** To use the substitution method, we substitute for one variable in terms of the other.

For instance, notice that we can make $y$ the subject of the second equation:

$$
\color{red}y=x - 2
$$

Substituting this expression for $y$ into the first equation, we get an equation that we can solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y & =4 \\ x+(x-2) & =4 \\ 2x-2 & =4 \\ 2x & =6 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution must have $x=3.$ But we also need to figure out what $y$ is. We can do this by substituting $x=3$ back into the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =x-2 \\ y & =3-2 \\ y & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x = 3$ and $y = 1$, which can be written as $\left(3, 1\right).$

**Note:** Whenever we isolate the variable in one equation, we have to substitute it into the *other* equation. We cannot substitute a variable into the same equation it came from, because this will not give us any more information about the variable." :tutorial/id #uuid "e1e8cb2d-3d4e-5cb9-8947-2bd9deb11b89" $$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y &=4 \\ x-2 &=y\,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

In order to solve the system without a graph, we will need to combine the equations into a single equation that can be solved using algebraic manipulation.

One way to combine the equations is called the **substitution method.** To use the substitution method, we substitute for one variable in terms of the other.

For instance, notice that we can make $y$ the subject of the second equation:

$$
\color{red}y=x - 2
$$

Substituting this expression for $y$ into the first equation, we get an equation that we can solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y & =4 \\ x+(x-2) & =4 \\ 2x-2 & =4 \\ 2x & =6 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution must have $x=3.$ But we also need to figure out what $y$ is. We can do this by substituting $x=3$ back into the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =x-2 \\ y & =3-2 \\ y & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x = 3$ and $y = 1$, which can be written as $\left(3, 1\right).$

**Note:** Whenever we isolate the variable in one equation, we have to substitute it into the *other* equation. $$
\{\begin{aligned}3p=15 \\ p+2q=9.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It doesn't matter which equation we pick first, so we choose the easiest one. In this case, the first equation looks like the easiest.

Using the first equation, we can isolate $p$ by dividing both sides of the equation by $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3p & =15 \\ p & =5\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $p=5$ into $p+2q=9,$ then we can find the value of $q:$

$$
\begin{aligned}p+2q & =9 \\ (5)+2q & =9 \\ 2q & =4 \\ q & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $p=5,\,q=2.$ So,

$$
p-q=5-2=3.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0a9225c0-5f39-5569-928a-3834451e9d52" :step/next {:db/id 17592186547152}} {:db/id 17592186547152 :step/content {:db/id 17592186546991 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b85cb2c-460d-5f91-86c0-674d13fae83e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-9" :db/id 17592186546309} {:answer/id #uuid "242eed59-c937-5dab-b478-b3a1accb9d4f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186546329} {:answer/id #uuid "463e0a8b-5e11-54a2-8cdd-72b176626176" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186546407} {:answer/id #uuid "6a785a85-c477-5db9-a10d-570f963f9181" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186546485} {:answer/id #uuid "f5ff80ce-ffb0-542a-ba50-ce8557612884" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186546805}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186546309} :answer-field/id #uuid "e282d81b-1bfe-5c5b-abe6-d91779057814" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186546940}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3b789afd-79c7-56fc-b94a-f894f177dfe2" :question/math-academy-id "q-18555" :question/problem "Given the system of equations below, what is the value of $a+b?$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2b=6a+14 \\ 5b+25=0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "We number the equations so that we can refer to them more easily:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2b=6a+14 & \,\,(1) \\ 5b+25=0. & \,\,(2)\end{aligned}
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $(2),$ we can solve for $b$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5b+25 & =0 \\ 5b & =-25 \\ b & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $b=-5$ into equation $(1)$ and solve for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(-5) & =6a+14 \\ -10 & =6a+14 \\ -10-14 & =6a \\ 6a & =-24 \\ a & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $a=-4,\,b=-5.$ So,

$$

$$"} :step/id #uuid "ca7de6ad-e459-52ba-851d-06dd86cc6059" :step/next {:db/id 17592186547164}} {:db/id 17592186547164 :step/content {:db/id 17592186546971 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "25d7a53c-5916-5db7-992b-ff7a626a51c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5" :db/id 17592186546336} {:answer/id #uuid "51399b6f-2763-5014-9b02-635633f0dada" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186546427} {:answer/id #uuid "9e23c320-e17b-534f-8a91-354568ebc163" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186546603} {:answer/id #uuid "a3f272eb-ffc1-5fb6-b622-055a0def12d3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186546617} {:answer/id #uuid "d9f37f2b-79d8-5ebd-8615-8e1bcfb28380" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186546732}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186546732} :answer-field/id #uuid "78ca5c4c-b502-5598-a6f0-d81d606b319e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186546881}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "1ad70587-af92-55e0-95cf-31aa82c10e13" :question/math-academy-id "q-52115" :question/problem "Given the system of equations below, what is the value of $a-b?$

#uuid "1ad70587-af92-55e0-95cf-31aa82c10e13" :question/math-academy-id "q-52115" :question/problem "Given the system of equations below, what is the value of $a-b?$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}a=7 \\ 3a+6b=15\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It so happens that the first equation is already solved for $a:$

$$
a=7
$$

If we now substitute $a=7$ into $3a+6b=15,$ then we can find the value of $b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3a+6b & =15 \\ 3(7)+6b & =15 \\ 6b & =-6 \\ b & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $a=7,\,b=-1.$ So,

$$
a-b=7-(-1)=7+1=8.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "e5c9a09f-e906-5432-9fef-4ec9ba80344e"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "25d7a53c-5916-5db7-992b-ff7a626a51c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5" :step/content {:db/id 17592186056069 :tutorial/content "Let's think about how to factor the following trinomial:

$$
x^2 + 7x + 12
$$

This trinomial is neither a perfect square nor a difference of squares. In such cases, the factoring process requires a little trial and error.

We can factor this trinomial in four steps:

- **Step 1:** Find the factor pairs of the constant term $(12)$:The factor pairs of $12$ are
$(1, 12), (2, 6), (3, 4)$.
- **Step 2:** Determine which of these factor pairs add up to the coefficient of the linear term $(7)$:
$\begin{bmatrix}1 + 12|= 13 & \cdot \\ 2 + 6|= 8 & \cdot \\ 3 + 4|= 7 & ✓\end{bmatrix}$
- **Step 3:** Using the factor pair identified in the previous step, write the linear term as $7x=3x+4x$:
$x^{2} + 7x + 12|=; x^{2} + 3x + 4x_(⏟)_(7x) + 12$
- **Step 4:** Factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately and then factor the expression completely:
$x^{2} + 3x + 4x + 12|=; (x^{2} + 3x) + (4x + 12)|=; x(x + 3) + 4(x + 3)|=; (x + 4)(x + 3)$

And we're done!

Before we continue, note the following:

- The process carried out in step 4 is sometimes called **factoring by grouping.** This is because we group two sets of terms and factor them individually before factoring the entire expression.
- We can check that our answer is correct by multiplying out the factors:
$(x + 4)(x + 3)|= x(x + 3) + 4(x + 3); = x^{2} + 3x + 4x + 12; = x^{2} + 7x + 12✓$" :tutorial/id #uuid "90a8aa34-4549-57c2-bdc2-24cc962cd306" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8891 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "add682be-a6dd-51b0-a261-ba8a3f84b958" :step/math-academy-id 178072 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055609}} {:db/id 17592186055609 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054658 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054476 :question/id #uuid "1e0116a2-6f90-5b57-97c1-6a64b45c9cef" :question/math-academy-id "e-14343"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3c9ba00d-9171-5732-8539-2e2943cce58e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048351} {:db/id 17592186051017}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055108} {:db/id 17592186055495} {:db/id 17592186055497} {:db/id 17592186233563} {:db/id 17592186233570} {:db/id 17592186233577}] :knowledge-point/title "Factoring Trinomials With Positive Coefficients"} :step/id #uuid "072ef290-5a3e-575d-a0fd-7d8084343f23" :step/math-academy-id 178073 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055610}} {:db/id 17592186055610 :step/content {:db/id 17592186056070 :tutorial/content "Let's now consider the following trinomial:

$$
x^2 - 2x - 8
$$

Notice that the constant term $(-8)$ is *negative*. So, when writing down our factor pairs, one number will always be positive, and the other will always be negative.

So, first, we write down all factor pairs of $-8{:}$

$$
(1,-8), (-1, 8), (2,-4), (-2, 4)
$$

Now, we find which factor pair adds up to the coefficient of the linear term $(-2)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{bmatrix}1 + (-8) &= -7 & \cdot \\ (-1) + 8|= 7 & \cdot \\ 2 + (-4)|=-2 & ✓ \\ (-2) + 4|= 2 & \cdot\end{bmatrix}
\end{aligned}
$$

Using the factor pair identified above, write the linear term as

$$
-2x = 2x-4x
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{2} - 2x - 8 &=  \\
&= x^{2} + 2x - 4x - 8
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately, and then factor the expression completely:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{2} + 2x - 4x - 8 &=  \\
(x^{2} + 2x) + (-4x - 8) &=  \\
x(x + 2) - 4(x + 2) &=  \\
&= (x - 4)(x + 2)
\end{aligned}
$$

Let's see another example." :tutorial/id #uuid "3b5a5752-232b-5714-b74a-1e50c4210b83" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8894 :tutorial/title "Trinomials With Negative Constants"} :step/id #uuid "232a2780-b6bf-56f2-b607-6b8d27ae3f25" :step/math-academy-id 178077 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055611}} {:db/id 17592186055611 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054659 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054478 :question/id #uuid "41c3e610-0259-59db-9494-3af6f47c7360" :question/math-academy-id "e-14350"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ac258511-5028-5fc8-9843-99309b36a38e" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055130} {:db/id 17592186055229} {:db/id 17592186055231} {:db/id 17592186459240} {:db/id 17592186480700} {:db/id 17592186487383} {:db/id 17592186491186} {:db/id 17592186498516}] :knowledge-point/title "Factoring Trinomials With Negative Constants"} :step/id #uuid "47e26748-840d-518f-8679-595bc9b0406d" :step/math-academy-id 178078 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055612}} {:db/id 17592186055612 :step/content {:db/id 17592186056076 :tutorial/content "Remember that to factor a quadratic expression, we must find a factor pair of the constant term that adds to the coefficient of the linear term.

With that in mind, let's factor the following trinomial:

$$
x^2 - 7x+12
$$

Notice that,

- the constant term $(12)$ is *positive*, while
- the coefficient of the linear term $(-7)$ is *negative*.

Since the constant is *positive* and the coefficient of the linear term is *negative*, we must first consider the *negative* factor pairs of the constant term $(12)$. These are as follows:

$$
(-1,-12),\qquad (-2,-6),\qquad (-3,-4)
$$

For each pair, their *product* is positive, and their *sum* is negative, which is what we want.

Now, we find which factor pair adds up to the coefficient of the linear term $(-7)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{bmatrix}(-1) + (-12) &= -13 & \cdot \\ (-2) + (-6)|=-8 & \cdot \\ (-3) + (-4)|=-7 & ✓\end{bmatrix}
\end{aligned}
$$

Using the factor pair identified in the previous step, write the linear term as

$$
-7x = -3x - 4x
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{2} - 7x + 12 &=  \\
&= x^{2} - 3x - 4x + 12
\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{2} - 3x - 4x + 12 &=  \\
(x^{2} - 3x) + (-4x + 12) &=  \\
&= x(x - 3) + 4(-x + 3)
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to get a *common* factor in both terms, we take an additional factor of $-1$ from the second term:

$$
x(x - 3) - 4(x - 3)
$$

Now that we have a common factor of $(x-3)$, we factor the expression fully in the usual way:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x(x - 3) - 4(x - 3) &=  \\
&= (x - 3)(x - 4)
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "25f481d5-38d8-5f35-95fc-dd74f97d0394" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9504 :tutorial/title "Trinomials With Negative Linear Coefficients and Positive Constants"} :step/id #uuid "47589875-8a7f-5cea-a2cf-0da701bb35ac" :step/math-academy-id 178082 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055613}} {:db/id 17592186055613 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054660 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054477 :question/id #uuid "f51ebe90-e58a-5712-84b8-4367ed18d58e" :question/math-academy-id "e-14346"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "65a95770-9419-5a8f-b264-58cca3e3c0db" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055109} {:db/id 17592186055131} {:db/id 17592186055496}] :knowledge-point/title "Factoring Trinomials With Negative Linear Coefficients and Positive Constants"} :step/id #uuid "87945626-63e1-5990-b1f8-6d13138cf85c" :step/math-academy-id 178083}] :activity/title "Factoring Trinomials" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186054931} {:db/id 17592186055608 :step/content {:db/id 17592186056069 :tutorial/content "Let's think about how to factor the following trinomial:

Now that we have a common factor of $(x-3)$, we factor the expression fully in the usual way:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x(x - 3) - 4(x - 3) &=  \\
&= (x - 3)(x - 4)
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "25f481d5-38d8-5f35-95fc-dd74f97d0394" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9504 :tutorial/title "Trinomials With Negative Linear Coefficients and Positive Constants"} {:db/id 17592186055613 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054660 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054477 :question/id #uuid "f51ebe90-e58a-5712-84b8-4367ed18d58e" :question/math-academy-id "e-14346"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "65a95770-9419-5a8f-b264-58cca3e3c0db" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055109} {:db/id 17592186055131} {:db/id 17592186055496}] :knowledge-point/title "Factoring Trinomials With Negative Linear Coefficients and Positive Constants"} :step/id #uuid "87945626-63e1-5990-b1f8-6d13138cf85c" :step/math-academy-id 178083} {:activity/expected-seconds 780.0 :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186134608} :activity/id #uuid "25739194-82c1-5788-9ee1-b6fee61cbd79" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049399 :topic/id #uuid "f1aa8ae2-23cf-5d91-8af0-a43e9db5e668" :topic/math-academy-id 2214} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134608 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135191 :tutorial/content "The explicit formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is

$$
a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d, \quad n \geq 1.
$$

Every arithmetic sequence can also be written using the following recursive formula:

![](images/a2/a2d28772cb4cb6078d2fccdca054ec1c2dccf27a5ea0b5972b9ac174eaad671f.svg)

For example, suppose that we're given the following explicit formula for an arithmetic sequence:

$$
a_n =2n+6, \quad n\geq 1
$$

To convert to a recursive formula, we just need to work out the first term and common difference. The first two terms are

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =2(1)+6=8 \\ {a}_{2} & =2(2)+6=10,\end{aligned}
$$

and the common difference is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={a}_{2}-{a}_{1} \\  & =10-8 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the first term is $a_1={\color{blue}8}$ and the common difference is $d={\color{red}2}.$ Therefore, the recursive formula is as follows:

$$
a_{n+1} = a_n + {\color{red}2}, \quad a_1 = {\color{blue}8}, \quad n \geq 1
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b6cd14c7-922b-5e05-9c8e-b842717155ad" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8910 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "02ae2395-79da-5dc3-9f17-a75936abdc07" :step/math-academy-id 191930 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134609}} {:db/id 17592186134609 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133746 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133531 :question/id #uuid "00113d76-b950-513e-a3ea-29eef91c9cec" :question/math-academy-id "e-14383"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9b8b10a8-f81a-5dae-b54e-b10959e3ad14" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050157} {:db/id 17592186050380}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134163} {:db/id 17592186134446} {:db/id 17592186560987} {:db/id 17592186561011}] :knowledge-point/title "Converting an Explicit Formula to a Recursive Formula"} :step/id #uuid "ed82570d-8cc5-564d-8da6-d86c3395fced" :step/math-academy-id 191931 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134610}} {:db/id 17592186134610 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133747 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133532 :question/id #uuid "e04ad3e0-888e-51c0-b60c-e816b7df514b" :question/math-academy-id "e-14386"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d36a3a61-e23b-5ce3-ac65-f7ac1691ec4e" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134177} {:db/id 17592186134447} {:db/id 17592186560975} {:db/id 17592186561005}] :knowledge-point/title "Converting an Explicit Formula to a Recursive Formula Using Function Notation"} :step/id #uuid "340d50dc-babe-5074-be5e-52e39f437e88" :step/math-academy-id 191934 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134611}} {:db/id 17592186134611 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135192 :tutorial/content "It's often more useful to translate from the recursive formula to an explicit one. So how do we find the explicit formula for the arithmetic sequence defined recursively as

$$
a_{n+1} = a_n + {\color{red}1},\, \quad a_1 = {\color{blue}6},\, \quad n\geq 1?
$$

The explicit formula is

$$
a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d, \quad n \geq 1,
$$

so we just need to determine the first term $a_1$ and the common difference $d.$

We are given that the first term is $a_1={\color{blue}6},$ and we can use the recursive rule to compute the second term, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & ={a}_{1}+1 \\  & =6+1 \\  & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Using the first and second terms, we can compute the common difference:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={a}_{2}-{a}_{1} \\  & =7-6 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute $a_1 = {\color{blue}6}$ and $d={\color{red}1}$ into the formula for the $n$th term:

$$
\eqalign{
a_n&= a_{1}+(n-1)d \[3pt]
&= {\color{blue}6} + (n - 1)({\color{red}1}) \[3pt]
& =6 + n-1\[3pt]
&=n+5
}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is

$$
a_n=n+5, \quad n \geq 1.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c6c5b9f8-4c71-5c1f-8841-3f22646e5074" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8914 :tutorial/title "Translating From the Recursive to the Explicit Formula"} :step/id #uuid "7cd53e1d-4c0c-570b-bef4-68f8081c2fef" :step/math-academy-id 191938 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134612}} {:db/id 17592186134612 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133748 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133533 :question/id #uuid "d732cfb5-9db5-535d-adb1-5d3292f1c497" :question/math-academy-id "e-14389"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "36e1e439-ec4a-5577-80d5-3b113bf36e74" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134056} {:db/id 17592186134164} {:db/id 17592186233564} {:db/id 17592186233571} {:db/id 17592186233578} {:db/id 17592186560995} {:db/id 17592186561033}] :knowledge-point/title "Converting a Recursive Formula to an Explicit Formula"} :step/id #uuid "2a238f59-a780-5248-bfa5-a217bec91d6c" :step/math-academy-id 191939 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134613}} {:db/id 17592186134613 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133749 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133534 :question/id #uuid "26b3b89d-d485-51ac-b964-8377ce3aff28" :question/math-academy-id "e-14393"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "baac268a-629e-5887-885a-49393c72776f" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134178} {:db/id 17592186134479} {:db/id 17592186560974} {:db/id 17592186561053}] :knowledge-point/title "Converting a Recursive Formula to an Explicit Formula Using Function Notation"} :step/id #uuid "c81f0b63-4b36-56b0-bc0f-1535d35453ef" :step/math-academy-id 191943}] :activity/title "Translating Between Explicit and Recursive Formulas for Arithmetic Sequences" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186134049} {:db/id 17592186134608 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135191 :tutorial/content "The explicit formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is

(The non-negative integers consist of the numbers $0$, $1$, $2$, $3$, and so on.)

Some examples of polynomial terms include

$$
x^2, \qquad \dfrac 1 3 x^6,\qquad x, \qquad 1
$$

Let's go through each one:

- $x^{\color{blue}2}$ is a polynomial term because the power of the variable is ${\color{blue}2}$, a non-negative integer.
- $\dfrac{1}{3} x^{\color{blue}6}$ is a polynomial term because the power of the variable is ${\color{blue}6}$, which is also a non-negative integer. The coefficient of $\dfrac 1 3$ isn't important.
- $x$ is a polynomial term because it can be thought of as $x^{\color{blue}1}$. So the power of the variable is ${\color{blue}1}$, which is a non-negative integer.
- Finally, $1$ is a polynomial term because it can be expressed as $1\cdot x^{\color{blue}0}$. So the power of the variable is ${\color{blue}0}$, which is a non-negative integer.

On the other hand, the following expressions are *not* polynomial terms because their powers are not non-negative integers:

$$
4x^{-2}, \qquad x^{1/3}, \qquad {\sqrt{\color{black}x}}, \qquad {\dfrac{\color{black}1}{x^3}}
$$

To see why, let's go through each one:

- $4x^{\color{red}-2}$ is not a polynomial term because the power of the variable is ${\color{red}-2}$, which is negative.
- $x^{\color{red}1/3}$ is not a polynomial term because the power of the variable is ${\color{red}1/3}$, which is not an integer.
- $\sqrt x$ is not a polynomial term because it can be written as $x^{\color{red}1/2}$. So the power of the variable is ${\color{red}1/2}$, which is not an integer.
- Finally, $\dfrac 1 {x^3}$ is not a polynomial term because it can be written as $x^{-\color{red}3}$. So the power of the variable is ${\color{red}-3}$, which is negative." :tutorial/id #uuid "a11e9fb3-6fe1-547c-996f-fb83d15a47d0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1578 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0500aa37-469a-53bd-a5da-8fbb0fe569cc" :step/math-academy-id 4106 :step/next {:db/id 17592186079458}} {:db/id 17592186079458 :step/content {:db/id 17592186078529 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186078153 :question/id #uuid "0690af9e-ae28-50a0-b2fd-0a9c3baaec3e" :question/math-academy-id "e-1280"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c12f648d-f276-5123-b6aa-b222ad108825" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049089} {:db/id 17592186050495}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186079068} {:db/id 17592186079149}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Polynomial Terms"} :step/id #uuid "ad32752d-72d3-5211-adbf-f50f0a51075b" :step/math-academy-id 4107 :step/next {:db/id 17592186079459}} {:db/id 17592186079459 :step/content {:db/id 17592186079622 :tutorial/content "A **polynomial** is a sum of polynomial terms, such as

For example, to evaluate the polynomial $2x^2+3$ at $x=5$, we substitute $x=5$ into the expression and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2x^{2} + 3 &=  \\
2(5)^{2} + 3 &=  \\
2(25) + 3 &=  \\
50 + 3 &=  \\

(The non-negative integers consist of the numbers $0$, $1$, $2$, $3$, and so on.)

Some examples of polynomial terms include

$$
x^2, \qquad \dfrac 1 3 x^6,\qquad x, \qquad 1
$$

Let's go through each one:

- $x^{\color{blue}2}$ is a polynomial term because the power of the variable is ${\color{blue}2}$, a non-negative integer.
- $\dfrac{1}{3} x^{\color{blue}6}$ is a polynomial term because the power of the variable is ${\color{blue}6}$, which is also a non-negative integer. The coefficient of $\dfrac 1 3$ isn't important.
- $x$ is a polynomial term because it can be thought of as $x^{\color{blue}1}$. So the power of the variable is ${\color{blue}1}$, which is a non-negative integer.
- Finally, $1$ is a polynomial term because it can be expressed as $1\cdot x^{\color{blue}0}$. So the power of the variable is ${\color{blue}0}$, which is a non-negative integer.

On the other hand, the following expressions are *not* polynomial terms because their powers are not non-negative integers:

$$
4x^{-2}, \qquad x^{1/3}, \qquad {\sqrt{\color{black}x}}, \qquad {\dfrac{\color{black}1}{x^3}}
$$

To see why, let's go through each one:

- $4x^{\color{red}-2}$ is not a polynomial term because the power of the variable is ${\color{red}-2}$, which is negative.
- $x^{\color{red}1/3}$ is not a polynomial term because the power of the variable is ${\color{red}1/3}$, which is not an integer.
- $\sqrt x$ is not a polynomial term because it can be written as $x^{\color{red}1/2}$. So the power of the variable is ${\color{red}1/2}$, which is not an integer.
- Finally, $\dfrac 1 {x^3}$ is not a polynomial term because it can be written as $x^{-\color{red}3}$. :question/problem "If $b-5c=c-4b,$ then $b=$" :question/worked-solution "We need to isolate the variable $b.$ To do this, we treat $c$ as though it were a constant and apply the addition and multiplication principles as usual.

First, we add $4b$ to both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}b-5c & =c-4b \\ b-5c+4b & =c-4b+4b \\ b+4b-5c & =c-4b+4b \\ 5b-5c & =c\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we add $5c$ to both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}5b-5c & =c \\ 5b-5c+5c & =c+5c \\ 5b & =6c\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides of the equation by $5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5b & =6c \\ \frac{5b}{5} & =\frac{6c}{5} \\ \frac{\cancel{5}b}{\cancel{5}} & =\frac{6c}{5} \\ b & =\frac{6c}{5}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "c76c91ea-1fa5-50f4-8d7c-4155dbbf366c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186495259}} {:db/id 17592186495259 :step/content {:db/id 17592186495052 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "01b21b33-50e5-5cbe-9b22-24f73902555e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1+2y}{3}" :db/id 17592186494322} {:answer/id #uuid "15ea45d4-5b0c-536f-977e-e4f7ad0b6a37" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3+6y" :db/id 17592186494357} {:answer/id #uuid "cabe9447-7e18-5fc2-b800-d12efc44ec31" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3-6y" :db/id 17592186494798} {:answer/id #uuid "eb9cf60f-e518-550d-b474-33adf1d185b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2y-1}{3}" :db/id 17592186494878} {:answer/id #uuid "f0e2634c-f79a-5536-b6e7-b72d016dd451" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3-2y" :db/id 17592186494889}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186494357} :answer-field/id #uuid "b4aba618-e4e2-5bd3-9df6-670dd46cecef" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186495003}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "041420d0-7112-5aa8-8e70-44b04f8459e6" :question/math-academy-id "q-135011" :question/problem "If $\frac{z}{3}-2y=1$ then $z=$" :question/worked-solution "We need to isolate the variable $z.$ To do this, we treat $y$ as though it were a constant and apply the addition and multiplication principles as usual.

$$

Then, we multiply both sides of the equation by $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{z}{3} & =1+2y \\ 3\cdot \frac{z}{3} & =3\cdot (1+2y) \\ \cancel{3}\cdot \frac{z}{\cancel{3}} & =3\cdot (1+2y) \\ z & =3\cdot (1+2y) \\ z & =3\cdot 1+3\cdot 2y \\ z & =3+6y\end{aligned}

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We need to isolate the variable $x.$ To do this, we treat $y$ as though it were a constant and apply the addition and multiplication principles as usual.

First, we add $y$ to both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-y & =y-x \\ 2x-y+y & =y-x+y \\ 2x & =-x+2y\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}2x & =-x+2y \\ 2x+x & =-x+2y+x \\ 3x & =2y\end{aligned}
$$

To find the axis of symmetry, we take the average of the roots, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2} \\  & =\frac{k-2}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{k-2}{2} & =6 \\ k-2 & =12 \\ k & =14.\end{aligned}

"![](images/b2/b27906f92121928be444d3b7f616becbcc7a849e1313ef50accd8c8bfd718bfb.png)

If we know two points on a parabola with *identical* $y$-values, we can find the $x$-coordinate of the vertex by taking an average of the two $x$-values. 

For example, consider the parabola $y=f(x)$ above. Notice that the values of $f(x)$ at the points $x=-3$ and $x=5$ are equal.

$$
f(-3) = f(5) = 3
$$

Therefore, the parabola's axis of symmetry must be equidistant from the lines $x=-3$ and $x=5.$ We can find this by taking the average of these two values.

If the parabola's vertex is $(h,k),$ then we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}h & =\frac{-3+5}{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $h=1$ is the $x$-coordinate of the vertex, and the axis of symmetry of the parabola is $x=1.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "23d4f6e0-c0a7-5551-bd88-80b3268a5b2b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13792 :tutorial/title "Extending the Formula"} :step/id #uuid "1b132072-c297-50ce-be49-d3a763e0a32f" :step/math-academy-id 502439 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111697}} {:db/id 17592186111821 :tutorial/content "![](images/b2/b27906f92121928be444d3b7f616becbcc7a849e1313ef50accd8c8bfd718bfb.png)

\dfrac{4x^3-x}{3x^3+24}.$" :question/worked-solution "To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to\infty.$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is $x^3.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by $x^3,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{4{x}^{3}-x}{3{x}^{3}+24} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{4{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}-\frac{x}{{x}^{3}})}{(\frac{3{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{24}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & =\frac{(4-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}{(3+\frac{24}{{x}^{3}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\dfrac{1}{x^2}$ and $\dfrac{24}{x^3}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to\infty,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(4-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}{(3+\frac{24}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & \to \frac{4-0}{3+0} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the horizontal asymptote is $y = \dfrac{4}{3}.$"} {:db/id 17592186048180} {:db/id 17592186049313} {:db/id 17592186088185 :question/id #uuid "a03f5577-2558-5fce-9fcf-4034bbb0803c" $$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{3{x}^{2}+2x}{6{x}^{4}-1} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3{x}^{2}}{{x}^{4}}+\frac{2x}{{x}^{4}})}{(\frac{6{x}^{4}}{{x}^{4}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{4}})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{2}{{x}^{3}})}{(6-\frac{1}{{x}^{4}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms  $\dfrac{3}{x^2}, \dfrac{2}{x^3},$ and $\dfrac{1}{x^4}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to\infty,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{2}{{x}^{3}})}{(6-\frac{1}{{x}^{4}})} \\  & \to \frac{0+0}{6-0} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$
